review:
I'm sorry to say, but this game just doesn't hold up.

And it breaks my heart, because I was a huge, avid fan of DDS original. I loved everything about that game. It was a meme, it was immersive, the music was delicious, the police were terrifying and a challenge... This one? It's... It feels weird. It feels like seeing an old friend and realizing you don't recognize them.

Let's break it down, small to big:

1. The code is still probably written in a lot of the original Polish, therefore sometimes random Polish words appear when you're trying to play the game, due to gaps in the translation.

2. The interface is not very pleasant. It just feels a lot less immersive and a lot less challenging than the original. To illustrate an example of what I mean: In the original game, you had to very carefully navigate around every inch of the ghetto and remember where the police might show up from. Now granted, having a bit more freedom of movement is cooler than being boxed in all the time, but it is extremely unbalanced. It feels more like running around Minecraft, rather than a challenging crime game.

3. The grind feels too harsh and too punishing. You have a very limited number of resources and revenue for most of the game, and you have to keep running around the island like a maniac to make the orders, leaving you very little time for anything else.

4. The story progresses in a very lopsided fashion. You have to continue grinding weed and fet, but you *can* technically speedrun to the end of the map and somehow get to the end.

5. Crafting feels very unorganized. Although that might be down to the person.

6. Again, this feels more like minecraft. You won't be taken through the essentials by Eddie or Marcus, you have to figure them out on your own, particularly discovering influencers and finding the recipe for new drugs and it left me running around like a maniac to deal fet and weed for 100 hours before finding Diego.

In conclusion, if you're a fan of the original installment, if you loved DDS1 and felt immersed by the equal parts memes, grind and badassness, you won't feel the same about this. It just isn't it.

I'm sorry, Byterunners. You failed.

review:
[h1] 252 Hours of Bugs and Pure Developer Failure – This Game is Used as a Torture Device in Guantanamo [/h1]

[h2] "If suffering was a game genre, this would be Game of the Year." [/h2]

I have all achievements in this game. 252 hours. I even played the demo before release and spent dozens of hours before achievements were even added. And I can say with absolute certainty:

[hr][/hr]

[h1] This game is garbage. [/h1]

The only positive thing I can say is that the soundtrack is genuinely good – but good music can’t save a broken mess like this.

I was genuinely excited for this game after the demo – the story there was actually guided, if I remember correctly. The demo also had tons of bugs, but people overlooked them – after all, it was just a demo and who knew what might be added later. I even thought that by the full release we’d see drivable vehicles, but those now seem to be "announced" instead. My thoughts on that are in the gameplay section. Then came the full release: the first ~5 hours were almost bug-free, giving me false hope. Then it all fell apart. Story-wise, I literally had a quest saying “Talk to someone”… I went there, and he wouldn’t talk to me. Save file broken. Restarting and various other attempts did nothing. Quest dead, game progress "lost"

[hr][/hr]

[h1] Bugs Everywhere: [/h1]

The biggest drug in Drug Dealer Simulator 2 isn’t cocaine or meth – it’s bugs. This game is so unfinished, even Early Access titles would be jealous.

[list]
[*]Quest scripts constantly break → Reload.
[*]NPCs act like remote-controlled idiots.
[*]Boat docks? Sure, you can dock… but half the time you can’t even get on land because the transitions are broken.
[*]The world feels like a copy-paste fever dream with zero polish or logic – I mean seriously, since when do bushes grow out of rocks?
[*]Many areas look walkable but just trap you in geometry because the map is so "edgy" and unrefined.
[*]Why is the yacht fast-travel system so broken that I dock in Dueno del Mar but end up in Paraiso Peninsular?
[*]Why are the same bugs from the open beta still in the game? It’s been out long enough. Are you too incompetent to fix them, or do you just not care? By the time anyone realizes how bad it really is, they’ve already spent too much time in it to get a refund.
[*]Why are some shopkeepers sometimes invisible, forcing me to memorize their locations just to buy something?
[*]Why does the interaction menu (hold R) sometimes completely fail to work for opening backpacks, maps, or anything else?
[*]At night, there’s a severe white flickering bug that’s been around since the open beta. It doesn’t happen every night, but when it does, it’s intense enough that even I felt sick – and I don’t have epilepsy. For something this visually aggressive, there is zero epilepsy warning – which is reckless and outright dangerous for anyone prone to seizures. How is this not addressed?
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h1] Gameplay: [/h1]

At the start, the game is about cooking or growing some drugs, selling them yourself, and using the profits to expand production and upgrade your base. Once you unlock your first distributor dealers, the stress ramps up. Suddenly, you’re less of a "cartel boss" and more of a delivery boy – risking your cash with thugs and your drugs with cops.

If you play solo, you’ll barely have time for special clients anymore. Instead, you’re stuck in a loop of buying supplies to make drugs just to keep your distributors stocked. If you play co-op, splitting the workload with a friend makes it slightly better, but solo? Forget it.

Shops only restock once per day around 6 AM, which means after buying supplies you’re forced to wait an entire in-game day. And since you can’t sleep during the day, you have to sit there and watch the clock crawl.

Got raided and lost everything? Too bad – now you’ll spend ages cooking just to recover. Growing weed plants takes about 35 minutes for 80g, and drying 100g in a single dryer takes ~45 minutes. All of this drags on endlessly before you can even get back on your feet. Sleeping at night doesn’t progress production – it literally pauses. Machines keep running if you’re away, but if you sleep? They tuck themselves in and stop too. Even the plants stop growing when you sleep. And as already mentioned, I don’t understand why you can’t sleep during the day to fast-forward time. Did I at least give them a bedtime story and a goodnight kiss?

The story is, as I said before, ASS. You can skip entire story elements without realizing it, only to see them later when they’re completely useless – like learning about the alternative route to the capital after unlocking fast travel there.

At one point, you’re tasked with supplying a cartel. This is where the developers’ "creativity" really shines:

You craft items and even steal some, which can take several in-game days because you have to wait for respawns.
You raid the military base for bomb parts. Sounds exciting, right? Wrong.

Sometimes there are no guards at all, and you can waltz in without resistance. Other times, if you get caught and thrown in jail, you keep the bomb parts after being released!

Instead of real gameplay, it feels like waiting simulator:

"Wait for X to contact you"
"Wait for Y to respawn"
"Wait for Z to finish"

These clowns clearly ran out of ideas and padded it with time-wasting nonsense.

As for the upcoming drivable cars: I already expect them to be terrible. You’ll probably get stuck constantly on bridges and other terrain. I’m sure FPS drops will be endless while driving. On top of that, the map is so horribly designed with all those scattered islands – which map designer was drunk enough to think this entire map was a good idea? Honestly, the fast travel points are the only saving grace in this game; they save time and spare you from seeing more of this abomination of a map.

[hr][/hr]

[h1] Multiplayer Disaster: [/h1]

[list]
[*]Why do I get FPS drops just because my friend is sitting in the casino or using fast travel?
[*]Why can I hear his snake bites across two islands?
[*]Why does the yacht teleport me to the wrong island entirely?
[*]Why can I see enemy health bars across the entire map when my friend is fighting them?
[*]Why can I see the distance between my friend and random dealers? Why on earth do I need to know how far my friend is from Dealer XY?
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h1] Developers: [/h1]

The developers are a disgrace to the gaming industry.These clowns put effort into the demo, even added a cutscene at the end – but in the main game? Not a single cutscene.

Honestly: ChatGPT could’ve coded this game better than you ever will. And the cherry on top? They seriously wanted to sue the dev of Schedule One. For what? For the fact that a single developer did a better job than your entire "studio"?

[hr][/hr]

[h1] Casino DLC: [/h1]

You buy the DLC and get access to the casino, which offers a limited selection of games:

[list]
[*]A single slot machine model, lazily copy-pasted about 250 times.
[*]Texas Hold'em, Blackjack, Roulette, All-In Poker.
[*]Low, medium, and high stakes options for all of them.
[/list]

You can buy skins for tables and slot machines, but they don’t change gameplay.

Then there are the so-called "passive casino profits", hyped up in loading screens:"Casino passive income has increased!"Sounds great, right? Spend 4,000,000 B to buy the casino and you’d expect serious money...

Nope.If you’ve unlocked Slavic stashes, the casino income is the same – about 150 B every 3-4 seconds. That means in real-world time, you wait 22 hours just to break even. Which really makes me think their combined IQ is about 22 as well.

The only extra perk? You get an extra hideout

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

If you’re going to buy this game, only do it if it’s free – because it’s worth nothing more 

And to whoever was responsible for the Steam achievements: please send me your address so I can ship you something huge to cram it where it hurts the most

review:
I tried to like this game, but ultimately couldn't. Here are a few reasons why:

1. Performance:
    The way the game runs is confusing, sometimes you get very high frames while on occasion (mostly) you are stuck stuttering between 15-30 fps. This cannot be noticed by a new player, because it doesn't affect the beginning island, however once you move on to the other side of archipelago it will be very noticeable. My system is not high end by any means, but it still crushes the required specs listed on the store page. The game does support dlss, but I don't think it should be necessary for a game that recommends you use at least a rtx 2060.

2. Mechanics:
   I can't say much on the mechanics, since there is barely any. Everything from the first game has been downgraded to timers and crafting menus. Instead of pouring soil or planting seeds, you click a few buttons on a menu and watch a timer go down. This wouldn't be very bad, if it weren't for the fact that the time it takes to do things in game takes between 20-40 minutes. Another note I have is with cars in game, yes you can buy them, but you cannot drive them, only fast travel. I do not think I need to say why this is disappointing.

3. The content (lack of updates):
    This game is lacking in many aspects, that being what there is to do in the game, except look at timers. The game does get updates, on rare occasion. Recently the casino dlc released, which A: should've been in the base game and B: Does not need to cost almost 7€. The dlc for this game should be free, like in the first game and there is no need to put new content behind a paywall. 

FInal verdict:
The game is not all bad, I have to give credit for the co-op mode, a lot of this game's many problems can be ignored while playing with friends. Still boredom will kick in within a couple of hours. I would hope that the devs won't abandon the game, but keep fixing and improving it, because it could use some Cyberpunk treatment. I do however, choose not to recommend it at it's current state, because most people will only be able to push out around 10-15hrs before ultimately getting bored and uninstalling. Give it a year or two, maybe eventually it'll live up to it's predecessor.

review:
Drug Dealer Simulator 2 has a lot of potential. Despite its bugs and missing features, it’s genuinely fun and has the makings of something great. That said, some systems could really use an overhaul—but that’s just my opinion.

The reason for the negative review isn't the gameplay itself, but the disappointing direction the developers have taken. Development on the main game appears to have stalled entirely in favor of working on a gambling-themed DLC. And honestly… who asked for that in a drug dealing simulator? A small in-game casino feature would’ve made sense, sure—but dedicating an entire DLC to it feels completely out of touch with what fans actually want.

What makes this worse is the feeling that the base game is being neglected. It seems like the devs are now just trying to salvage the DLC instead of fixing or improving the core experience. It’s frustrating to see a solid foundation get pushed aside for content that doesn’t align with what made the game fun in the first place.

review:
I played for about 3.5 hours, and honestly, it was a frustrating experience. I wanted to like this game, especially after enjoying the first one, but this sequel misses the mark on almost every level.

The gameplay feels clunky and unintuitive. The combat system is awkward and uninteresting — and the lack of firearms makes encounters feel meaningless. Progression is slow and unrewarding. Instead of immersing me in a tense, criminal underworld, I found myself delivering food packages to a cartel… which feels completely out of place.

Several other issues stood out:

Multiple bus routes that add little to nothing to the experience.

Frequent and lengthy loading screens between areas.

Boats that move painfully slow, killing any sense of momentum.

A broken POI/suspect system where getting into minor conflicts locks me out of my own house for 15 minutes under threat of a raid — it’s more frustrating than immersive.

Overall, the game feels poorly designed, lacks tension, and, most importantly, isn’t fun. There’s no sense of danger or reward. It’s a huge step down from the original, which at least had a sense of purpose and identity.

Unfortunately, I can’t recommend this title. And after this experience, I don’t see myself purchasing anything from this developer again any time soon.

review:
Contains a lot of stupid decisions.

"Special" customers provide a tiny income but require you to drop what you're doing and travel all over the map to roll them some blunts or bake them cookies.

You'll randomly lose rep/demand because apparently someone OD'd. Ok, well I'm selling the base product without any mix or cut so wtf. How do I mitigate that or stop it from happening again, the game certainly isn't going to tell me.

Distributors aren't worth it as they take 20% off the top, on top of the 15% the dealers take.

Chemists aren't worth it as they only know how to make make basic weed. Unless you spend half a million to train them! Wtf are they being trained by a celebrity?

Map is way too big, which wouldn't be an issue if you could get around in a convenient fashion, but the fast travel system sucks.

Clothes have durability, why? It's unnecessary tedium to have to visit a clothes shop periodically to buy new clothes. This isn't a clothes shopping trip game. Why does the stamina system exist? It's unnecessary tedium to have to stop every 100 yards to get your breath back. 

Game has half implemented features like hideout coziness, cartel level and street cred that do nothing. Devs have actually posted on the forums saying it does nothing, but it might in future. That was fine while game was in early access, but it's not now.They still haven't implemented a skill tree, so level means nothing.

Cops will walk past balaclava clad thugs wielding spiked baseball bats and dead bodies, but apparently I look suspicious.....I hope all the above gets fixed, because this could be a great game. However I doubt it as these developers abandoned DDS in order to work on DDS2, and they're already trowelling out DLCs rather than finishing the base game.

review:
After playing "a certain other" game of this genre, I had an itch that I wanted to scratch again. This time with DDS2 as the next best alternative according to Steam.
So in order for this review to be helpful for both the potential buyers as well as the developer, I will try and avoid simple "play this other game instead" comparisons and ignore any conflicts between the developers. I honestly believe that Byterunners can most definitely be a great competitor in this genre.

[h3]My experience after 2 hours[/h3]

I would describe it as follow: Imagine the map of Far Cry 3, but with less vegetation and the pirates want to buy substances off of you.
[list]
   [*]Different game "difficulties" that let you focus more on the violent or the economic part of the game if you prefer.
   [*]The map is barren and you just run from A to B for no reason. What was wrong with the dense DDS1 layout?
   [*]Houses are in random locations (why would anyone build a small wooden shelter on the backside of an island, with nothing nearby, nor any real pathway or road to it?). 
   [*]Infrastructure makes little sense (there are fences EVERYWHERE but nothing is walled off with gates. You just have to run around and you will reach your destination eventually. Like a rat in a maze.)
   [*]Random objects lying around just so it looks less barren. Why is there a stack of barrels on the beach? Why are there fences everywher
   [*]Currency could be standard dollars but instead you have 6-digit amounts of a foreign currency in the first hour
   [*]Contacts do not tell you where they will be before a deal
   [*]Contacts just appear and disappear from and into thin air before and after a deal (they teleport)
   [*]Contacts ask you to hook them up roughly at the same time (I guess all of their cooldowns are the same?). So if you accept 5 deals one after another, the next day you will get requests of roughly 5 people at the same time again. 
   [*]NPC behavior in general is that of a tree moving in the wind. They do not react to you bumping into them, you cannot talk to them, they do not walk around. The word "NPC" is not harsh enough for these bots.
   [*]There are a lot of shacks or buildings, but you cannot interact with them.
   [*]One way you get new customers is they just stand still in a random location and wave to all day. Until you come buy, to which they ask whether you have this certain substance. I guess the idea comes from waving a taxi out of traffic but it is very questionable in this context.
   [*]Clothing has objectively helpful bonusses (more bag slots, some are concealed so not found during searches), and rather vague ones (Swag?, Sussy?)
    [*]A lot of different items that can be bought in stores and don't spoil too much in their tooltips what they're used for.
   [*]The items seem realistic and kind of remind me of Escape from Tarkov, so it feels authentic to hold a bottle of 200 ml phenylethylamine for example, and not just a wacky "bottle of acid" with a flame on it. And you keep the bottle once you empty it. You can even use it as a storage container, or sell it, up to you.
   [*]Items are only "seen" in menu context. So you cannot pick up or throw items and see them in the 3D world. They just hop inventories: From the shop, to yours, to your grow box menu, to your drying rack menu, to your manufacture table menu, to your inventory, to your customers. Kind of like digital money that you never hold in your hands.
   [*]Tons of different recipes. Substances have different recipes. There are obviously different substances but you can also hollow out cigarettes, pulverize your fertilizer and other things that seem to have a more realistic way of mixing things than throwing a donut into your meth and call it calorie-dense.
[/list]

[h3]Aspects that would drastically improve the game experience in my view[/h3]

[list]
   [*]Map should be way smaller and dense instead. Various maps from Hitman WoA feel vast just because how they have layers upon layers in a small location. It's just the most bland experience having to take a bus from a dead island 1 to dead island 3 to meet a buyer that is standing alone in the middle of 3 wooden shacks. It cannot take me further away from immersion.
   [*](Option to) disable permanent UI elements. Keeping it clean is more authentic than this "we need a health bar, a stamina bar, a minimap with 20 icons, a 3D yellow blip with meters to my destination, hold tab to open phone, hold B to toss backpack, game autosaved" and whatnot. 
   [*]Disable UI popups like level-ups, reputation, quest completion. Show that at the end of the game. I don't need the game telling me what a badass cool awesome asskicker I am because I sold 2 grams of weed to John Pork over here and increased my lowlife reputation by +8. No one cares. This is not the source of dopamine hits the players play your game for.
   [*]Split stacks at customers with LMB or RMB, not this "drag here and use slider". It's just a cleaner feeling to throw this guy two RMB clicks of weed in his face. Sliders feel "more precise". 
   [*]The world looks and feels dead. Even your buddy is just standing in this one spot, doing nothing, 24/7, while things around him are growing or drying. 
   [*]Why am I not required to sleep? I just did all-nighters and nothing happened. If in your game time equals money, then there is no incentive to sleep. Either make it mandatory, highly incentive (through a malus on stamina and/or health or something) or remove it.  
   [*]Change the currency to standard dollars. It is much more intuitive to calculate what a reasonable price is if you start with 10 dollars a gram at the game and go from there. And no, bigger numbers don't make me feel more rich. I feel 2.000 dollars in my pockets more than 170.000 pesos or whatever that is.
   [*]Voice lines are perfectly fine but I feel that they do not add much and just cost you more in production value. Just lines of text are enough if it means your development resources are spent elsewhere.
[/list]

review:
First, let's talk about its advantages. The modeling is quite high-quality, and the overall graphics quality can be said to be at the top level among indie games. The gameplay is quite good. From production to sales and operation management, the Settings are quite good and deserve recognition. It is obvious to see the progress compared with DDS1.

But I really feel very sorry. After all, this studio is a small one. I can understand that it updates slowly and has relatively low technology. But I really can't understand your studio's half-hearted behavior. Not long after the release of DDS2, when bugs, game optimizations and player feedback were not well resolved, your studio began to announce that it would produce the next work. If the game optimization of your DDS2 is like this, even if your next work is done very well, do you think players will take the risk to buy it?
    
Let's not talk about anything else. Just take game optimization as an example. My laptop has an RTX4060, but the frame rate of games is always less than 30FPS(like in a villa or on a private island), and this is even when I have lowered the graphics quality. My Red Dead Redemption 2 can maintain a stable 60FPS at frames per second, so it's impossible that the equipment doesn't meet the standards.
   
 So, could your studio please do a good job with DDS2 first, optimize it well, and read more player feedback? Let's put the next work on hold for a while. As a die-hard fan of the DDS series, I'm really not afraid that your next work will be delayed for a long time. I'm only afraid that it will be as poorly optimized as this one.

There are some good perks: Like the idea that you can get mugged and lose your drugs and money to police and enemies. I love the way different clothes deteriorate making clothes more of a consumable needed to buy again to up keep the perks. Trying to accuse other games of copies as a publisher (In this case: Movie Games) just because there MIGHT be small similarities is no sportsmanship in this business. If every company goes like this, there wouldn't be as many games on the market nowadays and new publishers/devs would have to pay more attention on all legal rights than on actually working on developing games. See it as a competition and just give players reasons to join in on your game again. With these circumstances, I'll refrain from buying more games of this publisher for now.

Summing up: There are better and cheaper alternatives for a drug dealing game about building up a business. One definitely being Schedule I. Lmao investigating a lone indie dev for making a superior game is laughable.

Like, instead of trying to actually improve your game, your first reaction was to bust out the lawyers.

Pathetic. Absolutely embarrassing. You saw someone doing your job better than you ever could SOLO, with NO BUDGET, NO MARKETING TEAM, NO SAFETY NET and your fragile little ego just couldn’t take it.

So you whipped out the lawyers like they're a damn trap card, thinking you could activate them in response to getting absolutely obliterated by someone who actually gives a ♥♥♥♥ about making good games. Thinking that’ll erase the fact that ONE PERSON cooked your whole million-dollar studio with a passion project

You’re not defending your IP, you're defending your insecurity. You’re not protecting your brand, you're shielding your mediocrity from public exposure, and you're failing at even that.

Imagine getting your ass handed to you by one person with passion and vision, and thinking the right move is to cry to your legal team instead.

That’s not business. That’s cowardice in a suit.

EDIT (4/7/25) in response to the publishers forum post:

Due to repeated opinions that Schedule I is very similar to DDS, we were obliged to request a legal analysis from an intellectual property specialist. It has indicated that there might have been an infringement by the Schedule I developers in relation to Drug Dealer Simulator.

S1's "similarities" start and end at being in the same genre. You weren’t “obliged” to jump straight into legal saber-rattling. You chose to. Let’s not pretend this was some reluctant move. This whole “investigation” is a textbook case of bad faith. You know it. We know it.

Now we are obliged to follow up further, but we are yet to contact the Schedule I developers. Our goal at this point is discussing the situation with them and we have an open approach.

Still an absolute PR disaster. Instead of actually reaching out to the singular dev like normal people, you chose the route that conveniently frames you as the “concerned party” while setting the stage for legal intimidation.

Like we said, we need to start a conversation. It is not our intention to prevent TVGS from selling or developing their game.

Right, because nothing says “open dialogue” like legal threats dressed up as concern. Don’t insult anyone’s intelligence with your “we just want to check” excuse. It's about as convincing as those fake UPS texts I get constantly.

Overall, our goal is to support all devs, but we need to consider our legal obligations if law specialists determine that there are grounds to claim infringement. We even contacted TVGS via email just before the release, when the game was already huge, and wished them all the best - but that was before that legal analysis. Back then no one expected it to be needed, not to mention that it would bring these results.

Translation: “We misjudged S1’s success, and now that it’s in our way, we’re hoping a flimsy infringement claim will sweep it under the rug and out of the way.”

This is a very serious situation for us. We’re not a big corporation, but a relatively small indie publisher. There are other drug simulators out there with very positive scores and good sales. These are A-OK in regards to DDS according to lawyers.

Oh please, don’t use the “We’re indie too!” sympathy play. You’ve made a whole business out of churning out low effort simulator clones like it's a factory. Funny how you’re not going after other similar games. Could it be because they’re not threatening your wallet?

This entire situation reeks of desperation, greed, and weak legal posturing. If you were trying to make yourselves look like the villains of the month, congrats you nailed it perfectly.



EDIT (4/10/25)

Yes, I’m aware it’s the publisher and not the devs initiating the investigation. And yes, I know they’re claiming it’s a ‘legal obligation.’

Counterpoint: if this is just standard legal protocol, then where the hell are the public announcements for the other drug sims that share mechanics and themes? Where are those statements? Those investigations? Those legal letters? Funny how they don’t exist. Or if they do, they’re not announcing them.

So let’s stop licking boots and pretending this is routine procedure. Because if it was, we’d be up to our eyeballs in posts naming half the Steam storefront. Instead, They went straight for Schedule 1. Why? Because it’s gaining traction. Because it’s better. Because it’s competition.

If vague opinions are enough to trigger legal action, then Movie Games S.A. should be launching full-blown investigations into every drug simulator out there, not just the one that made their own game look like a relic from 2017.

This is a petty power play dressed in legal/lawyer speak.

And, this last bit, this is for you directly, "Movie Games"

You don’t get to parade around with your legal and then cherry pick what you "investigate" based on what bruises your ego the hardest. If you're gonna weaponize the law, at least be consistent. Better yet, if this is your poor attempt at transparency, be better and show us the list of games you've obviously had to reviewed under the same scrutiny since your "obligated" and "legally required". Publish the timelines. Publish the statements. Prove this isn't targeted.

But of course, you won’t. Because this was never about a lawful obligation it’s a thinly veiled corporate maneuver cloaked in the ceremonial robes of “due diligence.” What we’re really seeing is a early stage deployment of the "We Feel Threatened and Needed a Pretext Act." You call it an investigation. I call it laying the groundwork for a weak-ass legal ambush.

No lawsuits yet, sure, but just enough noise to rattle cages, stir doubt, and flex a little muscle. This isn't enforcement, it’s intimidation wrapped in a press release. It’s the legal version of shaking the vending machine because someone else got a better snack.

You didn’t rise to challenge Schedule 1, instead you looked at your “legal options” folder and hoped the threat alone would do the work. And rather than engage in Good Faith Development™ or Competitive Market Behavior Act compliance, you opted for Clause 5(a): "Oh ♥♥♥♥, They Made a Better Game Than Us."

review:
I tried to play this game, I really did. I wasn't gonna even write a negative review despite how bad and boring this game is. I even refunded it shortly after buying it because I just couldn't see myself playing it again and I still didn't plan on it. Then you went after Schedule 1. An Indie Game that is doing so much better than both your terrible games did that it damaged your ego thus causing you to try and dismantle it.

It wasn't even satisfying doing any of the bagging, cutting or planting in this game. It just sucks. There's really not much to it. For the remainder of this review I will be talking about Schedule 1. (Suck a fat one DDS).

Schedule 1 is an Indie Game kind of like DDS but way better. Developed by one person, this game is the pinnacle of simulation games blending kooky goofy fun and cartoonish graphics with solid realism. You start as a low level drug dealer, making small deals, growing pot, cutting it, bagging it and delivering it, but as time goes on, as you make more money and you grow your drug tycoon, it develops into a fully functioning drug dealing organization with dealers, growers, packagers, meth cooks, and so on. Its highly fun and addictive and 100 times better than DDS. I'd never recommend this trash ass game but I can assure you that Schedule 1 is what you're looking for.

review:
So, I have like 169 hours on this game so far, and just over 177 on DDS1 by the time this one came out. Meanwhile, I've already hit about 32 hours on Schedule 1 in less than a week. Why? Because it's way more fun than this is. And it actually runs without the frame rate randomly deciding to nose dive harder than this dev has since it came out.

Hearing the response to Schedule 1 has seriously affected my opinion of this game's dev. I believe the comment about it only being their publisher who is taking issue with it is an outright lie. Not to mention some claims of a potential infringement. Literally the only similarity is that its a game where you make drugs. Oh, and the fact you have to order a dead drop to get materials, like you do in your first game.

It would be like saying Nintendo owns platforming games because of Mario. or that Fromsoft owns soulslike games. And they even had the genre NAMED AFTER THEIR GAME, yet they STILL don't own it! Neither does Rockstar have any claim that something like Saints Row infringed on them.

None of this is infringement. Yall are made that a solo dev had an idea to make a different drug game, and it turned out better than yours did. Honestly, how has the frame drops not been fixed yet? I can run this damn game at lowest settings, and it'll still drop to under 20 FPS, sometime even single digits, at seemingly random times. And that's running with a 3080, an i7-9700K, and 32gb ram, well beyond what your min specs call for.

I loved this, and the first game, so, SO much. I loved seeing someone else come out with a different take on a drug making/selling game, and I would have gladly played both this, and Schedule 1. After this though, I cant say I rightly feel like supporting Byterunners, or the publisher, Movie Games, any longer.

Quit being whiny and salty about 1 guy making a better game than your whole-ass team did, and try, idk, FIXING YOUR FREAKING GAME!

To quote another player.

Pathetic. Absolutely embarrassing. You saw someone doing your job better than you ever could SOLO, with NO BUDGET, NO MARKETING TEAM, NO SAFETY NET and your fragile little ego just couldn’t take it.

So you whipped out the lawyers like they're a damn trap card, thinking you could activate them in response to getting absolutely obliterated by someone who actually gives a ♥♥♥♥ about making good games. Thinking that’ll erase the fact that ONE PERSON cooked your whole million-dollar studio with a passion project

You’re not defending your IP, you're defending your insecurity. You’re not protecting your brand, you're shielding your mediocrity from public exposure, and you're failing at even that.

Imagine getting your ass handed to you by one person with passion and vision, and thinking the right move is to cry to your legal team instead.

That’s not business. That’s cowardice in a suit.

EDIT (4/7/25) in response to the publishers forum post:

Due to repeated opinions that Schedule I is very similar to DDS, we were obliged to request a legal analysis from an intellectual property specialist. It has indicated that there might have been an infringement by the Schedule I developers in relation to Drug Dealer Simulator.

S1's "similarities" start and end at being in the same genre. You weren’t “obliged” to jump straight into legal saber-rattling. You chose to. Let’s not pretend this was some reluctant move. This whole “investigation” is a textbook case of bad faith. You know it. We know it.

Now we are obliged to follow up further, but we are yet to contact the Schedule I developers. Our goal at this point is discussing the situation with them and we have an open approach.

Still an absolute PR disaster. Instead of actually reaching out to the singular dev like normal people, you chose the route that conveniently frames you as the “concerned party” while setting the stage for legal intimidation.

Like we said, we need to start a conversation. It is not our intention to prevent TVGS from selling or developing their game.

Right, because nothing says “open dialogue” like legal threats dressed up as concern. Don’t insult anyone’s intelligence with your “we just want to check” excuse. It's about as convincing as those fake UPS texts I get constantly.

Overall, our goal is to support all devs, but we need to consider our legal obligations if law specialists determine that there are grounds to claim infringement. We even contacted TVGS via email just before the release, when the game was already huge, and wished them all the best - but that was before that legal analysis. Back then no one expected it to be needed, not to mention that it would bring these results.

Translation: “We misjudged S1’s success, and now that it’s in our way, we’re hoping a flimsy infringement claim will sweep it under the rug and out of the way.”

This is a very serious situation for us. We’re not a big corporation, but a relatively small indie publisher. There are other drug simulators out there with very positive scores and good sales. These are A-OK in regards to DDS according to lawyers.

Oh please, don’t insult everyone’s intelligence with the “We’re indie too!” sympathy play. You’ve made a whole business model out of churning out low effort simulator clones like it's a factory. Funny how you’re not going after other similar games. Could it be because they’re not threatening your wallet?

This entire situation reeks of desperation, greed, and weak legal posturing. If you were trying to make yourselves look like the villains of the month, congrats you nailed it perfectly.

review:
[h1]Unfinished, dishonest, live-service trash[/h1]

The previous game in the series was a bloated, lootbox-infested mess that took forever to load (longer than this one in fact) and took up too much space on disc (more than this one in fact) because it was built to push a CSGO style skin economy... and then they started putting gameplay-affecting items like GUNS in "DLC".

This product doesn't contain lootboxes but it is still ruined by microtransactions including literally the most dishonest and exploitative implementation of a Battle Pass that I have ever seen. 

[h1]Obfuscates unlockables to trick you into unlocking things you can't use without paying extra.[/h1]

Unlike other games with Battle Passes, like the Free-to-Play [i]World of Warships,[/i] this FULL-PRICED game obfuscates which items are exclusive to the paid Battle Pass and which ones you can unlock in-game until AFTER you have used your points to unlock them.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3633379236

This means that you use the points from the tedious and often buggy missions to unlock items only to find afterwards that you still don't have them because SURPRISE! Those are exclusive to the Battle Pass. 

They actually put the text saying that Battle Pass is required on the OTHER SIDE OF THE SCREEN and only distinguish the paid items with a different color AFTER you unlock them.

They don't want you to realize that you are wasting your points until after you have done so which they hope will make you more willing to buy the battle pass so that you at least get what you already spent your points to unlock. The pyschological manipulation here is similar to a trick used in [i]Killing Floor 2[/i] where you earn lootboxes by playing the game that require "keys" (purchased with real money) to unlock.

I sincerely hope that whoever made that decision ^ never makes another game again because that is so sleazy and deceptive that it should be illegal.

[h1]"Campaign" is just scavenger-hunt added to regular survival mode.[/h1]

Rather than actually having a true campaign or a series of individual coop missions like in [i]Vermintide, World War Z, Space Marine, Aliens Fireteam Elite,[/i] etc., the "campaign" of this game is just that it adds some scavenger-hunt type objectives and radio chatter to the game's regular wave-survival mode. 

Not only is this unsatisfying as a "campaign", it also make the regular wave-survival worse since it means whichever player currently has campaign objectives in the map which you are playing will be scurrying around trying to find those rather than being a team player... all while a wave-survival mission is going on.

This actually turns out even worse than it sounds because...

[h1]Campaign-Objective markers don't work[/h1]

The campaign-objective markers in this game disappear when you get close to your objective... Which means that you will find yourself running away from your search objective (while being chased by fast-moving zombies) in an attempt to figure out where you are supposed to go by looking from far enough away that you will get your objective marker back. 

It gets worse though because the objective markers are OFTEN in the wrong places. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3633364545

Less than 3% of players finished that ^ particular mission, probably because the objective marker actually points to the wrong body... which is worse than having no objective marker at all. 

This happens a lot so I don't know if this was simply incompetence or if it was designed that way on purpose as some weird way of stretching the underwhelming, threadbare content. If the latter, I hope that whoever thought that a scavenger hunt in the dark with a GPS that tells you to go the wrong way was a good idea for a campaign takes a few seminars on game design. 

[h1]Games with microtransactions should be free.[/h1]

As if it isn't bad enough that these incompetent devs made an underwhelming, unfinished game and decided to charge $80 for it, they ALSO had to fill it with microtransactions AND the most dishonest implementation of a Battle Pass that I have seen so far. So much so in fact that this game actually feels more exploitative and incomplete than a lot of free games that I have played.

[h1]Can't see the character you customized in the base.[/h1]

I actually liked being able to walk around my home base (though it would have been a LOT better to make that part third-person so you could SEE the character you customized.) 

[h1]Upgrade system punishes you for upgrading weapons.[/h1]

I wanted to like the weapon customization system in this game... 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3628176337

However, it is inherently broken because customizing weapons makes them more expensive which means the more work you put into improving a particular weapon, the less often you will be able to use it. That's because In this game, you have to buy your weapons during each match with the money earned in the same match.

If they had NOT raised the price on the weapons to punish you for grinding to improve them, the weapons customization could have been a decent, if grindy mechanic. However, like so many other aspects of this game, they simply threw some ideas together without apparently realizing how they would get in each other's way.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Even if you liked [i]Killing Floor 2[/i] (which I kind of did despite the bloated installation, bugs, long load times, and scummy business practices) I can't recommend this sleazy, shallow cash-in.

review:
[h1] When a Dev does too much: Has Killing Floor lost its soul? [/h1]

I have over 600 hours in KF2 and probably more than a thousand in KF1. I would consider myself a big fan of the previous two entries but the third one hasn't really captured me so far. It's not a bad game on a technical level and a lot of the changes made don't seem objectively bad - they just aren't Killing Floor.

Whenever I see some of the newly implemented features I think "Killing Floor but Apex Legends" or "Killing Floor but Doom" and not "Killing Floor 2 but better".

[h2] The Weapons [/h2]

The premise is very simple: Kill things before they kill you. Weapons ensured your survival and they just felt great to use. The experience of scoring a headshot was always thrilling in a way that other zombie shooters I played never matched up to. And just firing your weapon had this sense of realism.

But KF3 somehow fails to capture this. The weapons I tried are all somehow like they are made of plastic. The Commando's pistol really seems like none of the shots have any impact. And where's the M14EBR's laser? I don't know if I just missed it but it's not on by default and neither does it activate with "alternate fire mode". 

[h2] The Zombies ("Zeds") [/h2]

I immediately noticed, just like when first playing KF2 that suddenly everything felt more alive. More movement patterns, more abilities, and especially with the jump to KF3, what seems like more intelligence (Husks in particular). Many Zeds now come with some kind of ranged ability and some Clots now crouch while Husks use a jetpack to fly/hover in the air. Stalkers are more acrobatic than ever and Sirens can now extend their necks plus their scream actually pushes the player away only to be then hit by the Scrake's new grappling hook ability. 

This all seems very cool but it all makes combat more difficult and thus comes with some player-side buffs that were previously just not necessary. Also it feels like everything has become more bullet spongy. I don't know why I need so many headshots to take out a single Siren. Stalkers can be killed by a single headshot most of the time but they move in such erratic patterns that it becomes really tricky to do so. Plus they are less visible than in KF2, meaning you won't as easily pick them out from a distance where they still walk predictably.

[h2] SHINY NEW THINGS (but why?) [/h2]

[list]
    [*]Players now have some kind of ability whose cooldown refreshes about once per wave. In the case of the Sharpshooter it's a drone that automatically attacks Zeds in melee, killing most weaker ones in one hit and exploding in the end.
    [*]You can now upgrade your armour so it can take more of a beating.
    [*]There is now a hub from which you select missions rather than just going from the main menu.
    [*]Players are now required to complete a rather patronising tutorial.
    [*]There are story missions now.
    [*]The Berserker perk has been replaced by the Ninja.
    [*]Players can now use ziplines.
    [*]Players can now slide on the ground.
    [*]Players can now pull themselves up onto a ledge.
    [*]Players can now perform glory kills like in Doom.
    [*]A dozen or so different crafting materials for weapon upgrades can now be collected.
[/list]

I don't think that any of these changes make the game better than its predecessor. They make it feel more gimmicky. The previous entries in the series were distilled down to a very satisfying gun experience with a lot of "make one mistake and you're done" urgency. It didn't need a tutorial because things were self explanatory. It didn't need a hub that just feels like a barrier to actually getting a game started. Why do you have to walk to the other end of the building just to change your perk? You can just do it by pressing ESC and clicking a thing in KF2. Why, after selecting a mission and confirming your selection, do you have to walk up onto the helicopter platform and get in the vehicle and then wait 8 seconds and watch the same takeoff clip every time? What's the point of glory kills? And while many might disagree, what's the point of story missions?

My best guess is that the devs wanted more immersion and also to capitalise on what other successful games had already done. You can slide around in every shooter since Apex and also people seem to love the new Doom games. So they put in a bunch of these popular features seemingly without wanting to preserve the soul of Killing Floor. You may get this higher sense of immersion but to me you lose the fun and relative simplicity of Killing Floor 1 and 2.

[h2] The Actual Gameplay [/h2]

Killing Floor 1 and 2 had this "get gud" feeling about it where everything felt really threatening and once things get too close to you it might be over. But KF3 just expects you to get hit which is why you can upgrade armour. It expects you to get overwhelmed which is why it gives you these extra abilities that kill Zeds for you when you're swarmed. Since almost everything can shoot you from a distance now, just outrunning them isn't enough. It feels like you always need to be around the corner or behind a wall so that they can't get you. But that also means you're shortening the window in which you can get them. 

The boss enemies so far don't do it for me either. Just like in the previous games, they obviously can't be taken out so easily and they are likely to get close to the players here or there and get in a few hits. But so far I haven't experienced those fights as tactical as much as a more graphically intense version of Clicker Hero. The Patriarch in Killing Floor 2 was a good example. He doesn't have that much HP. But once he's hurt, he will retreat, heal, and come back with more aggressive abilities. This gave the players the choice between trying to hunt him down before he heals or waiting it out, setting up a new ambush, and tending to their own wounds. KF3 boss enemies so far appear to all just relentlessly chase you until the HP bar hits 50% and they relent even less than before.

Also, is welding doors shut still a thing? It was somewhat of a core mechanic previously and I haven't even been able to confirm whether or not it's possible anymore.

KF1 and 2 were beautifully simple by comparison. By no means easy, but streamlined. After launching the game it takes a few clicks and you're already loading in the map. You don't need to use a mission terminal or a levelling up terminal or a perk selection terminal, it's all just quickly accessible in the game's menu. Weapon upgrades were also a thing in KF2 and they were handled at the trader pod. You didn't have several options for several different weapon part upgrades either. You just clicked "upgrade" and that's it. But I don't think you need more than this either. 

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]

In my view, Killing Floor 3 desperately tries to put a new spin KF2 that it just perceived any change as an improvement whether or not it would be. In the process of this evolution it lost its biggest asset which was its satisfying simplicity. They felt raw, to the point, and satisfying. KF1 and 2 were one-trick-ponies but they performed their trick elegantly. If the first two games in the series were a scalpel, #3 tries to be a Swiss Army Knife with a Casio wrist watch strapped onto it. But that's not what people that enjoyed the other games associate with the series. There is just an overwhelming amount of not actually playing the game in the third release.

If you never liked Killing Floor because it felt static, KF3 might actually be for you. If you look for a more polished version of KF1 or KF2, you're about to be disappointed.

I'll keep it installed and I'll probably play for a bit here or there. But without relatively major changes, I don't see myself enjoying it anywhere near as much as its predecessors.

review:
As a veteran of the first game, I have mixed feelings about this title.

Visually, it’s not bad. The ZEDs are modeled in an interesting and detailed way. Unfortunately, the maps themselves feel weak and uninspired. Everything takes place at night, which gives the impression that the developers are trying to hide graphical shortcomings rather than create atmosphere.

Performance is average at best. I clearly remember earlier versions running better and being more optimized. I’m also not a fan of the new limited medpack system — it feels restrictive and unnecessary.

Another major issue is matchmaking. There should be an option to manually choose servers, because the current system simply doesn’t work. I either end up alone on a map or connected to a server with terrible ping.

Gunplay is where the game falls short the most. It feels extremely underwhelming — even when using a powerful shotgun, it feels like you’re shooting a slingshot rather than a heavy weapon.

At its current state, I’d give the game a 6/10.

review:
The Good:

- Weapon modding is a feature that wasn't possible to add to KF2 for dev time/remodeling reasons, and is a pretty nice addition to this game. It adds some variability to your loadout, especially with the G33 grenade launcher, even though most are just strictly a bonus over the base gun. Like the iron sights? Too bad, get a red-dot for that extra accuracy!

- Crawlers crawl on walls, like was promised in KF2, but was a technical impossibility at the time. Neat!

- The Ninja class, which was rumored to be the final class in KF2 (which, instead, turned out to be the Survivalist), is in KF3. This is another neat thing, despite replacing the Berserker (if only for now, we'll see what the future holds and if we get the zerker back or not.) Which is also neat.

- The new mobility options are nice I suppose: ziplines giving you a get out of jail free card if cornered near them, dodges and slides letting you avoid attacks, even if I'm still getting the hang of them.

The various tools are interesting, from adding turrets or environmental traps to the battlefield to kill the zeds and opening new routes with the multitool, to adding an ammo refill or syringe refill to the team, deployable shock traps to stun big zeds, or various other effects. You start with a class-standard tool, and can swap them out at a trader for a small fee. Adds more customization to your build, and useful utility. Btw, yes, REFILL your syringes. They're limited. That'll be discussed in The Bad.

You can very your build more than in KF2. You have new perks every 2 levels instead of 5, and gain "proficiency points' to let you upgrade your favorite perks to a much better version of themselves. Sadly, there are no class-unique 'zed-time' perks (ultimates, essentially) at level 25, as it's basically just a slow-mo and damage boost for all classes now, even if some class perks do alter zed time.

The game looks pretty nice in general after they revamped it before release, except for some of the zeds' aesthetics, and that every map is set at night in a dilapidated military setting, and that most guns look like f'in Amazon boxes with LEDs on them (Discussed in The Bad section.)


The game is GENERALLY pretty shallow levels of fun, WHEN you can play it. (Discussed in The Bad.)


The Bad:

It loaded shaders for about 20 min at first launch, but is done in seconds every time after. Very bad first impression.

First game after tutorial was a server disconnect. So it started, so it has been. In my ~9 hours of playing at first time of writing this (~8 hours in), I've had about 8 or 9 server disconnections, and one full crash to desktop. Instead of retrying the connection, you're instead having to waste 2-3 min setting up another connection attempt, cuz it, for some reason, the game QUITS YOU TO THE START SCREEN instead of to the HUB when you disconnect. Then you have to go through all the startup bullsh**, choose a map, run to the VTOL...wastes my time, and I hate that. JUST START ME NEAR THE VTOL WHEN I DISCONNECT DAMMIT! Meanwhile, KF2, you DC, go to server browser, choose a new one. 20 seconds max. Compared to 2 min. Tripwire please. What the fu** even are these servers? What the fu** happened from KF1/KF2? Also, it will occasionally just hang even when connected, forcing me to hard-stop the game via Steam.

From a technical aspect, this really should be an early access game, and we're all beta testers. This is basically a (partially) working proof-of-concept that needs at least another year-plus in the oven to iron out all the bugs and kinks, and release all of the roadmap content to make it a full release. The cake's not just half-baked, it's not just the raw ingredients, this sh**'s still growing in the fields or forming in the animals.

Animations are lazy trash compared to even KF1's, let alone the beautiful mocapped ones of KF2.

It's laggy, unoptimized sh** even on the lowest graphical settings.

As for the gameplay, it's extremely chaotic (in a bad way.) Unlike in KF2, KF1, or even the KF mod from UT, some of the enemies are extremely samey in design (especially the SC, FP, and husk, all looking like tall, bulky, metal-armored profiles) and are literally all over the place, especially in the husk's case. Contrast this with the other KF games, where you could identify the zeds easily from just their outline and outfit: the SC wore a WHITE butcher's/medical smock and a CHAINSAW, the FP was the big BROWN nude/metal man with a BIG, YELLOW OR RED CHEST PUMP and MEATGRINDER HANDS, and the husk was smoldering and VERY ORANGE. These new designs are just muddled and confusing, just like the whole gameplay loop. Husks fly with jetpacks and shoot from the air or rooftops. Every enemy has a ranged attack now, even the cysts.

Every map's SO DARK! Why EVERY map? Some is fine, BUT EVERY?

Syringes/healing are now limited, including to the medic, and you can't heal others with your syringe(s). This changes the gameplay dynamics and makes the game a lot harder to clutch. Yes, you can use the trader mid-wave to refill your gear, and yes, you can get syringe bags to gain one additional syringe per bag, but you're still limited to dosh or syringe bags to heal, unless the medic is healing you, instead of it being free but timed per use like the previous games. Oh, and you get one free full heal upon entering trader at end of wave. Woohoo? BAD!

The guns' aesthetics look and feel like sh**. Literally look worse and blockier than any modern guns, and they're supposed to be the future of weapons. Doubt guns will look like Amazon packages with LEDs or giant glowing polygons in the future, really. One would think guns would be more effective in the future, not looking like a gunsmith's "Bubba'd" first work. 

The voice lines. Overall a jumble of AI-slop-esque 'corporate-badass' one-liners ala Back 4 Blood, with very weak, one-note, and all-miss-no-hit 'humor'. Where's all the British + random silliness? Oh, Mister Foster is kinda British? in a very flat, not-funny kinda way? In fact, ALL of the deliveries just feel flat, like they're just talking to the wind instead of each other like in 2. Overall, they range from a nothing-burger to borderline annoying. Rate it didn't laugh once outta ten. All too serious.

The Other:

Sirens turned into go-go-gadget-extendo-necks, and their base attack is projectiles, with her AOE scream being her charged attack.

Stalkers are very tanky, just like everything else, instead of the fragile assassin type they've always been. Not sure how to feel about that.

All classes feel pretty wonky and unbalanced (especially the Ninja in general) and don't really have their own identities like in previous games (ESPECIALLY the engineer, who is a mishmash of demo, survivalist, and support from KF2). It's getting better in recent versions from what I saw it used to be during earlier versions, but it's still got a LONG ways to go.

Edit: After more playing, the game SERIOUSLY needs a 'long' 10-wave mode. With 6+boss waves only, you are barely are able to afford 2 fully-modded weapons by boss wave while getting armor/deployables each wave ON NORMAL, let alone hard or hell on earth where money is even more tight. The economy feels broken.

Conclusion:

I can see why there's only ~300 players on Steam. Guess most people are waiting to see what happens; if this game gets better, or dies ala Payday 3 or many other modern games.  The same thing I should have done, and that you should do. Wait and see in about 6 months to a year, then get it if this game is better...or don't if it's totally dead. Else, if you REALLY can't wait, at least get it on sale like I did. It's not even really worth that $24 I spent right now though, given I can't even really play it much...

TLDR: Really sad to see such a great series go down this way. Here's hoping TWI keep improving it, and Embracer Group keeps further meddling to a minimum. I really want this game to be great, but right now, it just...isn't.

review:
Brimmed with jank, unbalanced mess of a game. Difficulty curve is absolutely terrible. There are only 3 difficulty options and jumping from Normal to Hard is extremely though than jumping from Hard to Hell on Earth is even more steep.

Earning XP is slow which doesn't help to ease difficulty spikes. You need to "survive" 3 missions to upgrade a weapon mod to the max. Weapons have several mods. So, maxing out a weapon takes ages and also there's even RNG mechanic! This just to slow down the game to increase player retention and nothing else.
 
This whole progression system makes the game extremely unsatisfying. You need pretty much to max out your gear and your perk to win Hell on Earth. But maxing out takes too long.  So, you will stuck on lower difficulties and that lower difficulty that you stuck will become extremely easy and boring. 
Funny part is that the enemy behavior is completely different on HoE difficulty as well. This effectively prevents you from learning the game while playing on the lower difficulties.
This is absolutely a terrible way to balance a game like this. Hell on Earth should be the default difficulty that everyone should play on. And lower difficulties should act like expanded tutorial. Players should level and gear up quickly on lower difficulties so that they can play on HoE. And then you can introduce some new modifiers to make HoE more difficult or add a new game mode/difficulty for those who mastered the game on the default difficulty. 

One other baffling design decision is that there's no requirements to play on Hell on Earth. So you can literally play on the hardest difficulty as soon as you start the game first time! Yes, game allows level 1 players to play on the hardest difficulty. Thus public lobbies full of people who wants to be carried by others. Or potentially low level player join HoE to quickly level up their perks because once again levelling is slow!
There needs to be some level restrictions to play on higher difficulties. You can eliminate these restrictions on solo play. 

So, the game needs more difficulty options to smooth out the transition. Also progression needs to be speed up and the RNG aspect of weapon mods should be removed. 
 
All in all, the game is such a frustrating mess. And the funny part is the "hardcore" players of this game ignore all these criticism. They just want this game to be more difficult, more unforgiving... Even though the game has absolutely broken difficulty and progression system.

I also have tons of criticism for gameplay but I don't think it will change... Like, add some lingering dodge frames to dodges, make shove have some range, make it so if you are surrounded the enemies deal less damage to increase survivability, make the game more visible without me fricking toggle the flashlight every single round, etc. etc.

review:
I don’t know what’s more broken right now — the game or my patience. Killing Floor 3 is currently suffering from that issue, you know, the one that makes the game borderline unplayable unless you enjoy staring at loading screens, broken systems, or features that clearly weren’t finished before someone yelled “ship it.”

This doesn’t feel like a sequel; it feels like a tech demo that escaped containment. Core mechanics stumble over themselves, basic functionality behaves like it’s held together with duct tape, and whatever is going wrong right now completely kills any momentum or fun the game might have had. Nothing ruins the thrill of surviving waves of enemies like fighting the game itself.

What’s especially impressive is how this issue manages to undermine everything Killing Floor used to be good at. Tight gameplay? Nope. Smooth sessions? Absolutely not. Confidence that your time is being respected? Laughable. Every match feels like a gamble where the house always wins and the player always loses.

And let’s not pretend this is some obscure edge case. This is front-and-center, obvious, and embarrassing. The kind of problem that makes you wonder if anyone actually tested the game under real-world conditions or if the plan was just to let players QA it for free.

Right now, Killing Floor 3 isn’t intense, chaotic fun — it’s frustration wrapped in potential. Maybe someday it’ll be worth revisiting. Today is not that day. Until this issue is fixed, consider this less a game and more a warning.

Verdict: Wait. Or don’t. Your blood pressure will thank you.

review:
A fun game. Commendable size of only 22.09 Gigabytes as of time of review, however, it's not worth the asking price. Weapons are based on a rarity system, so higher tier weapons are objectively better than most others, which means there's really no reason to play with the middling weapons ever, as there's not even a damage upgrade system like in Killing Floor 2, meaning the gameplay variety is a little stale unless you [i]really wanted[/i] to use another, weaker gun. Too much grinding as well. Leveling your Class and completing your selected Battlepass takes forever, though, credit where credit is due, Battlepasses are permanent, which I feel is something plenty of games can take a note from. Talking about customizing guns however, you [i]can[/i] get a few crafting resources from winning a round, but I'd still say it takes a while to earn enough to max out a single gun, letalone all guns from a single Class... not like that matters though, since, again, all guns except for your Starting Weapon and Tier 4 are pretty much irrelevant.

Killing Floor 2 is almost 100 gigs but is way more fun for the <$5 you can spend to get it off CDKeys / Loaded. Check back on this game in a few years, if it manages to survive for that long...

Compiling Shaders...
Compiling Shaders...

I have had tons of fun with this game so far with the time I've had with it. I've only played the Ninja class and have leveled that to 25, and the melee combat is the best in the series! It feels smooth, cutting up enemies is satisfying, and parrying even more so. The skill trees are nice and has a lot of great abilities to improve gameplay and give you something to grind toward. The game does lack some features of its predecessors such as some classes, guns, and features like first person spectating, but it improves on the core mechanics from the previous. 

Currently, it has enough content to last someone well over 100 hours if they wanted to max all current classes/make all ideal loadouts for classes, though it could still use more maps, guns, and features to improve it even more as it only has 9 maps right now and about 5 primary guns for each class (there are 6 classes) 

KF2 is definitely still the better game right now just because it offers steam workshop and a lot more content, though I'm sure 3 will pass it with more updates to come!

No statements/official reports from Devs in their official discord about the current health of the game, no update in over 3 months, no bug fixes in over 2, and no new word about their current roadmap and or plans on updating the game. review:
Lack of communication ruins the game.

The game relies entirely on voice chat for communication, and as a result, about 99 percent of matches are completely silent. Most players do not use voice chat, whether due to language barriers, comfort, or simply preference. This turns a cooperative game into a disorganized solo experience.

Even on higher difficulties, many players do not purchase essential items like healing pistols. This is not always intentional griefing. In most cases, they simply do not know. The real problem is that there is no way to inform them. There is no text chat, no meaningful ping system, and no basic command options to communicate simple needs or strategies.

Something as basic as saying “let’s go together” or guiding the team to a specific position is impossible. While this may sound minor, it has a massive impact on gameplay. Cooperation breaks down completely, and difficulty becomes frustrating rather than challenging.

Because of this, I find myself going back to Killing Floor 2. Even though it has fewer maps, limited content, and fixed wave structures that become repetitive, it still functions better as a cooperative experience. At least the core gameplay does not collapse due to a complete lack of communication tools.

This is not a player problem. It is a design problem. A cooperative game without accessible communication systems is fundamentally broken.

review:
Killing Floor 3 doesn't understand neither the modern gaming landscape it's in or what it's supposed to be, creating a game that acts as gaming offal, a common garden variety of detritus that has been shaven away from a much higher quality game of old. I'm going to be harsh in this review but fair as i possibly can be.

Killing Floor 3 does have a certain level of enjoyment to be gained. The same way a certain level of enjoyment can be gained from a pizza ordered at 3am from the kebab shop or a tacky arcade game at the seaside designed to pilfer you of coins. It is a ghost of a far cry from the survival horror action game it was, Rarely worrying about ammo, healing or even money and if that's what you want. A simple shooting gallery with targets aplenty and a light sense of dopamine, that's not bad inherently but this game is called Killing Floor 3.

Killing Floor 2 was already a stark and very strong departure from the first game and while the visuals of KF3's enemies and environments are all with the modern day contemporary glitz and glamour they also equally have the same flaws as every other modern title given a cursory amount of care. The game's performance is inconsistent, which is shocking considering how long this game has been out for. I have a RTX 5070 Ti and an i9-14900KF and i still experienced some hitching and even stuttering in high intensity moments. While the game does look better than Killing Floor 2, it doesn't look that much better. That's not the only problem, the art style feels hemogenous, under all of the gore and halloween party decor scattered across it's levels it's utilitarian architecture feels done to death. Every other level in KF2 looked similar. It's a tired aesthetic and instead 3 should have brought back more of the grindhouse artstyle of the original, there are hints here and there of it but caked in buildings styled in dull modernism. The Zeds are given a fair facelift but it's again styled in that same sci-fi utilitarian artstyle that was tired even back when Quake 4 released. We've seen this. Nothing here feels truly fresh or unique and that is a serious problem for this game.

The most critical detriment to the game is style and spectacle, the game lacks any sort of gratiutity or fun in it's weapons. Instead looking like every science fiction loadout you've seen in the last 10 years. Killing Floor 2 generally did a good job of having standout weapons that felt memorable with debatable balancing decisions. Killing Floor 1 was famous for it's bombastic loadouts, crashing and ripping AA12s, snapping and popping zeds with akimbo desert eagles. A buzzsaw flying through the air sending a scrake's head flying into low orbit as it connects with his neck. KF's level of what i can only describe as melancholic malaise as far as spectacle goes is reflected in the class abilities which feel incredibly underwhelming. There is little spectacle in what should be an emergency button to pull victory from imminent defeat. ZED Time, a slow motion mechanic that previously kicked in seemingly at random moments of gameplay flair felt tailor built to make those moments of badass hero moments. KF3 has a bar at the top of the screen telling you when it's going to happen and it takes away from how organic those moments are and completely ruins ZED Time for me. It's now just a damage meter that triggers slow motion when it's hit. Every magician knows to not ruin the magic by explaining the trick. Fire damage is ingeneral much worse than KF2's. It's incredibly underwhelming in comparison to cooking Zeds alive in that game.

The gameplay of Killing Floor 3 is the charades version of what you might think Killing Floor is omitting the style, tension, the important gameplay decisions as the game's pace continues on. Even the classes feel half-completed in certain aspects, obviously a leftover of the fact that classes were previously locked to specific characters in the beta. Ammo back in previous games was the great balancing factor and it rose the tension of the game as you started to run low, as you started scrounging and looking for more to possibly fight back the aggressive tides. Dodging enemies left and right and weaving through the map looking for that holy green box of ammo. No more. You can instead just straight up buy and deploy ammo at your own leisure, killing all tension. Who cares making decisions about which weapons i should take and what loadout options are best for ammo conservation? I can just sidestep it all and toss large amounts of ammo whenever i need it. This is a change obviously meant for a more casual audience and while that might work to a degree to make the game more digestable, it makes the game less fun as a result.

This also extends to the weapon system, Weight was a deciding factor into what you could carry before. You could carry 3 or even 4 guns of varying strength or carry an incredibly powerful weapon and maybe a backup one. The weight system made you make more organic decisions on a class by class basis and it was fun to make those decisions. Instead you're locked to 2 weapons and a sidearm. Previously in the beta you were class locked to weapons of your class but that changed at somepoint, thank god. Weight is no longer the prime decisionmaker. It's now the weapon blueprints you make before the match, how expensive they are.. all wrapped in a crafting system that seems aimed at laboriously rerolling perks on attachments endlessly to get what you want. It feels uncannily similar to modern call of duty titles and it's zombies mode, aping something that Killing Floor never was. 

As for the live service nature of the game, it feels several steps behind modern day titles. Helldivers 2, Deep Rock Galactic all understand how to successfully spice it up and how to bring people back and most importantly without punching fans in the wallet. Killing Floor 3 feels put into the camp of Destiny 2 or Call of Duty, jump through hoops and perform laborious tasks to keep you in the game for longer. Fun be damned.

I'm going to wrap it up here, ultimately Killing Floor 3 is exactly what i described at the start. It's serviceable, consumable but lacks any sort of emotional sustenance. While it's fun might work initially, it doesn't have the lasting impact. I've only played maybe 3-5 hours of the current game as of writing and i'm bored. I'm not going to rag on anyone for enjoying this, ultimately fun is subjective and it's down to you as to what you enjoy. If you're however new to the series then i highly recommend the previous two titles. While Killing Floor 2 isn't as robust as it used to be, it's still vastly more enjoyable than Killing Floor 3. Killing Floor 1 might feel archaic to some but it really has a unique grindhouse artstyle and feel that i think is worth visiting even in 2025.  For anyone who has even had the slightest resonance with anything that i've talked about in this review, i am as equally in mourning for the series as you are but perhaps dead is better. To those who are still living in copium thinking the game will be turned around, i'm sorry. The issues are too fundamental for them to change at this point, the cake is baked. If you want to believe otherwise, i can't change your mind.

review:
Personally I like the game. It doesn't hold a candle to KF2 or KF1, but I find it enjoyable and kind of addictive. Performance is pretty hefty and optimization is definitely lacking, but it runs okay for the most part. Expectedly, the game is a little bare on content. It's much better since the new update, but I think it'll take another 1-2 updated to make it feel 'complete'. I don't mind personally when you compare it to KF2 on launch.

My one major gripe is the price of the game vs what you get. It's just too high; wait for a sale. Let's also not pretend like the season pass/cosmetic shop business model isn't horrible, because it is. But I feel like that's Embracer's doing rather than TWI's. A lot of the season pass cosmetics are pretty lazy reskins too. Maybe that will change in the future.

Credit where due for TWI making necessary changes too. Why they didn't listen to the comminunity before? Who knows. But it's better than nothing. A kind of average, but fun 6.7/10 for me.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Updated review: It's been a couple months now. The game is on sale during a new season, so it's the perfect time to update this and explain why I'm changing it to a fat "NO".

Performance has become worse this update, somehow. It's been my biggest issue with the game from day one and not only is it not fixed, it's worse. This is after a recent driver update too; I really expected better. Nvidia tweaks help, but you shouldn't be forced to do so for basic stability on a moderate system. Ontop of that, this update broke a bunch of keybinds and the last update caused booting issues with EAC. I'm fine with .ini, control panel and boot tweaks, but many people aren't. Being FORCED to deep dive to make the game function is ridiculous.

Content: Obviously there's more now, but it still feels bare, like there's not enough and the season passes are just a joke. This one is by FAR the laziest one we've had yet - it's literally the same 3-4 outfits copy/pasted onto every character; that's the whole pass. The game is already in a poor position with fans and recurring players and TWI's answer is to be MORE lazy? Come the f**k on.

I had fun with the game initially, but it's one slap in the face after another and I genuinely regret buying it now. Do not buy it for anything less than a 50% sale and please do not buy one of the special editions - the "supply passes" are not even remotely worth it.
