review:
I like this game; it has a lot of potential, but after 2 days in the demo and another 50 hours in early access, my frustrations are reaching their limit. While the first sector of the first biome felt designed, intentional, with new discoveries on every island, by midway through the second sector, you begin to see the gameplay loop. Shortly after reaching the second biome, things start to get stale. It's at this point that the limits of procedural generation show their true colors. Some islands, even within the same archipelago, are virtually identical, which makes it extremely confusing to remember if you've explored an area on an island already, or if that was a different, identical island you explored. Many islands starting in the second biome / 2nd ring are just...mostly empty. They have foliage and whatnot, but in terms of resources or blueprints, there's nothing of note for islands upon islands. As opposed to the first sector in the first biome, 75% of the archipelagoes feel like pointless filler.

There's also no real reason to keep playing -- while an ancient civilization is hinted at, there's not really a story after 50 hours of gameplay. I LOVE exploration (but not when it's literally the same "map" over and over again) and I LOVE crafting (but only when it's in purpose of a greater story). Perhaps they're withholding the narrative for final release, but...if so, why?

By far the most frustrating issue has been the near-total lack of explanation for....anything. I'm currently stuck being unable to build over a dozen machines and items because I can't make planks. How do I make planks? It doesn't say. I assume I need a sawmill, since I saw broken machines that looked like sawmills in the very first sector, but have yet to come across a fresco, anchor, or knowledge stone that will give me its blueprint. Similary, I unlocked the blueprint for candles, but seem to be missing an ingredient -- it looks like the icon for wool thread, which I have, but no, it's not -- and I have no idea what it is, because there's no text explaining what the icons mean. Perhaps flax thread? I have the flax breaker blueprint unlocked, but alas, it requires planks -- which I can't make. There is no way to search, in the game, for WHICH island contains a specific blueprint that's blocking you from making progress, For all I know, it's on an island I visited already but somehow missed.  The amount of time-wasting guesswork the game requires you to do is deeply aggravating, and, over time, makes the game increasingly un-fun to play. I have smaller preference items (like the ability to toggle on/off the "glimmer" on resources -- I filled up on rocks very early in the game. I don't need more rocks. Please stop shining at me every time I pass a pebble., etc) but the two biggest issues come down to lack of guidelines / tutorials / menu text / icon explanations / key legends, and painfully repeat gameplay where the novelty quickly wears off.

I will say, one thing I have absolutely NO issue with -- the music. It is sublime. It's so soothing on my brain. I love it. Please don't change the music, and give your composer a raise; it is the single best redeeming quality of the entire experience.

I actually do enjoy the game and hope, as development continues, that they will address some of these pain points. If so, I'll happily change my review to "recommend." Until then, I'd save your $25 until this game is further down the road.

review:
This is a lovely looking game that I'd would like to love.  Right now, it's mostly just an exercise in frustration.
I'm using a controller, which is probably the source of some of the issues.  The others playing with me are using keyboard/mouse.  They're still experiencing some of these issues, but not all.

Gliding:
It's perfect when using a controller.  Don't change a thing.  It feels really good and, so far, is the most fun part of the game.  For keyboard/mouse, not so much.  It's possibly just me, but I can thread a needle with the controller, but with keyboard/mouse... it's a disaster that goes down like a plane without wings.

Island Piloting:
The controller mappings are bonkers for piloting.  The keyboard/mouse controls at least make a little sense.  I tried to remap the controller, but some options don't seem to be allowed.  Please allow us to map the X axis on the left stick to steering left/right.  I'm a little confused why this isn't the default.  Putting left/right on triggers and up/down on shoulders just makes for seriously confused flying for me personally.  I'd prefer left stick Y, as is (speed), left stick X = left/right, and left trigger = down, right trigger = up.  I might actually be able to fly this island then.

Combat:
I personally find the combat extremely difficult.  Blocking is so slow it its almost impossible to block reactively.  I can hold block, but it doesn't actually seem to have much effect; I still take nearly the same amount of damage, I just get don't get knocked back as far.  The combat combos are interesting, but I can only perform 2-3 of them, then I'm out of resources.  For our multiplayer server, we just end up dying repeatedly while hopefully getting a few strikes in so we can cleanse an island.  It's not fun.  Maybe we've missed a part of the progression, but we visited all of the islands in the first area before going to the next, and in that second area, we're just getting our asses handed to us.

Crafting:
Crafting/inventory is confusing with all of the different tabs.  I struggle to find where things are supposed to be, and where they're supposed to be crafted.  I'm constantly trying to craft something in wrong place.  We're are also running into recipes we cannot make and we're not sure why.  Sometimes there's an ingredient that we've never seen and there's no clue where we're supposed to be looking for it.  Is it something we missed?  Is it something we're not supposed to have yet?  Especially with the wool sails.  We have three recipes for different wool sails, but they all take a some kind of cloth (there nothing in the UI that tells me the name), I'm assuming it's some kind of wool cloth.  How do you make wool cloth?!?  Did we miss something?

Inventory Management:
With a controller, this is clumsy and cumbersome.  Many other games have figured this out, please take some notes from the others.  With keyboard/mouse, it's just OK, I wouldn't call it smooth.
Controller-wise, could you please move "destroy" from holding down one of the sticks (R3), when holding down the left (L3) is what's used to move items.  That's not a good idea.  We've already had two stacks of items destroyed in our multiplayer game.

Cleansing Islands (muiltiplayer)
They need to get the multiplayer side of this fixed.  Each person on our team has different information for the same island.  My Field Guide will say 100%, but the others aren't there.  At least for us, it seems to be something with the insects.  It's like each of us has to add our own insects to the island to make all of the Field Guides happy.  That doesn't make sense.

I really do want to like this game.  It looks amazing and we love the style.  It's a bit resource intensive for what's there though.  I'm hoping there will be some optimization as part of the later development stages.  
We are into the story of the game, even if it's a bit thin at this point. I hope this is expanded on.  If the game improves, I will change my review, but right now, it'd say, even at the current price, this one needs to cook a bit more, especially if you're doing multiplayer.

i'm gonna keep at this for a little longer, and this is a review from the early access version of the game, so I hope it doesn't age well, but I don't recommend it at the moment. The concept is incredibly novel, the game is beautiful, and the design is perfect for a cozy experience. The problem is, if you're going to make a survival building game, the survival and building need to be enjoyable, and at the moment, they aren't.

The gathering action is bad. It's not responsive enough, so it takes a half-second of staring at a thing before you pick it up. That sounds like not a long time, but there's a lot to gather here. There's a function in the game that occasionally highlights gatherable objects, but it's gone so fast, you'll see something out of the corner of your eye, but not find it, and there's no way to re-trigger that effect except to sit around and wait for it to happen again. All in, it feels clunky.

Tools are incredibly unfun. Basically, you click to swing, and then a timer pops up, and if you click again at the right time, you swing again, a little faster. Fine, in theory, but if you time it perfectly, swinging feels cumbersome and a little slow. If you time it wrong, it is positively glacial. Nothing about it is tactile, and, much like the gathering, if you're not pointed exactly where you need to be, you won't hit it.

Then there's combat. A game like this doesn't need a LOT of combat, but it should feel exciting, or at least interesting, when you do it. You swing your weapons exactly like you swing your tools, which means there's no way to attack quickly. The weapons injure enemies, but they don't react to being hit, so you'll hit them mid-swing, and they'll follow through and hit you. And when they hit YOU, you are thrown backward, and have to run back toward them to fight. It's not HARD to figure out how to fight them, but it's ponderous, slow, and again, there's nothing kinetic about it. Much like in material gathering, I don't feel like I'm HITTING anything.

This is early early access, so I'm hoping these things get resolved. But until they do, I just can't suggest playing the game.

review:
Game is fun for the first 3 hours but it gets tedious fast after that. Mainly because it being EA, there are a ton of much needed QoL and UI upgrades. 

1.	The Inventory/hot bar management is outdated. Hot bar allows you to have 8 items max equipped at a time. If you need to use a new item, you must open inventory, take one item off, equip the new item, use item, go back to inventory, unequip, put back in storage, equip previous item. Daily tasks like watering plants, shearing animals becomes extremely tedious having to switch in and out of tools.

2.	Crafting and cooking is just a big sigh at the moment. The game needs to show item name/description/quantity when you hover over them, so players can see how many we resources we currently have and how many we can make.

3.	You can only cook one dish at a time, which is time consuming. Cooking can benefit from the compost’s mechanics; its skill check and it allowing you to cook X amount at a time. 

4.	The workbench helps players know which items combine to make a new recipe. They should apply this to cooking too. Currently, it’s throw random ingredients together to see what ya get, which is wasteful because some of these ingredients are hard to get.

5.	Cooking via a recipe. Some recipes will take any vegetable to make the dish without letting you decide which vegetable to use. This becomes a problem when you’re saving certain vegetables for certain dishes. 

6.	The game needs a “send item to storage” or “deposit” option. Inventory space is limited given how many varied items you find. 

7.	Building: you currently cannot move anything you’ve built once you’ve made it. Your only option is to break it down, get the resources back and then rebuild. However, do this at your own risk because it isn’t consistent with all buildings. I’m having to travel all the way back to an earlier island to find a single worm because I lost mine trying to “move” the worm bin closer to the compost bin. 

8.	Cost to make certain items is just way too expensive. The aforementioned black stone. Takes many hits to mine and once you’re done, you only get one stone. Granted, one stone can make 3 curved wood, it’s unfortunate because every crafting recipe wants a few damned curved wood and more. Black stone being so scarce, you’re having to pick and choose what to make, which isn’t fun because a lot of these recipes are qol upgrades. 

9.	The same goes for mushrooms. If they spawn on an island, you can get as many as 6-8. But that’s just about it. It has to spawn on the island. It can be another few islands before you see another island with mushrooms.

10.	Sharpening your weapon and tools currently feels like a big joke. You guessed it, it requires black stone and its only temporary. I assume the devs are trying to keep it realistic where your tools eventually dull. However, again, black stone is rare and since its needed in so many recipes, its not worth sharpening your weapons/tools at this time. The game could benefit from permanent upgrades to weapons/tools so that players feel a sense of progression and that their time invested in playing is rewarding.

11.	Game needs a manual save in the options. Currently, the game auto saves for you. You cannot go back to a previous save file, which sucks if you screw up.    

Game is ultimately repetitive after the first map: Go to an island, cleanse, learn knowledge. Rinse and repeat. Without any real progression i.e. gear, level, skill/weapon upgrades, it’s a farming simulator on wings. And even then, it doesn’t do the farming part that great. However, if they implement a bunch of QoL and progression upgrades, the game could be a really fun farming simulator.

- Charcoal can be very difficult to acquire in larger player games, as it is a found resource and cannot be crafted. It's used for sketching/learning new building pieces, lighting fires, some construction, and clean water recipes.

Combat
[hr][/hr]
Combat is a bit painful. You have the option to hit, or dodge. There's a block in this game but it can only be used after about a half second after you swing at the earliest. Usually resulting in you trying to block, but not being able to until after you've been hit. (You have a little cooldown/combo bar that shows up as you swing, and cannot block until the bar completes it's cycle.)

Killing the fungus orbs from too far away with the Bow, can soft lock that corruption tree growth and soft lock you. (Possible fix is to exit to main menu and reload save.)

[hr][/hr]
Again, the game has potential but it feels like it needs a little more TLC before I can really recommend it. Any other aspect not listed I have had fun or very few frustrations with. (Animals, Building*, Sailing a ship.) I'm still playing it with my spouse and enjoying it for the most part.

[hr][/hr]
* In regards to building, it's not bad, but the textures are moderately offset on one axis, so that rotating a floor piece for example 180 degrees, will cause alignment issues with it's neighbor. Also curved and triangle pieces do not have a mirror option so you will always have that one derp corner.

Like all other bad games out there with terrible developers.  This is why I cannot recommend this game or this developer.  They really don't care about their community when they are happy shutting people up with technical problems and not helping them.

This game feels like its inspiration came from an environment like World's Adrift.  There is a little bit of everything from survival, crafting, exploration and discovery.  The game is pretty forgiving when it comes to handling your demises.  There is no PVP (at least not intended).  Instead of building Air flying ships, you can pilot floating islands. Overall its pretty good if going about it with yourself.

Where the game fails miserably is the implementation the developers did for their dedicated server support.  A game like this, which supports up to 8 players in multiplayer, needs a headless dedicated server support.  Instead of providing that, the developers half assed server into two separate Powershell scripts.  One that creates the world, and another that loads the world. I have no idea why on god's green earth these people chose to release a multiplayer instance like that, this is probably the worst approach they could have taken.  

I had to literally engineer a solution that let me deploy the world and launch the server.  To make matters worse, the "platform" if you want to call it like that doesn't support locking your server behind a password.  It uses "Invite Codes" which don't work because the server still appears on the poor excuse for a server browser, they have, so locking your server to play with your friends only behind an invite key, is not yet possible. My friends and I have not been able to hop in to play together, given that the server can't be locked behind a password and the invite code system is broken so I have to resort to launch the server manually every time we want to play which pretty much makes having a server our friends can jump whenever useless.

As a single player game the game is great and if thats your intent, then buy it... but if you want to buy it to play with your friends, either suck up the terrible server design or wait till they release something better designed than a five year old that made it. So, this is a thumbs down review, but not because of gameplay reasons. Rather, it's targeted specifically for people who've had motion sickness in games and for those who intend to play solely in third-person. If motion sickness isn't an issue for you and you intend to play exclusively in first-person, feel free to ignore this review.

I, myself only occasionally experience motion sickness in first-person games, but this is the first time I've ever experienced it in third-person mode. Despite lowering camera sensitivity to 25% (below which it felt too slow to be playable), I still logged off feeling mildly ill and having a headache. I'm sure this isn't something everyone will have a problem with, but if you've ever experienced motion sickness in a game before, I'd go into this expecting a refund to be in your near future.  

Additionally, I found the third-person mode to have very poor animations and more challenging targeting. This does not feel like a game in which equal levels of attention and resources have been applied to both modes, it feels like a game developed primarily for first-person with third-person added later. (This review could be changed in the future) When games are cocky enough to release themselves in early access, I'm cocky enough to leave an early review. This game is a very good concept and I honestly think that the actual gameplay is very fun. Here are my issues with the game:

1: THE ISLANDS ARE WAY TOO SMALL and there are not a whole lot of resources that you need on most of them. For example, when I was making my first island ship, I didn't have enough rope to build enough sails because I had already milked all the resources that i needed in order to make rope on all the other islands resulting in me having to create MULTIPLE new games just to get more myker fibre to make more rope and then bring it back to my original world, but in conclusion, for this problem is that if the islands were bigger, it would just be a lot more fun to explore and I feel like it would make the game FEEL a lot fuller and obviously the problem with finding resources could easily be fixed with having MORE islands to explore which leads me to my next issue.

2: THERE AREN'T NEARLY ENOUGH ISLANDS. In survival crafting games like these, you should be able to get an INFINTE amount of resources, but things tend to run out when you have a very limited amount of space in the world, which was what led me to have to create multiple new games to get the myker fibre on the corrupted islands to make more rope. I don't think this game is proceduraly generated. I know the starting islands aren't, but that could be something that they could think about doing later on.

3: IT IS VERY UNCLEAR ON HOW TO PROGRESS. When I glide around to other islands and learn a bunch of new crafting recipes, almost all of them require ingredients that I have never seen before and have no idea on how to get. With my experience playing this game, as of right now I have 3.5 hours of play time and I have probably spent 30 minutes on google searching how to find or make something in this game, because there is no clear guide in the game.

CONCLUSION: I know that this game is in early access, but they knew that harsh, but truthful reviews like this one would come out as soon as they released it. I will still continue to try and play the game for the time being, and hope that they make changes in the future, but sadly, most early access games never make any changes. Let's hope this one's different. That's why there needs to be more people like me to advise the developers as soon as the game releases on what they are doing wrong so they can't make too much money at first so that they can end up making a good game overall once it's out of early access. As right now though, as fun as I think this game is to actually play, I cannot recommend this game. I made this review so detailed because I want to believe in it and I think this game has a lot of potentiel. If I just flat out hated the game, I would've just left the review at "not recommend" and wouldn't have said anything. Please make me change my opinion in the future.

review:
Ok, so first off I want to say that I will come back to thumbs up the game if they fix one major issue with the game. But I cannot recommend anyone buys it in its current state and waste their money. The TLDR is that there's a bug that causes your tamed animals to disappear and it bricks your progress, making the game have an artificial road block to stop players from experiencing the game and seeing the lack of current content.

 I understand this game is in early access, but there's a widespread bug in the game that's affecting many players where if you tame and put animals on your home island, they will randomly disappear even though they still exist on the island's log (list of current animals.) The animals will be on the log, on paper, but not exist on your island. What this means is you will continue to lose animals you put the effort into collecting and they will just be deleted. 

You may ask yourself why this matters if you haven't played the game. Well in order to harvest loot, materials and even progress/tech, you must make sure an island is cleansed AND balance its ecosystem. The most difficult part of attaining 100% balance ecosystem is making sure there's enough animals on each island. You can remove excess animals from healthy islands, but the moment you take one and it's -1 animal, that island is suddenly locked and you can't take anymore resources from it unless you return that -1 animal. What ends up happening is that you will continue to find corrupted or imbalanced islands and the demand for animals quickly overwhelms your supply. It's essentially impossible to "balance" every island you come across and you eventually just take what you can and leave the previous island imbalanced and move on. WELL, if the animals you collect on your home island randomly disappear, your progress can easily get messed with and bricked. You can and will find yourself "Stuck" not being able to properly access new islands for progression, whether its due to an animal or even having the right insect.

In order to get to the 2nd biome of the game, you need to get a loom in order to process wool to make wool sails to sail into that biome. If you need animals to access an island on the way to unlocking that loom, you can get completely messed with thanks to the bug and its frustrating. I'm currently in the 2nd biome, but my last sheep/llama just disappeared, which means if i want to continue getting wool, I need to return to the first biome and suffer even more. Also the new biome animals (birds) i tamed are disappearing now as well. It's just not worth the headache.

The game as it is now gives you a VERY simple gameplay loop. You may or may not find that simple gameplay loop enjoyable. I'm not saying this game doesn't have a decent simplistic concept or foundation, but i am saying that whether you like it is a coin-toss. Also, the bugs that literally brick your experience and stop your progress, making you feel like you wasted your time.

Edit: I apologize for the long review, but I wanted new players to understand what they might be getting into before buying it.

I loaded the game after yesterday's patch. Same issue as before. Also tried sleeping and despawning/respawning island to see if the animals would respawn properly. It's entirely possible that the island I chose is the issue, but if the animals are gone or inside of the island or just bugged, you can't get them out and the issue will just continue to remove new animals. It's very possible starting a new save might resolve it post-patch, but I'll just return after the next patch or a week from now and play something else.

From a gameplay perspective, this is a fantastic game with excellent sound design, music, and, I would say, atmosphere—though I can’t fully experience it. You’d expect a game set in what’s essentially an empty void with scattered islands to run well, but the reality is quite the opposite.

I encountered performance issues even with the demo. Granted, I run the game at 1440p, but even on the lowest settings, I could only manage an average of 40-50 FPS. Performance would frequently dip even lower when exploring or when more islands came into view. While the developers have made significant improvements since the demo, the performance is still far from acceptable. For a game that appears so lightweight, this level of optimization is, frankly, disappointing.

As much as I love the game’s concept and unique design, I sadly can’t give it a positive review in its current state. The only way I managed to achieve a stable 60-70 FPS was through AI frame generation—which is hardly a real fix. Without further optimizations, the performance remains a major drawback to an otherwise incredible experience.

review:
I'd probably leave a positive review if the overall rating was "somewhat positive" or lower. It wasn't bad. The art is pretty good, the characters are pretty good, the puzzles are okay, the office politics are pretty good.
I don't know why the game description likens itself to Obra Dinn. The central puzzle mechanic is incredibly similar to Golden Idol. You go around and collect keywords, use them to complete sentences. Solid system.
That said, I had a friend over yesterday. I showed him a few games I'd been playing, and this wasn't one of them. I also have no interest in playing the sequel. If that isn't "I don't recommend this game," the what is?

As others have said, the base price is a bit high for the game length. I played two games of similar length this week, one was five USD and one was free. I enjoyed both of them more. Neither of them had a full roster of voice actors, so I understand the why this would have a higher budget than a solo endeavor or a college thesis.
That said, the vocal performances are very exaggerated, in a way that feels like part of the joke. I was definitely very amused when I first heard this duck doing his grizzled detective bit, but by the end it just felt like distractingly bad vocal direction from the whole cast. I would've preferred to do without.

At the end, you get to decide who's arrested for their involvement in the great salami caper. During your investigation however, you learn about other crimes like [spoiler]blackmail, kidnapping, and embezzlement,[/spoiler] and those aren't presented as considerations. Some characters were immune to punishment for their crimes because they weren't involved with the salami, and Eugene was hired to investigate the salami, you see. As a player, I personally didn't give a duck about the salami by the end of things, but I couldn't express that indifference in the final decision. While you can select any arbitrary combination of perps to take the fall, you can't select nobody.

2/5, doesn't tell you what the salami is made of.

There are only two, both are basically very similar - it's either a text with gaps with drop-down lists of suggested words, or a group of photos of all suspects where you need to fill in the names with the help of... drop-down lists! There is no room for mistakes, because you see at once if the word you've chosen is correct. I mean, where is fun in that? Puzzles have to puzzle! 
All things considered I find this game a little overpriced, because I've spent much longer hours playing similar games for a similar price.

It wouldn't have been so bad if they were just red herrings but the story isn't set up that way. For example, when identifying the Salami Bandit, the answer the game wants is that it's [spoiler]Manfred[/spoiler] because his [spoiler]handwriting is identical[/spoiler], but two other characters [spoiler]have more similar handwriting to the Bandit, including one that you know at that point is engaged in blackmail and fraud[/spoiler]. The answer the game wants you to give is contradictory to the reason it wants you to give it.
Slightly less confusing deducktions, or deducktions that are confusing for the right reasons, and this could easily be a recommend.

(I hate the rating system on Steam. I don't think this game is bad, I just wouldn't recommend it)
This is a very close recommendation from me, but it's just not there.
The art is nice, the voice acting is great, the humor is cute, dumb and silly.
I do like the actual story - it's very silly, but rides that silliness all the way. And for the most part, I liked trying to piece together the story.

But, man, I've played quite a bit of detective games now, and some of these puzzles were just... whack. Too often I just looked at a "quest" and thought "Why is that relevant for the case?" or "I have literally no information on that". But most egregiously, I was able to easily brute force solutions (which I hate even being able to do, because I want to SOLVE it), because there are so few combination of inputs, that you can just kinda deduce from that instead of from engaging with the story/gameplay. There's still a handful of them that I don't know how you were even supposed to deduce.

The puzzle I disliked the most was [spoiler]cracking the safe code[/spoiler]. It just made no sense narratively to me. Why would Duck Detective (and the player for that matter) ever think that [spoiler]there being two desks[/spoiler] was significant in any way?? [spoiler]They're just randomly highlighted numbers[/spoiler]! Or the fact that you had to piece together that [spoiler]Margaret was planning a surprise party.[/spoiler] Why was that important to progress? And how was I actually supposed to figure it out? I have a bad feeling, that some crucial information is given ONCE in a cutscene, and if so, that is ridiculous.

After the [spoiler]safe[/spoiler] puzzle, I just kinda hit a point of annoyance I couldn't bounce back from, and I had a hard time enjoying the rest of the game. Which is a shame, because there's a lot to love!

review:
Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 80:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆☆☆ (6/10)

You play as Eugene McQuacklin, a depressed duck detective who loves bread and takes himself a little too seriously. You investigate missing lunches at an office, which sounds like a pretty silly case, but apparently there's more going on than stolen sandwiches. The concept is cute, the art is charming, and the voice acting is great, but unfortunately, the detective work falls apart. Too many deductions feel like guesswork rather than logical conclusions, and the story doesn't do much to make up for it. It's a shame, because there's a fun little game in here somewhere, but I came away feeling pretty underwhelmed.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] The concept is adorable. A noir detective game starring a sad duck in a trench coat is a funny idea, and the art style fits it really well.

[*] The voice acting is great. Everything is fully voiced, and I don't have any complaints here. The performances give the characters some personality and help sell the whole detective-noir thing.

[*] The humor works at times. Some funny lines and silly moments made me smile. The contrast between the serious detective tone and the fact that you're playing as a duck investigating missing office lunches is pretty amusing.
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] The deductions are frustrating. This is supposed to be the main mechanic, but many answers don't feel well supported by the clues you find. Instead of actually solving the mystery, I often felt like I was just guessing what the game wanted me to say.

[*] Keeping track of clues is a pain. The game might tell you you're missing information, but it doesn't do a great job of showing you where to find it. Sometimes you're expected to remember a random line of dialogue from much earlier and somehow connect it to something else. 

[*] The story and characters are pretty forgettable. The characters have some personality, but most feel more like jokes than real people. The mystery itself isn't particularly interesting, either, and the story doesn't really go anywhere surprising.

[*] It's extremely short. You can finish it in around two hours, and there's not much reason to replay it afterward. With the deduction mechanics being as frustrating as they are, I wasn't exactly itching to go through it again.
[/list]

review:
I wanted to LOVE this game so much. I love detective/mystery/puzzle games. And I love cutesy/cozy games. This feels like it's right up my alley. It made me a bit sad. :( 

It simultaneously felt too easy and too difficult. I felt like I could have done more if I had been given more options, more freedom. The focus of the game for me ended up being trying to find out what exact, specific words they were looking for that didn't always make sense. I wanted to focus on the clues and putting them together. The fill-in-the-blanks didn't always make sense to me, like I said, so that made the game difficult and frustrating. I ended up needing hints which was super annoying for such a short game. 

Finding the clues was super fun, but I wasn't able to deduct things from the clues. It was as if I was finding clues just to find them. Because the focus was...the fill-in-the-blank stuff. Ugh. That probably made intuitive sense to some people's brains, and they probably loved this. It's just not what I expected. 

The vibes are so fun, goofy, and engaging. The voice work, story, and animation are stellar. I wish it had a replay value, because I would have loved to have experienced all of that again. I really, REALLY enjoyed that part of it. I wish I could give it a "maybe." But, ultimately, I don't recommend it, unless maybe it's really on sale.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
The gameplay is just SO frustrating... 

Since the mysteries are quite superficial, you can often form multiple valid answers that would fit into a deduction. However, you then find out that the game wants them solved in a specific order. Instead of trying to actually solve something or put clues together, you spend most of your time guessing through trial and error which one the game is asking you to solve now, which completely ruined the experience and made it frustrating instead of fun. 

The good reviews and cute graphics pulled me in, but the voice acting (while well performed) are nothing like how you'd expect the characters to sound like and became a huge turn off. I'd honestly preferred if they used random animal noises instead of those voices. Btw I was hoping that the characters being animals would've been used as a plot element at some point, but nope, its left unexplored.

Even though I bought it on sale, it feels like I paid a pretty penny for such a short and shallow game with zero replayability. You get to play as a [b] Duck [/b] who is a [b][i] Detective [/i][/b], which makes it even more disappointing that it's just not a fun game and I can't recommend it.

The hint system doesn’t actually hint at anything, but just explains the obvious gameplay over and over again. The deductions are either painfully obvious or just trial and error - even with a walkthrough, it’s not clear how you're supposed to figure out some of the things that are going on, other than by guessing.
When you look at playthroughs you can see that people are just clicking through the few options, instead of actually figuring out the answers by clues. 

It’s not really hard to piece the story together, but there is hardly any actual proof to be found for anything.

review:
Duck Detective: The Secret Salami – A Stylish but Flawed Mystery

Duck Detective: The Secret Salami presents itself as a charming, artistic take on the detective genre, but beneath its stylish visuals and strong voice acting lies a gameplay experience that struggles to deliver on its investigative premise.

Presentation & Voice Acting
One of the game's strongest aspects is its aesthetic appeal. The visuals are beautifully crafted, offering a distinct, artistic charm that makes every scene enjoyable to look at. Complementing this is the top-tier voice acting, which brings personality to the characters and enhances the game’s atmosphere. From a production standpoint, the game is polished and well-executed.

Gameplay & Investigation Mechanics
While the core gameplay feels fluid and responsive, the detective mechanics leave much to be desired. The process of gathering clues often feels pointless, as much of the information provided is unnecessary and cluttered. Rather than guiding players toward a logical deduction, the game relies on trial and error, forcing you to randomly experiment with different words until you reach the correct conclusion. Conversations with suspects are superficial and lack meaningful depth, making it difficult to truly engage in the investigative process. For a detective-driven game, this is a major flaw, as it removes the satisfaction of solving the mystery through genuine deduction.

Value & Replayability
At full price, the game’s value proposition is questionable. I purchased it at a discount for around $6, but at full price, it's difficult to justify paying for a two-hour experience with no replayability. In an industry where even shorter indie titles offer some degree of replay value or narrative branching, Duck Detective feels limited in what it provides beyond the first playthrough.

Final Verdict
Despite its overwhelmingly positive reviews, I believe this game needs a more critical perspective. While it excels in style and voice acting, its flawed detective mechanics and lack of replayability hold it back from being truly great. If you’re looking for a stylish, casual mystery game, it might be worth picking up on sale—but at full price, it doesn’t offer enough depth to justify the cost.

Score: 6/10 – A visually appealing but ultimately shallow detective experience.

review:
This is a cute idea and a short game with a cute premise, fun writing, great animation, and great voice acting.

Unfortunately, it feels more like ad libs the game rather than actually solving a mystery. I spent more time just arbitrarily moving around words to see what stuck rather than actually questioning people or looking at evidence. There are clues and it does encourage you to think through things. But it's more annoying than actually exciting to solve anything, and some stuff I truly don't understand the reasoning for. After figuring out who was who, I got an, "Yay, that's over" feeling whenever I "solved" a section. I'm not sure if it's meant to be pointed that the detective reaches random conclusions about all the information he comes across, much of which is useless or contradictory, rather than leading straight to the solution.

I'm also not sure why looking at someone's public Blue Sky page, seeing a book promo, and checking out the book, is considered stalking. I know the protagonist is meant to be a parody of a hardboiled (lol bird puns /end sarcasm) detective, and thus hyper paranoid and also an asshole, but this particular rehash of "Facebook stalking" where people browse publicly and easily accessible information is very stupid.

I appreciate the idea of smaller point and click-style games rather than, say, the much longer Monkey Island or Grim Fandango-style ones, because those just take a while to go through (worth it for the journey, but longer games can be difficult investments). And I appreciate that, rather than having to visit everywhere again or write everything down, your inventory keeps images of all the clues you can easily browse back through. This is far more accessible than any other similar point-and-click game I've played. And I applaud that.

But I won't be playing the next one. I wish these developers the best, though!

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
Duck Detective: The Secret Salami is a short, sweet game that needs less short or more sweet. What's there is nice, but it feels underbaked.

This game has two support beams: Gameplay and tone. And if just one was improved, or was just leaned into more, I think that would be enough to support the downsides of the other. But a light breeze can knock it over as it is.

So first, gameplay. The literal gameplay is just walking around, obtaining words, and figuring out which words to put in what order, but the actual gameplay is that of deductive reasoning on your end, sometimes compared to The Return of the Obra Dinn. This game isn't trying to be Obra Dinn, obviously, like, OBVIOUSLY. But it is basing the core of its gameplay on providing scant information to the player and have them be the ones to put it together. However, most of these deductions weren't done via evidence and investigation, but through relevance. You're given new words as the game goes on, and so most of the time, it's just figuring out what new words you're gonna use.

Furthermore, the information given ranges from basically just writing out what your trying to deduce, (e.x. trying to figure out someone's name, and the "information" given to do that is just their name tag), or is so obscure that the conclusions reached from it, while not an unreasonable leap of logic, are unsubstantiated. And because the game only progresses from the words obtained through conversation and investigation, it told me that I didn't need to pay attention to other things. And frankly, that's kinda true, because I was able to beat the game through guessing, without completing the external deductions the game expected of me.

Next, tone, which I describe as aesthetic and writing. It's sad the most charming and hilarious bits of writing were the "tips" featured in loading screens. They had a fun tone that was just not present in the rest of the game. A game called Duck Detective: The Secret Salami made me expect some cartoonish logic and comedy, but it was pretty muted. Not absent, just, yeah, just muted. I think they really really should've leaned into the absurdity of the situation and tone.
The vocal performances helped the charm of this game, but they weren't enough to save it.

While not a bad way to spend 2 hours, I wouldn't call it a good way either. I didn't hate anything, there was plenty I liked, but a lot I was disappointed by.

review:
So disappointing. It's two hours long and I didn't even want to finish it.

On the positive side, it looks nice - the Paper Mario style works really well, the UI is clean and the main character's voice acting is great (although some other characters sound like they're doing a bad impression of an accent - the janitor has the worst English accent since Al Pacino in The Local Stigmatic).

But it just doesn't hold up as a detective game. The story itself is boring and the "collecting clues to make deduc(k)tions" mechanic falls apart quickly. Half of the game is trying to guess what the game is thinking as it hasn't given you enough information to form a proper conclusion, and the other half is the game propelling itself forward by inventing things out of thin air. The most effective way to play is to brute force answers by picking the words which look like they'd fit the sentence most closely.

The process of collecting clues is also tedious. Examining characters to find out more about them is mildly interesting (although it's nothing more than pointing to a feature and the game using it to leap to a conclusion on your behalf) but traversing the small environment is slow and the map, which tells you which characters or items you need to interact with at that point, is inconsistent - it shows a coffee machine and a work bag as apparently important items, but you can't interact with either at any point.

Not for me unfortunately.

I didn't enjoy it at all. The presentation is excellent, but the underlying game is very frustrating.

Frustration 1 was the controls. I felt like I had to click multiple times to get the character to respond. It quickly made navigating the areas tedious. 
Frustration 2 was some of the logical leaps. (Adjusted to avoid spoilers) One clue asked me to figure out who did a crime, so I scoured the area for hints and hand shapes and writing styles only to have to look online and find the solution was "The thief". Other instances required logical jumps that made no sense, even with the answer in front of me.
Frustration 3 was conversations not being logged with all the other notes, meaning repeated conversations to check for missed info.

Too much frustration, not enough clarity of logic and clues.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
The art of this game is very cute, charming, and the voice acting is solid. The mechanics of finding words and slotting them into the ducktective's ducktections was also fine. The main gripe that I had about this game was that a lot of the deductions that you need to make are just tenuous guesswork. The clues towards the end of the game don't really point you in any direction, so instead of being a puzzle to solve, it ends up at times being a case of just brute forcing your way through suspect names.

For a game that's as short as it is (around 2 hours), I would expect the story and the puzzles to be airtight. Sadly Duck Detective appears to have forgone logic and puzzle design in favour of (admittedly adorable) art.

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
This game has enjoyable aspects but ultimately feels like a demo for a more full game. The visuals and voice acting are lovely and there is some fun parts to the writing but the mechanics have a lack of feedback and satisfaction that some tweaks could really add to - as it stands, the mystery solving is sadly far more unsatisfying than I would hope for a game in this genre. The short playtime doesn't give us enough time for the characters to feel properly memorable and frankly it also just doesn't quite feel worth the asking price. My biggest issue overall is probably the ending. 

If you are interested here is my explanation: 
[spoiler]Toward the end of this short game, two characters are revealed to be embezzling money from the company. You uncover this with evidence and they even admit to this crime as well as blackmailing openly in multiple endings. However, despite the game giving the player the option to arrest three characters in the end (including one who was unaware any wrongdoing was occurring) there is no option to arrest the embezzlers or resolve this in any way at all. With how unlikable much of the cast is and how many of them are implicated in the finale, I think an ending where you can arrest even more characters would only add to the comedy - you, a washed up duck effectively wiping this bus company branch off the map is a ridiculous snowball effect of being hired to investigate a stolen lunch. [/spoiler]

I hadn't intended for this review to sound so negative. The passion poured into this game is apparent. It is just frustrating that with a range of positives this game exemplifies, these fundamentals aren't quite there for me. I am very excited to see what these artists and devs make next and hope this in no way gives discouragement - I just wanted to be honest with my experience.

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
Not Quite What I Expected

I was drawn to Duck Detective by its overwhelmingly positive reviews and my love for deduction games like Obra Dinn, Case of the Golden Idol and Chants of Senaar. However, this game falls short of those standards.

Pros :
- The UI is clean and user-friendly.
- The art direction is charming and unique.
- The quirky universe is genuinely fun.

Cons :
- The writing is subpar.
- The investigative elements, which are the core of the game, are poorly executed. 

You can easily finish this game in 2 hours so unless it’s priced under €5, I wouldn’t recommend purchasing it.

review:

The game forces you to make certain assumptions that are simply nonsensical for all the previous context that was given by completing phrases with words from different categories.

Overall, it's a fun and cute little game, but the whole “detective” premise fails to hold up, and the whole thing felt like watching a YouTube video.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review: I liked the visuals, voice acting, and general play style of the game, but the story leaves much to be desired. I feel like there wasn't a good conclusion to all the stories. Why would you introduce a character at the beginning of the game, to not have any conclusion with it?
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
The art is cute, and the price is okay for a short 2hr game.

But what really bothered me about this game is that there's not enough information in the game to support your deductions! The loop, which happens 5 or 6 times, is that you walk around talking to people and looking at objects and getting information, then you're asked to conclude something that's not clear at all from the information you're given. As an example, at one point you have to conclude that a certain object is in a certain place. But you're never given any information at all about where that object is! You just have to guess based on the grammar of the conclusion sentence they've written for you.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
I like this game, but I can't recommend it. a lot of people want a sequel and I do to, but I probably wouldn't buy one... why? this game has fun and unique (to me at least) little puzzles for solving the plot points and continuing forward on the mystery front, but there's very little challenge. not the worst thing in the world, certainly better than having too obscure of clues for people to find or making connections that beggar belief. but the simplicity and briefness mixed with the quality voice acting and fully developed art style left me feeling like I had played a demo of a much larger game, but I already bought it... and I finished it in one play session...
which brings me to why I probably wouldn't buy a sequel or more follow-up games, if this was level one of 4-5 levels in a ~$30 game I would probably be giving it rave reviews, but being game one in a 4-5 game series... I couldn't invest my time into game 2 without knowing for sure that games 3 through 5 were coming out and I would have some sort of satisfaction or overarching story to care about. The frivolity of a mystery like the secret salami, while fun, lacked impact. so good luck to the developers, this was polished till it gleamed, but I can't recommend this game to anyone who wants to leave satisfied, and I won't commit to playing any (theoretical) follow ups.

For now it only feels like I played the tutorial.

I would only recommend this game on a discount, or if more gameplay (several cases) where added to it. Or maybe for children! :)
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
As much as I liked the art and voice acting (as well as the dedicated quack button ^^), I unfortunately found the game to be more irritating and boring than enjoyable- you essentially are in one building (and its small outskirts) with a handful of characters and there's very little incentive given to investigate right from the start- we don't know why we are there or who hired us, and the more time passes, the more turns are presented that all just don't get enough time or room to develop. 
Coupled with the fact that the fill-in-the-blank mechanic has been done much clearer in the Tangle Tower games and it shies away from being as nonchalantly silly like Frog Detective, I just really couldn't finish this one, even though detective games are my favourite genre!

So ultimately, it's simply to shallow in gameplay, too thin on substance and too unfocused in tone for me to play through, despite the neat main character itself. But the rest just did not speak to me much. 

5/10

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
I’ve seen my fair share of animal detectives over my years: Frog Detective, Chicken Police, Tails Noir, even Pikachu has found his way to sleuthing and investigating.  Most of these titles bring a certain characteristic to the table, be it charming humor, determined wit, or a real thinker of a good puzzle.  For Duck Detective: The Secret Salami, the opportunity is there to grab all three, but takes empty grasps at all of them.

For Eugene McQuacklin, the road traveled has been a tough one.  Recently separated, down to his last dollar, and looming on the last hit of toast he said he wouldn’t do, the Duck Detective is contemplating selling his badge to make enough for rent.  Approaching his lowest moment, his phone rings to the tone of a concerned individual looking for a sleuthing intervention regarding…something, the detective was too busy getting out the door to take in all of what he was supposed to be there for.  But fret not!  Eugene’s powers of deduc(k)tion will help fill in the blanks and help him crack the case of the Salami Bandit!

You arrive at your destination with little info but a lot of questions, and to that you’ll use your deduc(k)tion skills.  You’ll start interacting with the diverse cast of characters who are employed at the BearBus station, from giraffes to cats, buffalos and bears.  Each character is fully voiced and comes with a range of emotions on how their day-to-day is going at their workplace.  You can choose to talk to them which give you small quips on their current state, interrogate for additional details, or inspect their demeanor: all to add “clues” to your notebook to work out your deduc(k)tions.

These are tackled with a fill-in-the-blank style puzzle, taking in all the clues found throughout your searches and piecing them together to get closer to solving the big puzzle.  At first these are pretty cut-and-dry and help understand the situation at hand but diving into the later puzzles where you start getting deeper into the Salami Bandit’s hands the expectations of piecing these together become a little tedious due to how open some of the deduc(k)tions are.  The beginning ones may have 2-4 gaps in the puzzle, but the later ones have you almost completing whole sentences with nearly 30 words to choose from that could realistically fit multiple scenarios though you’re only needed for one specific detail.  It becomes less of an A-Ha moment and moves to jamming square pegs into round holes to figure out exactly which part they want you to talk about.

The whole case runs a little over 2 hours which I felt was a fair amount of time to dedicate grilling six different staff members and investigating clues in essentially 4 rooms worth of content.  Some of the puzzles outside the deduc(k)tions were very clever, specifically finding out Margret’s work computer password, but there were very few of these to chew on outside of the heavily leaned on fill-in-the-blank criteria.

Where most titles within this genre find a niche to latch on to like explained before, the problem I found with Duck Detective is that it doesn’t quite hit any of the goals you would expect from this kind of game.  There were very few humorous bits to progress the character traits and motives, the flexing of your brain muscles never really hit a good elasticity as the puzzles are either cut and dry or do too much to be obtuse, and the wit from the main detective doesn’t carry enough to feel motivated to push through this case to its fullest.  There is a good foundation with the art, style, and presentation, but if there ever becomes more of the Duck Detective, and I do hope there is, it will need to pick what style of detective it wants to be and to stick the landing like I’m sure it can.  Otherwise this detective might be the thing it’s trying so hard to stay away from: Toast.

review:
I wanted to like this a lot more than I did. I was in the mood for a point-and-click mystery and while this is cute and the characters and voice acting are fun, the mystery leaves a lot to be desired. I really liked the mechanics of how the investigations are done and conclusions are reached, but the vast majority of clues are spoon fed to you. Literally, there are screens where you can't move on to something else until you find all the clues. That makes the few times that there's a subtle clue so easy to overlook, not because it's hard but because it doesn't have a neon sign flashing "CLUE HERE!" in your face. But, if you do miss them, it also doesn't matter because you can just keep guessing at solutions until you get it right (and some of the solutions more or less force this approach since the wording doesn't always make it obvious what you're supposed to be concluding). When I finished, I actually checked to see if I'd accidentally turned on easy/story mode, but it was still off, which makes me wonder how much easier it can be.

Hoping this studio follows up with a better mystery and maybe a harder mode. I don't want it to be impossible, but I also don't want to feel like an eight-year-old.

review:
I really wanted to like this game. It's made with a lot of love that shines through in everything: the art, music, dialogue... 

However, the actual detective work isn't very satisfying. You mostly need to fill in blank words in sentences. Quite often, the types of options you get matter more to finding the solution than the actual in-game clues. Some deductions are hard to piece together from clues (at least in my experience) but are easily guessed from the sentence structure and how you can fill the blanks. When you get them, it doesn't feel rewarding. Other deductions are very easy to get instinctively right based on clues, but it's easy to get stuck on a nearly correct answer. The worst example, without giving any spoilers, is a deduction where you might think you need to select a name but you actually need to choose "The Bandit". If you choose a name, even if it's the correct name of the bandit, you can't proceed. Also, the option "The Bandit" is all the way at the bottom making it easy to overlook that it exists. 

In the end, the deductions weren't very satisfying and it felt like a bit too much gaming the system and not enough actually being challenged to solve the puzzle. I do hope they make a sequel. If the actual deductions are a bit more polished, it'd be a great game.

In the beginning you're just like "ah well it'll make sense soon" and by the end of the game you're either putting in the very obvious bits of information you gather or you do guesswork for the rest and it just feels random. I get the fact that the game wants to be humorous, and it does that a few times, but it seems like in this case it hinders the gameplay of actual puzzle deduction. For a spoiler, I'm not the only person here mentioning the [spoiler]kidnapping of Sophie and her current location[/spoiler] being information that is just guessed out of thin air.

In case you'd rather play something more serious about deduction, I would recommend Golden Idol instead.

Art style and voice acting are great. There were some majors details I noticed in the beginning, and so I immediately guessed on my own who the culprit was. But apparently instead of inputting the name of my primary suspect in the "deduc(k)tion", I had to key in "the Salami Bandit" because... I guess I wasn't supposed to have it figured out right from the get go? Even though it was kind of obvious who it was?

Other reviews have described the mechanic of the "deduc(k)tions" as something you can brute force by trial and error as long as you have all of the information. And I kind of agree with that. As I progressed through the story, my initial suspicions were backed up by the little clues I found here and there, but instead of feeling rewarded for guessing correctly from the start, I had to deal with collecting enough info to fill in enough blanks. And even though I knew where the game was taking me, I spent too much time mixing and matching the information just to see which combination or string of words would even fit.

Maybe others found it fun, but it's not my fave mechanic.

Game was cute. It has potential. But I guess I just had different expectations.

review:
I give it credit for its art style and voice acting, but this is not a game that I would give a glowing review for.

The story is just very confused and muddled, and the goofy, nonsensical tone of the game doesn't help matters either. While I usually get on most other mystery game's cases for holding my hand too much, this one I found did the exact opposite. The clues are typically vague, and the suspects hardly ever give you any useful information. I STILL don't understand some of the conclusions that the detective came to, even after revisiting every piece of dialogue multiple times, and yet the game will act like it's all connected even though a player would still be very understandably confused like I was. Not even the hint system would give me a push in the right direction if I happened to be stumped; it constantly gives you the same generic advice of "I should make sure to talk with everyone" or "I should make sure to inspect everything." I sincerely don't understand why that was implemented if it's not going to provide anything substantial to the player.

Even the paltry fill-in-the-blank style gameplay just feels sorely flawed, and often feels like trial and error; I didn't feel like I was solving the mystery because I was connecting everything together, I was solving the mystery because the game was telling me that my word fields were wrong. Instead of it becoming a goal, it just became an inevitability because of the game allowing the player to brute force each deduction, which is a HUGE problem.

It's cute at best, but this is a mystery game worth skipping.

review:
Am surprised for the number of positive reviews for the game, it wasn't bad but it didn't break any new grounds nor gave a real compelling mystery or anything spectacular, there have been other detective games like tangle tower, Case of the Golden Idol and Sherlock Holmes games that actually did it better and offered more than the game. That said, I wish there was a neutral rating you can give to the game.

Good
+ Superb artwork, love the 2D cutouts reminds me of Wildermyth style, cutesy and fun.
+ Superb voice acting, the voice actor for the duck detective is funny and oh so natural, not so for some of the others.
+ The detective noir vibe is good (but will never beat Discworld Noir the GOAT).
+ Wish there were more mysteries or the game was longer, it felt too short for its potential.

Bad
- Too short, I paid how much for a single mystery and 2 hour game play to solve the puzzles?
- Some of the puzzles are to obscure and not so intuitive, the hint system helps but not by much.
- you can brute force some of the puzzles but not as well executed as the Obra Dinn or Golden Idol did for their games.
- The interaction and crime solving are superficial, the clue check is too simple and automatic, the dialogues don't really offer much in choice, there were two major puzzles which does take some deducting but also wasn't intuitive.
- Nothing groundbreaking in the genre.

All in all the game has potential and I hope the developers will look into a sequal and expand upon this unpolished gem and how best to keep its good points while addressing the shortcomings, it wasn't totally bad but just not outstanding.

review:
I really don't want to come off saying that Duck Detective is a bad game. The art style and visuals are great, the audio and voice acting are solid, and the mechanics behind the mystery gameplay are engaging.  And the low price point certainly lines up with the short play time.  But seeing that this is currently rated as Overwhelmingly Positive, I can't really bring myself to say that I recommend it.

The title character, Duck Detective, is woefully underutilized.  On paper, it is such a great character concept, with a catchy name and a striking visual design.  But there is very little relevance to the Duck part of the character.  I can only name three things: There is a dedicated Quack button, a core detective mechanic is a pun in which you make DeDUCKtions, and the character has a drug-like addiction to bread.  All of these are experienced within the first few minutes of the game.  For the rest of the game, nothing about being a duck is relevant, not mechanically, not narratively, not even for comic relief.  This game could have been Dog Detective or even Human Detective, and it would have been a nearly identical experience.  None of the other animal characters have any relevant animal quirks either.  For a game that screams "You are a DUCK!", they really don't seem to embrace that detail.

While the core mystery solving mechanics are enjoyable, a lot of the execution doesn't really come together.  There were a number of moments throughout the game where I felt like I had all of the information available to me, but I still didn't understand what DeDUCKtion the game wanted me to come to.  Because there's no penalty for getting it wrong, and you are just immediately informed when it is correct, there's incentive to just keep guessing until you stumble into the right answer.  Even after seeing what some of the DeDUCKtions were meant to be, I still didn't understand how you were supposed to come to that conclusion.  The game clearly marks everything you can investigate, so I feel confident that I didn't just miss something.  It would have been much more satisfying and enjoyable if the details of the case had come together more cohesively, instead of just arbitrarily coming up with conclusions that seemed entirely out of left field.

Those two major elements left me unsatisfied with the Duck Detective experience.  If $10 is no object and you want to see the game with the cute duck, by all means, go for it.  But if you were hoping for a genuinely great duck-centric mystery solving game, then maybe just keep your fingers crossed for the sequel.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
This game feels much less fleshed out than I was expecting. 

It feels like answers don't really come naturally in this game. It expects you to waddle around checking everything then just guess by putting words into a sentence, or shove names together until it works. Like, okay, that's Freddy. Cool. How was Duck Detective supposed to deduckt that? You don't go "oh, this guy must be Freddy, and I think that because [evidence]" you actually go "I have five first names and one of these is going to work if I guess" and it does. 

A few times I went "Okay, I know what's happening. But how does Duck Detective know what's happening? How was the dev expecting me to piece together this info based on what he is observing?" And I couldn't think of an answer. I think I'm expected to just guess.

It seems the dev wasn't expecting people to do things out of order either. If you approach the door in the reception office before talking to the receptionist, the game gives you a voice line as if you've already spoken to the receptionist. Stuff like this happened a couple times. Lacks attention to detail. Kinda sucks for a game that reacts to nearly everything by giving you some voiced lines, but the voiced lines can be out of order if you don't do things the "obvious" way. I thought we were investigating, not being led by the nose through a story.

If you're just looking for a silly couple hours, and aren't expecting anything, this would probably be fun for you.

However for me in the end, I feel like this game is a cute concept, but not detailed enough gameplay to be fun. It's like one of those Youtuber games. Surface level gameplay, but ultimately it's just an avenue to deliver voice acting from familiar people. I wanted Phoenix Wright, instead I got Word Jigsaw Puzzle: Celebrity VA Edition with a Quack button. 

I refunded, but maybe the game is cute enough for you to not be bothered by its shortcomings. It's not a bad game, but it's not for me.

It's cute, but very short. Voice acting, character designs are pretty well done, but there's no substance. Would make a cute short kids game, but that doesn't seem to be the target audience given the deduction logic has some major stretches tl;dr not worth the full price. 

They did a lot of framework it just needs more content than it currently has, 10 or so deduction puzzles and 5 rooms. Pretty standard gameplay, find an item or dialogue, receive a clue word to use to make a deduction. ad-lib your way to solve the specific puzzle. You can solve the puzzle without finding all clue words as long as you've found the right ones. 

I felt a number of the puzzles were a bit of a stretch. Non-spoiler: Some of the dialogue is not repeated so although you can meta-game the answer (no consequence for guessing!) it's not ever explicitly stated. I'd be fine with that given it's a deductive reasoning type of game, but it really didn't vibe well when 99% of a puzzle is straightforward with 1 dangling piece that's a complete guess (and you can actually just brute force it) which happened three times for me because the sole clue seemed to be the proximity of a character to an object regarding the action taking place. 

For the spoiler: [spoiler] Kidnapping vs murder, zero context other than Sophie is gone. The bus as the place she's been placed. There's literally nowhere else I guess? I guessed that because the character I thought responsible was standing in that area. That's a hard stretch imo. The blackmail subplot, the puzzle that starts it pretty blank. So it's also a stretch because why would it even factor in? I thought that puzzle would be about the accomplices at first. Also severely disappointed I couldn't hand out consequences to the blackmailer. That's a crime too. [/spoiler]

Overall, I liked the concept as I love this genre and I'm happy to see where this developer goes, but I can't really recommend it for most unless it's either more fleshed out or on sale.

review:
Duck Detective: The Secret Salami is short. All told, there are just about a dozen "deducktions" to make. As I write this the game has been out for five days and 70% of players have beaten the game, suggesting a majority of players beat it in one sitting, like I did.

It's cute, and the voice acting is good, but it wasn't very memorable since none of the puzzles were all that challenging or surprising. I did need to use the in-game hints a couple times, which are well designed: They gently suggest which clues you should pay attention to without spoiling the real puzzle.

I felt like a lot of my time was backtracking (to see if the suspects had any new clues) and waiting for loading screens, which seems strange because there are six rooms total. I think they did a good job with the characterization of the characters, but the paper-doll animation was very plain. Having them cycle between emotions (e.g. surprised, suspicious) would do a better job of drawing me in to the story. 

Feels bad giving this a downvote, since it was made with some care, but can't really recommend it as is. Definitely "almost there"; I would have enjoyed it more if it had another act, or some side mysteries to solve just for fun. The gimmick is good, but not good enough to give the rest a pass. 

Buy it on sale, maybe you'll like it more than I did.

While it did have some cute moments of animal humor, the vast majority of the game was repetitive and unrewarding.  I found myself committing to the slog so that I could just get it over with.  There were no real moments where I was glad I played the game aside from the first five minutes when I found out that you could make titular Duck Detective quack, he had an addiction to bread, and had a deep voice that made me chuckle at first.  If you are really bored, this might be fun for you but if you are looking for a really great detective romp, look elsewhere.  The best part of the game was the Paper Mario style art design that allowed for a whimsical take on a gritty noir mystery.  While it wasn't for me, it might be something that others enjoy.

review:
I'd love to love [i]Duck Detective[/i]; I love adventure games and I've played through all of the major deduction (deducktion!) adventure games on Steam. It looks great and the mechanics are well situated to make for a good game. The mechanic, which you can see in the trailer, where you inspect something and the art asset transitions from an impressionistic sketch into a detailed view as you move your magnifying glass over it is awesome. The production values are good and the full voice acting is highly appreciated (though the lead is in the orbit of "ProZD trying to do Vincent Price" and your mileage may vary as to whether that's what you're looking for). It's got a good user interface. And the case depicted in the game is actually reasonably complex and involves a fair amount of deduction (though none of it very difficult). At $9.99 for 90-120 minutes it's a little on the short side, but I appreciate that the developer is between a rock and a hard place in that having to build another entire case might drive the budget up high enough that it would alienate buyers. It gives me zero pleasure to leave a negative review on a small team's labour of love.

But the reason this is not a recommendation for me is the writing and the choice of story told with the case. Think of the puzzle and adventure games that jump to mind as the best of the best -- in [i]Obra Dinn[/i] you investigate a ghost ship from the age of mercantile capitalism that turns up years after being missing and magically delve into the fate of its crew. In [i]Case of the Golden Idol[/i] you investigate a curse spanning generations of a noble family against the context of Glorious Revolution era-England. God, you just get hooked on these games from the get-go. Not that everything needs to be adjacent to politics or feature the supernatural. I quite enjoy [i]Gone Home[/i] -- a game that is literally just a young woman returning to her home and walking around and revisiting memories. Quotidian is fine, everyday is fine. I just don't think the scenario here is any good.

In [i]Duck Detective[/i] you're a detective exploring a six room office for a bus dispatch company to solve the mystery of, like, well, I guess technically who stole someone's lunch, but even when you learn all the complexities and twists it's like... it's just this weird little thing. I think the developers are going for the juxtaposition of the serious and the absurd (there's a smuggling ring!!! lol but they're smuggling salami the detective's personal life is a mess and he's an addict... addicted to BREAD!) and it just comes off as a little twee and charming but not engaging.

Twee is where most of the writing lands, too. It's supposed to be pretty funny, and it's got a funny premise, but the "jokes" are... they have the shape of a joke but they don't make you laugh. You get load screens with "funny" facts like "Did you know there are no ducks on the moon?" and "There are over 1,000 ducks" and "You can't fold a duck more than 7 times". So the gag here is that these sort of remind you of "funny facts" but with the word duck added. More "tee hee" than "ha ha". 

If this was a vertical slice to pitch to a publisher, I'd say it's a very good one. The developers have built a series of mechanical systems, they've managed to plot out a mystery that unfolds in several sections, they have a great art style, great voice acting. You can really see the potential here. And I suspect this is why the demo was so well regarded. But if I was a publisher, I think I'd ask the developers "are you [i]sure[/i] this is the story you want to tell in the setting you want to use?".

review:
The game is decent, has superb setting and voice-acting, but as a puzzle deduction game it falls flat in a couple key areas.

One is that the 'Clue words' you need to fill out your deducktions are obtained from conversations that have little to no relevance to the mystery itself, just off-hand comments within which are buried the Magic Word™. You could have all the info you need to logically deduce the clue, but if you didn't interrogate an unrelated character about an unrelated object, then the word you need to finish the drop-down won't be available. 

The other issue is that the later deducktions are so vaguely worded that you could have multiple 'correct' deducktions that work with the words you have, but it might not be The One The Game Wants Right Now. Such as later when a Thing happens to a Character, and you have all the information and clue words to deduce Who did What to Whom and Why, but actually the game wanted you completely ignore the plot development and the Thing that Happened, and instead deduce a different thing that had zero relevance to the unfolding mystery, just a little fact that was revealed in passing when you collected the information that was actually relevant to the mystery. But with the way it's worded in the journal, you would have no choice but to start brute-forcing the answer or looking up solutions to figure out the game wants you to deduce this other, unrelated fact instead of the fact relevant to the case itself. 

If a logic puzzle game requires you to make illogical and irrelevant decisions to reach illogical and irrelevant conclusions, it's not a good logic puzzle game. 

6/10, +1 for dedicated quack button

It did mention it was a short 2 hour game, and the price is low enough that it's fine at that, but for this type of game, I feel like it held back on complexity of the puzzle that it just didn't do much for me.

Big part of the problem was the deductions were all just point and click on characters and it gives you a random word to use to plug into a puzzle. You also pull random words out of conversations, no choice it just gives them to you, to also plug into drop down puzzles.  This makes the observations non-existant (though there is some thought behind how to get to the answers for the puzzles but sometimes you can just pick something at random since the word list and character list is too short that guess and check can just work.)

On the positive notes - the art, music, voice acting and writing was all great.  Very silly/cartoony and fun, which was enjoyable. So if you like easy laid back games you can get enjoyment out of it.  If you're looking for a challenging puzzle though, this is not it.
