review:
Editing review because the game has released and I have very strong thoughts about how it's been 'improved' since early-access. It's still a cute game, but the issues definitely outweigh any fun to be had, and considering the game has been fully released for a while now there's been more than enough time to address the problems it has:

PROS:
- Super cute artstyle
- Unique NPCs you'll (usually) recognise whenever they pop-up again
- Simple but fun puzzle-based gameplay to uncover the trinkets
- Tool and workspace upgrades you can get throughout the game
- Almost-fully customisable rooms and furniture

CONS:
- The RNG is absolutely atrocious - a customer will ask for a specific trinket and I'll spend at least two or three in-game days to find it, which creates a massive backlog of dirty trinkets everywhere, and then the customer will leave at the end of the day anyway so my efforts were wasted, PLUS the replacement customer won't want anything I've got lying around so I end up either repeating that same experience or just refusing anyone service unless they want what I already have
- Most new equipment and upgrades won't say enough about what they do before you buy it - a couple examples are that the pay-what-you-can box doesn't say it initially only holds one trinket at a time, and the soap bucket doesn't say it only works overnight
- You can upgrade more than just the attachment tool now (I still can never remember the name) so they actually feel useful and fun to use, but there's other stuff to spend money on so you have to weigh all your options and figure out if breaking blocks easier is more important than being able to store all your random trinkets no one wants
- The sponge works well on about half the trinkets, while the other half it cleans much slower and harder with no indication of if it's related to size or material or whatever, so only at max-upgrade does it feel any ounce of ease
- The only way to 'dispose' of trinkets you don't want/need is a limited-slot box that you have to wait overnight to see any results from, so you very easily get a massive backlog and have to spend all your money on shelves and stash upgrades to hope to hold it all, which obviously cuts massively into the money you could otherwise spend on tool upgrades or customization

I can't say it's a fun game at all, as there's way too many problems that remain unaddressed that massively cut into any fun you could have. I wouldn't recommend this game at all, as the developers don't seem to understand the massive RNG issue that's ever-present throughout the game so there's no hope for them to fix the foundational problems, instead focusing on letting you make your workshop slightly prettier while you drown in a sea of unwanted and unremovable trinkets.

I'm hoping that once it gets out of EA and has a full release, it will feel more full-- maybe chests to organize trinkets into, ability to leave the shop to gather trinkets to clean, external shop decor, internal shop expansion, more tools to rotate through, something else. review:
A decent core attempt at a 'cozy' game but I cant recommend it as it is now, It's just missing any true depth unfortunately, which is a shame because I was really excited when I first heard about the game. As it is, all there is, is the primary game loop, get given a quest, dig through trash till you get said item, wash it and sell it for the given price, seemingly no haggling allowed. meanwhile you end up with mountains of trash you can do nothing with until a random npc (which you can only have one of at a time) requests it. This makes the game deeply unsatisfying as time progresses since you ahve no agency, all the money can be used for is buying more worksurfaces to put more trash on when your bag overflows or to upgrade the combining tool, the only tool that upgrading doesnt make the primary loop more efficient.

I dont want the review to be all negative because as I said at the start of the review, theres a great core here and with fleshing out the game could be something awesome. The main requirement as far as i can see is fleshing out the secondary and tertiary loops. Firstly the secondary loop, I want money to mean something with useful upgrades (bigger/faster sponge, slow auto cleaner/chipper that i have to load up and keep an eye on, etc.) and for more agency in how I make money, its a shop, why cant I put items on display to sell them? then have the character npc's make special requests, this immediately makes the player choose whether to sell something for temporary gain or to save it for a bigger combine and money boost later, or to just stockpile for a potential quest. Money can then also be spent on upgrading the shop, more selling shelves, higher quality shelves to sell things for more, etc.

Then the Tertiary loop, what are my overarching goals? why do i keep coming back to play? Having meaningful upgrades to the shop and tools will help as then I can aim to maxing out the shop, but maybe also a collection log, that way holding on to pieces to see if they will make a unique combination enters the agency argument from before. The game doesnt need to be challenging, I understand its meant to be a chill cozy atmosphere kinda game, but these games still need a destination otherwise players will just stop pretty quickly.

Obviously the games in development and some/all of what ive suggested might be in the works, hopefully far better ideas even, I cant wait to see where the game goes and will check back again to see if I can turn the recommend to a yes!

review:
No stakes, no skill or strategy involved in any way. You simply exist in a small building, randos come by and demand something from you that you might or might not get based on RNG, if you don't get it you lose time and eventually have to start a new day until you finally get the thing you need and then you can sell it to the rando for a fixed amount which you don't control. You do not price. You do not walk. You do not do anything that could bring any sort of gameplay aside from the repetitive drudgery of pick pick pick, sponge sponge sponge, maybe glue something together that nobody will buy. The rando will also take 5 seconds before you can dismiss their dialogue box as well, so you'll be furiously clicking until they finally decide you can close the box, and they won't leave until you fulfill their order, regardless of how long it takes or what you may want. You are not in control. You have no agency.
You can experience nearly the same thing you do in this game at your regular job - repetitive drudgery with no end or goal in sight. Maybe you can earn enough to decorate your workspace a little, just like IRL. You don't get to go out into the possibly colorful world hinted at by smatterings of dialogue from two-dimensional randos, but no, that's for other people. Not you.
Stay in your little hole, Goblin. Dig through your trash. You have no value aside from what others ascribe, and there is nothing you can do about it. Your world is your four walls. 
I could have saved money on kickstarter if I'd realized that there would be nothing else to the game aside from a depression simulator.
The game brands itself as "fantasy powerwash simulator." However, they missed the part where it's actually a game, you can move around, you can choose how and what you do, and you can choose where you go and what missions you take. They missed that purchaseable upgrades should actually affect gameplay, or that skill could factor into how a person plays. Each person has a different way they approach powerwash simulator - there is only one way in Trash Goblin.
Don't waste your time.

review:
There is an increasing trend in the popularity of cosy games. For many, gaming is no longer — or never was — about hacking and slashing through fantastic worlds, or shooting past wave after wave of enemies. Rather, gaming is about a sense of escape, and a chance to relax and decompress from the stress of the world. 

Cosy games can be best understood as games that don’t necessarily require much thought or planning, aren’t particularly ability or skill-focused, and are very forgiving of mistakes. This isn’t to diminish these games, or to diminish the skill of the people playing them. It is, however, to say that there is a world of difference between the consequences of a mistake in Cat Cafe Manager and, say, Counter-Strike. 

With this focus on accessibility, there comes a point where a game can be excessively accessible, to the point where it is nothing but mindless repetitive actions with no challenge or interest to be derived from it. This is especially true in job sims, and is what I’d argue is the fundamental failure of a game like Plane Accident. 

It’s also the fundamental failure of Trash Goblin. Trash Goblin veers too far into cosy, forgetting that it is also meant to be a game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633511 

Trash Goblin is a cosy job simulator. You play as a goblin, collecting, cleaning, and refurbishing trinkets to sell in a fantasy junk shop to whatever fantasy customers happen to pass by. As the days go on, you get brief glimpses of your customers’ lives, colouring in the world beyond your walls. 

To be clear, despite taking place in a shop, this is not a shop simulator. This is a cleaning and assembling game. There is no real way to set inventory, no way to set prices, and no way to grow the stop. While players do have the option to upgrade their tools, the tools upgrade in a fixed order, leaving no room to think strategically about which skills to upgrade, or whether to upgrade a skill at all. 

Indeed, calling the actions in Trash Goblin “skills” is itself a bit of a stretch. The goblin’s day consists primarily of cleaning and chipping away at objects, then hoping a customer interested in that object comes along to buy it. However, rather than the process of cleaning being based on the player’s own skill, the size of the object, or any external factor, the game instead assigns a fixed amount of time to each cleaning or repairing action, limiting what can be accomplished in any given day. The ultimate impact of this is that the player has no real agency. They, like the goblin they play, are trapped in an endless loop of grabbing an item, discovering it’s not what the customer wants, and being forced to waste more time grabbing another and another and another, with no real way to improve or break out of the cycle. 

So it is a job sim, then. Just maybe less cosy than the devs intended.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633348 

Beyond the lack of ability to change anything about the gameloop or the shop, save for its aesthetics, Trash Goblin has no plot or progression. While a customer will sometimes show up at the window and not leave until they get their single, very specific item, these customers have no real bearing on the shop. The brief glimpses into their lives based on the items they buy are too shallow to give them true character, and the fact that they gum up the store with their demands made me dislike when I saw one showing up. 

With no way to improve and grow in a way that meant anything to the game, and no reason to distinguish one day from the next, I got bored and frustrated very quickly. Adding in the various bugs I encountered (one of which made the entire cleaning and chiselling loop impossible by disabling my left mouse button), and the entire experience was a far cry from cosy. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633095 

The most tragic element of Trash Goblin, though, is that it didn’t have to be this tedious and dull. There are some fantastic elements throughout that made me want to believe there was more to it than what I’d seen. The art and design of the world, for example, are beautiful. The trinkets are fun, and I enjoyed what few snippets of story I did get. There is the potential for a good game in here, one with a dynamic shop and the ability to actually have some degree of agency over the game. Currently, Trash Goblin is not that. Instead, it is a tedious, monotonous experience, riddled with bugs, and failing to answer the question of why I should press on through any of them. 

Throughout my playthrough, I was reminded of another disassembly-based job sim that illustrates why Trash Goblin doesn’t succeed, that being Hardspace Shipbreaker. While the settings and gameplay loops are wildly different, the fundamental philosophies undergirding them are not. Both are games being in a world centred around one’s work. Both are cosy job sims, focused on the player doing the best they can with the tools available to them. Both are games fundamentally about capitalism, the whims of a system beyond our ken or control, and building ourselves a world that works for us within it.

Where Hardspace Shipbreaker succeeds and Trash Goblin fails, though, is in giving meaning or purpose to the job. Hardspace sees its job accentuated with a plot, mystery, and a sense of progression and choice. The player shares their world with three-dimensional characters, choosing how to approach their work, and becoming better and better at it over time. The player’s skills build with the character, giving everything a meaning, a purpose, and a sense of something bigger than just clicking buttons. 

Trash Goblin does none of this. It traps the player in the same actions over and over, with neither meaning or control. If we call both job sims, Hardspace is the job sim for the job we wish we had — something satisfying, meaningful, and not too overwhelming. Trash Goblin is the job we actually have — rote, boring, and a reminder that, even though life is finite, we’re trapped in the limits of our rooms, with no real prospect of ever getting out to actually live. 

I’d rather play in a world of imagination, personally. As such, this goblin does not recommend perusing through this particular bag on the workshop bench.

review:
In its current state I can't recommend it.  It is an interesting concept, but is just missing any sense of progression or achievement.  The gameplay loop gets stale after about 1 hour.

From my perspective, the following game mechanics would be expected in a game like this and they're just missing:
- Trinket gathering minigame/dungeons (just having it magically appear on your bench is really weird).
- Regions to gather trinkets which have different loot tables to try to get specific items.
- Bartering with customers (many others have mentioned this)
- Upgrading tools to be quicker/more efficient.
- Ability to expand number of "active customers" at a time.
- Ability to put items up for sale for "window shopping" with different components having different values that change like an active market. This would also open up "rushes" of demand for a specific object.
- Regular customers that come more frequently but expect better prices.
- Customers have a specific amount of time they're willing to wait.
- Different unlocked decorations change variables like demand for objects, customer patience, rate of finding "rare" trinkets, etc...

Those features would at least put this game in line with its competition. 

I'll keep my eye on development, but this release plays more like a rudimentary demo. The only thing you can do is chip away relics, clean them off and attach random things together. Customers are more of an inconvenience than part of the game, unlocking new decorations in your shop is meaningless and just a money sink.

review:
Needs more time to cook.

Fun concept but has too many rough edges to recommend right this second (day of release). 

First the good. The game is fun and cute. It has that relaxing, doing chores but don't have to move to do them, gameplay loop. There is a promising game in there.

Now the bad.

-The story is meh. Nothing amazing, nothing terrible. But a game like this, I'd prefer a little more story.

-Controls and hit detection need work. Things like setting your tool down after chipping or cleaning a relic is way too fussy. I don't like that you have to hover your mouse over the "Continue" button do advance dialog or tutorials. It would be nice if you could just click anywhere for next.

-The cleaning in particular can be bad, especially if you have another item on your bench. The game is extremely picky about where you can touch relics to clean them. It's not so bad on the larger objects but the skinny ones like the magnifying lens or a hair pin are downright painful.

-It's annoying you can't sleep without using up all of your energy. Sometimes I just want to put the game down but there's no way to go to bed early. Maybe that's not really a problem, but see my point below.

-Perhaps worst of all, the game gives you no indication of when it saves AND you have to finish the tutorial before you can save your game AND the game doesn't indicate that at all. I ended up having to restart the game because I didn't cross the invisible line between the tutorial and the "proper" game. Likewise, I don't know *when* the game saves so I don't know if I can just stop and quit with one time segment left in the day, and I can't sleep without completely using up my time, so I end up having to keep playing until I can go to sleep so I don't lose any progress.

So I think this is a game worth watching and I'm not going to refund it. But if you're reading this at release and the game hasn't been updated, I'd wait a bit before buying it.

For starters this game seems very Well made and like it has a good team behind it that put some care into it.
I do not know much about the developer or the future plans for this game at this time.
I understand that this game is in early access and will most likely receive updates to improve on its gameplay.

With that being said.

Core functions of the game 
you start out clicking through a barrage of text as there is No voice dialogue from what I experienced there are only groans when you 
click to your next text box. then it proceeds to show you, your four "Stations" the workbench, the customer table, the bed, and your staircase where you talk to the, idk owner I guess. Hope you like these cause its where you spend the whole game from what it seems. It prompts you little text boxes telling you what these stations do and are used for. then you get to test them out in the tutorial by serving a customer who needs an item that you must clean up to sell to him. the basic function of this game is to hear what a customer needs then go open a bag that will likely have that item in it, get the dirt off the item with a chisel tool, clean it with your sponge, then sell it to the customer and maybe you upgrade it. that's the entire game. there does not seem to be a real "Shop" element to it where like you can put items on a shelf and customers can offer on them or anything like that yet. these chisel and cleaning "minigames" feel mindless and boring and don't really add any kind of fun factor to the "Game". there does seem to be a lot of items to discover and maybe new shops to be seen further down the line but the desire to progress in this gameplay is just not there for me its not keeping my attention or scratching what I wanted out of this game.

Time management system
they have opted to go with this odd time management system that feels as if it was pulled straight from a mobile game where you have time blocks for your day, and certain
actions require certain time blocks. Lets say I wanted to chisel a trinket and clean that item, Well that just took 2 of your 5 time blocks away before you have to go to bed. so it makes it near impossible to serve 2 customers in a day this system gets old real fast I played this game to run a shop not sleep every 10 mins just to get to help 1 maybe 2 customers. I think surely they could find a better system to implement here.

Play-ability 
I really loved what they made this game sound Like, Honestly. I have not even 30 mins in the game as of this review and I'm having to have a youtube video up on another monitor just to keep my entertainment up. I sure hope they add more of a Game in future development. sometimes you are just kind of sitting there cleaning items cause customers are few and far between at times or at least very slow to come. leaves a empty feeling in the game world no consistent flow and in all honestly not sure how you could manage a consistent flow with the time management system. NPC's in the game are these 2D PNG images that just kind of shake and groan at you and don't do any real movement or talking.
If you need a mindless game to play while you are doing something else I guess I could see this being something, but for me I just do not enjoy it.

seems to be a few issues but the development team seems to somewhat be responding to those in the discord, I hope the team keeps up with development and maybe moves in the right directions, But from how it seems this is the game they wanted and may not deviate to broader shop style concepts. If you are looking to me to give a recommendation on this title, for me I'd say avoid this game or at least give it some time to add more to it If that is something the development team plans on even doing.

review:
I love the concept of this game, but the execution is lacking currently.  Yes, it is early access, but based on the demos, it seems like the time since then has more been spent on additional content rather than expanding or fleshing out the core concept (imo).

Up front, The biggest issue is there is not really any "game" to be had here.  There are no fail states, no impactful decisions (whether that be time management, conversation or gameplay choices), no true "game".  From a gameplay standpoint this is essentially just an extremely low budget, bare bones VN with some busywork thrown in.  You might think that this is some sort of puzzle game based on the screenshots and trailer, that you get these objects that you need to figure out how to identify, clean and sell, but not really.  That's the busy work.  When chiseling a new object, there is no way to fail, no way to do it "correctly", no way for you, the player, to effect anything.  All you do is mash the cursor on anything and everything.  You can't damage the object, you can't do it wrong, you can't make a wrong decision via your actions.  You just keep clicking until it's done.  THAT IS IT.

Outside of the chiseling/sponging "minigames", you are clicking through typical text fodder between customers and your shopkeeper.  To be frank, these characters are low quality, flat JPGs.  I had hoped that some more effort would go into the NPCs after seeing the demo, thinking that these cardboard cut-out looking characters were placeholders, but that doesn't seem to be the case.  The conversations between you and NPCs, if it can even be considered conversations, is extremely basic and safe.  It is genuinely suitable for a children's book, that's how basic we're talking.  I'm not advocating for a complex novel of dialogue here, but something that doesn't feel like it was designed for literal 5 year olds.  Maybe that explains the lack of a fail state, or any real gameplay to speak of.  It would certainly make sense why this game could be described as little more than a digital fidget toy rather than an actual game.

A good comparison would be Potionomics, which I suspect the devs of this have played and used as some level of inspiration.  Potionomics has things like VN style conversations, time management and actual player agency, decisions and interactions.  If you spend too much time doing things that are unproductive, you suffer and will fail.  If you don't make intelligent, planned decisions in your potion brewing or customer interaction, you will suffer and fail.  This is what game design is, and it's where the "fun" comes from in a game.  The ability for a player to test their wits and understanding of the games mechanics and suffer or succeed.  Without consequences, it's not a game, it's a toy.  That's what Trash Goblin is, in its current state at least.  On top of those things, Potionomics has quality 3D models and animations for their characters, whilst Trash Goblin...does not.  As I said, they are relatively low quality looking jpgs that look distinctly out of place in the 3D modeled environment.

Most worrying on this aspect is I think I've seen others mention this and the dev has responded that this is how they want the game to be and don't have plans to really deviate from this path(?).  If that's the case, it's unfortunate.  I couldn't recommend this game in any capacity if this is the intended design.  I was really hoping this would scratch that 3D Picross itch in SOME capacity, but it doesn't.  

Ignoring design issues, there is also the added fun of the game not saving, so twice now I've gone through the mind-numbing tutorial.  I'm not going through it again.  I don't think this game is ready to be released even in early access, and given the core design of the game, or lack thereof, I don't think it ever will be.

review:
I bought the game because I like games of this genre, which I've played countless times, and the graphics and interactivity from the developers were quite promising.
But I didn't know that it was possible to ruin a promising game like that.
So, I'll go straight to the disadvantages.

1. The inventory doesn't close with the same button, needed to look for Escape. This is always inconvenient, and in conditions of increased danger, when you can be shot at from any side at any time, this is clearly meanness on the part of the developers.

2. The font of the information messages is small and dirty.

3. To chop a tree with a sickle, and even stone and ore? The logic is fantastic. Well, in that case it was necessary to make it at least a laser sword from Star Wars.

4. But small trees and bushes aren't cut down by anything, they just exist.

5. There is no auto-battle for holding down the mouse button, you need to constantly click.

6. CAMPFIRE!!! They had to manage to make crafting a basic item so counterintuitive. I fiddled with its creation until night (when I just moved on to the next task of going to kill zombies). First I looked in crafting, and, of course, I didn’t find it. Then I created all the items in crafting according to the logic that the campfire will open only after crafting all the previous items, and, of course, I was defeated in the fight against the mind-blowing logic of the developers. Then I cut down all the trees in the area, because I assumed that the creation of a campfire was conditional on the presence of a large amount of wood. Then I threw wood and fat on the ground in the hope of setting them on fire - but only with anal fire, because I'd neither a lighter nor a firearm. Then I went online for a guide (I'll say it again, they really had to try to complicate a simple task like that), found it, because it turns out that I'm far from the first one to start looking for this information (which is good, because in this game I was already starting to doubt my own sanity), and found out that, according to the developers' logic, a fire is a type of house, so its creation is in construction menu. I started clicking on creation and, of course, was defeated again. I looked at the creation conditions - this includes stones, which I had happily spent on useless crafting of the previous things. Okay, I chopped up some stones with our laser Jedi sickle, chose a suitable place for a campfire pit for the umpteenth time and started clicking on the creation of a fire again, and, of course, was defeated again - was it possible to expect a different result? It turns out that a campfire cannot be made in a "safe" zone, i.e. near the campsite (I still don't understand why it's safe, because zombies and cleaners run around and kill freely there, including indoors, while the sellers look at them with frostbitten eyes - point 7) - needed to go further into the wild zone, closer to the warm friendly company of zombies and cleaners.

I went to clean up the zombies, almost died, because can create bandages only from the skin of killed animals (point 8) - the clothes of killed zombies and even cleaners aren't suitable (not feng shui, not kosher, haram, and in general not according to the concepts of brutal guys - only hardcore), finally convinced myself that we clearly have different logical paths with the developers and returned the game.

review:
I really wanted to like Dreadzone. It has a gritty, post-apocalyptic vibe concept that could’ve been a hit—but right out of the gate, the pacing felt slow and uninspired. The intro tasks dragged, and it took far too long to get to anything engaging.

Once I started exploring more, a few things stood out in a frustrating way:

Cons:

Enemies are tanky and respawn way too quickly—sometimes before I could even finish looting. They weren’t challenging, just annoying.

Weapon selection early on is extremely limited: just a knife and a pistol. And with no HUD ammo counter, I had to constantly open the inventory to check.

The AI followed me for unexpectedly long distances, which felt unbalanced.

Human combat encounters felt stale and repetitive.

Even after adjusting DLSS, resolution, and other settings, the graphics still left a lot to be desired.

I only played on keyboard and mouse, so I can’t speak to controller support.

Pros:

The concept has potential. There’s a solid foundation here if the devs continue to refine and build on it.

I'm willing to leave my purchase as a donation to the developers in the hope they can turn this into something special over time.

Final thoughts:
Dreadzone feels like it needed more time in development. I’ll check back on it periodically, but as it stands now, I’m having a hard time finding the motivation to keep playing. I truly hope the team puts everything they’ve got into polishing it up—because there’s a chance this could grow into a game worth the time and money.

My Feedback on the Game (Survival-Based Game):

The idea of the game is great, especially as a survival game that resembles other titles in the genre. However, the technical issues are many and they ruin the experience.

The character movement, such as walking and running, needs improvement—it feels clunky and unpolished.

All zombie sounds are the same, which kills the immersion. It would be much more enjoyable if each zombie had unique sounds or traits that set them apart.

Loot crates often contain items that aren’t useful. It would be more rewarding if, after fighting through a horde of enemies in a cave or an abandoned place, I found a loot box that actually gave me a good weapon or armor as a reward.

The world lacks points of interest to explore—besides trees, there’s not much to see or interact with.

The cover system (crouching while aiming) doesn’t really add any strategic benefit.


Overall, the game has a lot of potential, but right now it's held back by these issues. This is just my opinion, and I truly hope to see improvements and updates in the future.

review:
Overall this game feels way more like a UE5 tech demo than an early access game. Everything that isn't baked in from UE5 is kind of awful.

The game looks VERY decent at first glance because of all the UE5 shenanigans like nanites, vegetation, and godrays but the moment you interact with anything the developers actually made, it falls apart super hard. Strong UE5 Asset Flop vibes.

[h2]Zombies & Combat[/h2]
These aren't zombies, they're just [b]kind of walking health bars[/b]. Super wonky hit differentiation:
[list]
    [*]Headshot? Same damage as shooting the torso
    [*]Blow their head clean off? They keep chasing you
    [*]Bleeding system? Only a visual effect, they bleed infinitely with no effect
[/list]

[h2]UI/UX & Menus[/h2]
The interface feels like [strike]early access[/strike] pre-alpha placeholder. Think like Garry's mod but magnified to shits for people legally blind. Everything is clunky, poorly organized, and missing basic QoL features. Even simple inventory management is honestly a big chore. No way to search through to avoid the tabs either.

[h2]Core Systems[/h2]
[list]
    [*]Movement: Very "Wobbly", I guess it's passable?
    [*]Mining: Really annoying trying to figure out which rocks are real vs decorative asset flips
    [*]Crafting is very meh, some recipes make 0 sense like 2 leather = bandages. [i]Sure, why not? I guess [/i]
    [*]Woodcutting is a bit dank, cutting the tree, hearing it fall down but it's in one piece after wood magically spawns in your inventory
    [*] Everything else is in a meh state
[/list]

[h2]The "Tutorial"[/h2]
It [b]REALLY REALLY[/b] feels designed to waste your time and push you past the refund window.

Every. Single. Step:
[olist]
    [*]Mine rock → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Cut wood → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Make campfire → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Place wood → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Place food → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Light fire → run back to base and tell NPC
[/olist]

God forbid you combine some steps together.

[h2]Technical & Game State[/h2]
[list]
    [*]No dedicated servers
    [*]287 players on launch day (honestly feels a bit DOA)
    [*]Visual issues on ULTRA despite UE5 is kind of crazy lol - shimmering on weapons, blur despite motion blur off, all puddles are mirrors, unless staring 90° at it
    [*]Audio: No directionality - zombies always sound like they're breathing down your neck
    [*][b]AI:[/b] Wildlife attacks trees in circles, NPCs shoot the ground while bears maul them, big oof.
    [*] Meh performance, but that comes with UE5 as a whole and Early access game so I won't really ding them too much on that
    [*] Dev and Community Managers are going on the Steam Discussions
[/list]


And honestly all of these things would [b]BE OKAY[/b] if it weren't for the fact that they're asking this much money for this thing. $38.99 CAD for this is [b]OUTRAGEOUS[/b]

Maybe $9.99$ or $14.99 sure. $38.99? Lmao.

review:
This game is more of an alpha than an early release. The movement is clunky. Animations for swinging weapons needs to be smoother and register the hits better. I think the melee needs some more range so there is any chance to kill zombies. Leaning with guns needs to include leaning with your body... not just hands. I think it would be good if people in game can see aiming and leaning animations of others. The map on the GPS looks horrendous and should be either simplified to show a basic terrain and topography lines and POIs instead of the green mush it currently is. The item icons also should have some rework because it looks like not much design was put into them and they were AI generated. More NPCs with more quests and more interactions would be cool and give the game some sort of story mode. The building system is fine but I would enjoy a more interactive and customizable system like RUST or sons or Ark. The crafting system is fine but it doesn't show whether or not you have the materials needed to craft anything.

I would love to say the game has potential but I could just go play STALKER and would have a much better time. There is just no obvious direction this is going. This seems more of a game concept that never should have had an early access at least for another year or 2 of development.

review:
This is not an early access, this is an alpha. It isn't getting review bombed, it is not in a good place and so it gets negative reviews. I have a 2080 TI that runs pretty much everything on high and does it well, despite it's age. Everything looks very grainy, even tried playing with the settings and it still didn't clear up. My other issues with the game are:
Zombies do not appear to de-aggro, they will still know exactly where you are, despite breaking line of sight or distance.
Zombies with no head can still track you perfectly. How? Doesn't make sense.
You cannot see your hotkey list from the inventory menu.
The building system would be better if you could pre-place and then add materials, it is a gather the mats and perma place it type system.
All the inventory icons look the same, just white shapes. As far as UI goes, it was very much a let down that they did the actual bare minimum. 
You have to crouch to hit a lot of the rocks, why?
The shotgun feels terrible weak.
Crafting and cooking feels meh, very lacking and not unique at all, you can tell not a lot of thought was put into it. 

On the plus side, the gun play felt nice and unique. You can't lean, but you kinda shift your weapon left and right.
Most of the crafting systems seem to work, even if they are the bare minimum. 

Needs more time to cook and for the devs to do more than the bare minimum on certain systems. I can see how they think this is ready for early access, but it really isn't. I'll check back in 5 years.

review: They tried. The game looks pretty (If you're playing on a 4090 like myself), and you can see how the gunplay could have a tiny bit of potential. Fighting the mutants is a nightmare because it is so janky and dumb. They hit you while you're hitting them and it feels terrible. Headshots only remove their heads on normal mode, and their headless bodies still fight you. This makes it pretty awful to fight a group of them. Fighting the A.I. Humans is absolutely terrible. They just pursue you with no intelligence and fire endlessly. If you don't have solid cover, you have to run away or you're eventually going to die. They seem robotic and are just too aimbot-ish. review:
I had great expectations for this game, yet I find myself completely dissatisfied. I understand that it is currently in alpha, but it is quite disappointing. I played for just over an hour, completed all the initial quests, and experimented with the building features.

   I would create a list of pros and cons for the game; however, unfortunately, it only presents cons for me. The inventory system is poorly designed; assigning items to quick slots is cumbersome, and there is no scrolling option available. The map is also inadequately constructed, lacking a scrolling feature despite the indication of a zoom function in the bottom right corner. The quests were manageable until I reached a task that required hunting raccoons. Given the graphics and the absence of any indicators, I anticipated that this quest would be nearly impossible and chose not to invest any further time in it.

   The crafting, building, and gathering elements are arguably among the worst I have encountered. Locating suitable placements is challenging, there are no snap points for construction, the hitboxes for gathering are poorly designed, and extremely limited building options.

   The combat system is significantly underdeveloped; some zombies require a headshot and body shot to defeat, while others can be taken down only by expending an entire magazine, even without a head. The portrayal of the zombie movements was also disappointing. The hitboxes for both firearms and melee weapons are also poorly implemented, and I refrained from trying the bow, suspecting it would perform even worse.

   The graphics are notably underwhelming for a game utilizing the Unreal Engine 5 in the current era.

review:
This game is lacking quite a few QOL features and has a few annoying bugs.

Some examples, you cannot press TAB to go into your inventory, and then TAB again to exit the inventory. You have to use ESC.

In the build menu, you must use Q/E to navigate the tabs, you can't click on them. But, in other menus, you can use Q/E or click on the tab.

If you are trying to build something and have the blueprint visible, you can bring out a weapon at the same time and the build blueprint will stay on your screen.

Some of the menus are on timers. You have ~5 seconds to click "Yes" or "No" when doing things like exiting the game, before it auto chooses "No". Very weird concept and honestly not sure why they did that. 

There's a weird "arcade" feeling to this game that is off-putting for it's genre. 

I just think it's very obvious that there wasn't much QA testing done before this release.

Other might enjoy it, but I don't think it's for me.

review:
So I had hoped to be able to write something better, but I can't in the state the game is currently.  As I have said in reviews in the past, Early Release does not mean Beta Test.  I understand that the idea of an early release is that there might be a few things to tweak, but not bugs upon bugs.  This should have been taken care of in a 'beta', not in a 'this is ready for public consumption'.  Without further ado here are a few things that stopped me dead in my tracks.

[u]Things That Didn't Work[/u]
1) Guests are running into eachother: Game breaking pathing should not be a thing at the public consumption stage.  When two guests run into eachother into a hallway and continue to walk into eachother and never leave the hotel, that is a bit oversight.  Two rooms are now off the market.  Sure I could try to find a workaround to see if I can't kick people out of the hotel, but i shouldn't need to go to that extreme with a released product
2) Maids leaving with linen: Yup.  That was a thing.  So if you have a room being cleaned and it hits 2200h, the twits will walk out of the hotel and go to their minivan with the linen that they just washed and they don't come back with the linen.  In fact they will come back into the hotel and stand in the room like a moron wondering where the linen was.  Room is dirty, I can't get linen on the bed, and so yup, gonna take a hit.  Again, how is this a thing.
3) Take a long time to decorate: Decoration for a room takes a long long time.  It is not very streamlined.  This is especially annoying with the damn bell going off every few seconds.  So doing about 1.5 rooms takes me most of the day and I will be yawning like a crazy person and have to pause my work cause I can't see anything
4) Yawning all the time: I get it dude.  It's 2200h, you are a bit tired..., but suck it up Twila, you have some work to do.  The non-stop yawning and vision blurring makes me want to smack a llama.  I have work to do buddy, shut up..., nope here he goes again.  I find this part triggered me a lot.

[u]Things That Could Have Been Better[/u]
1) The Lobby: You enter the hotel and it felt..., blah.  I honestly didn't give a crap about the place.  There is a hotel design game that starts you in the lobby in terms of giving that a facelift.  I think that that would have been a good place to start making you care about the hotel, and also other people coming into it.  Having some sort of tutorial that starts with that to teach you about design, placement, coloring, etc would have been a good touch.  First impression leaves a lasting impact on a customer, and I have seen bit rate hotels leave me with a better taste than the lobby in this game.
2) More accessible laundry room: Having to run downstairs instead of having your 'cleaning' room readily accessible for you/staff, for me that is annoying and I think that this would have had a better feel and taste.
3) Weird room placement: This is just my OCD speaking, but opening rooms 6-9 instead of starting with 1 and going onwards, this bugged me.  This is just me, but I would have felt better if they would have let me start with room 1 and move onwards.  Not a deal breaker, but this is just something that would have made me feel better

At the end of the day, the bugs, and the time it takes to decorate are the cake.  The icing on that cake is the yawning.  The first three are things that should have been taken care of, and if people are going to say 'its early release', no these are Beta Testing things that should have been covered in that phase.  If you go buy a car and find out that you can't ever turn left in it, and find out it can't be fixed for the next 6 months while they order hardware, that's a big problem and it's not a 'your turning signal sometimes doesn't work' kind of an oopsie that can be handled in the wash down the road.  If the auto industry can't sell that, then what the heck are we doing with games clearly not ready for play.  But that yawning makes me put the game away.  I want to try this down the road and I hope to be able to re-review it and give it a thumbs up.  But the ingredients that they put into the cake, didn't really turn out well when it was done the baking process.  In my opinion, it's not ready for purchase, and I would wait for a while to see if they fix it enough for it to be truly ready for public consumption.

review:
For now, the game just isn’t worth the money. 

There are quite a few unfinished parts, especially in the Polish translation – many things are simply translated wrong (for example, Grapefruit as Winogrona [Grapes], Chips as Chipy [?]).
It’s a 10-hour game at most. After that, everything is maxed out. Each club takes around 3–4 nights before you move to the next one.

The first two clubs are pretty fun. There’s a lot to learn and do - one person takes orders, another mixes drinks, someone else cooks food, and another serves customers. Everyone has a clear role, no one gets lost, and it’s genuinely enjoyable.

The third club, though, feels completely disconnected from the rest. It’s the least polished and simply not enjoyable. There are only a few drinks and a bunch of drugs. Most of the work falls on one person handling the orders, while the rest just stand around bored. Customers order a ton, and the order board text is so long it constantly scrolls – meaning you waste time waiting for it to loop back just to check if you've prepared a correct order. It’s easily the most frustrating part of the game. The person at the bar ends up doing everything, while the "warehouse" crew have nothing to do. This club really needs better task distribution so one person isn’t overloaded.
Also, I really missed the cigarette stand that was in the demo. A separate stand would’ve helped balance the gameplay a lot.

Another issue: personal money. You can buy all the character customization options super fast – and there’s not much of it anyway. A few hairstyles, a few clothes, in mostly black color, and that’s it. Once you buy everything, there’s no reason to keep earning money. That's when the game gets boring.

On the positive side, the game offers funny moments, such as a llama or bizarre customers, which add some humor and lightness to the experience.

review:
Unfortunately it turned out to be really really hard to play this game and enjoy it. 
I would say I've played and watched my fair share of simulator games, and this simulator is simply just too difficult. Some of the issues being bigger, some being smaller. I got to the second club and unlocked quite a bit, while playing with 3 friends. So we were 4 in total. We even ended up hiring a cashier, because we were swarmed and everything had to be done at such a pace, we couldn't keep up.

For starters, the little screen you see the orders on is just bad in so many ways. It scrolls constantly (and not in a continuous way, like it hops back constantly), when you have an order that's a little too long to fit on the screen.
It only holds up to 3 orders at a time.
The orders, once you upgrade to the club and get food as well, are extremely intricate, too much if you ask me. 
The very very little time you get from the customers before they get mad. That's at the bar as well as when they've put an order in.
The bottles for all the drinks holds and insanely small amount of liquid. Like a gin holds 4 servings... I wouldn't mind paying more for a bottle if it meant I didn't have to throw one out and get a new one every 30 seconds.
Once you upgrade to the second club there are sooo many drinks, which also just makes it less fun 'cus you can't remember all of them and (I at least) have to spend a lot of time looking at the board to find out what I'm making. You should perhaps be able to choose which drinks you're serving - and perhaps also if you're a club that serves food or not. That would make it more playable for more people I would think.
Many orders (double and even triple checked several times) ended up failing with the customer for "being wrong". 
Many surfaces and cupboards you aren't able to place things on/in.
There's no indication of what order number is currently on your tray.
It also sucks that any tiny order must be on a tray to serve it, especially because the tray serves no purpose, when it's just a drink, without the order number.
The UI when you're on the different screens is very inconsistent. Like the back button is never really the same.

Having to keep up with all these things, taking orders, making food, making drinks, while doing the dishes, and fighting the occasional customer... just makes it a bit too much for me at least.

As I said, some smaller, some bigger issues.

The gimmicks are funny and it had so much potential. But these things all put together, just make it extremely hard to enjoy...
I've been looking forward to it for a long time, so this really sucks. Perhaps it'll be better in the future with updates to the way many of their current game mechanics work.

review:
I was seeing this game on Steam for a long while before I decided to finally get it. I was mostly hesitant from the reviews, but loved the idea of it. The concept itself is awesome and unique and I just wish it was implemented better.

I tried to like this game, but it truly fell short in my opinion. Yes, I understand that it's Early Access, but keep in mind that I've got nearly 1300 hours baked into 7 Days to Die, the king of Early Access games. Better yet, I'm probably at 3000 hours in Escape From Tarkov, the runner-up for the title.

This felt like Desolate, but worse. However, it is substantially better than Subsistence.

The melee combat is so static and boring and it doesn't feel like you're actually hitting the enemies. The base "management" is slim to none, with everything that you need already being available from the start. The only things to really do with it are plant seeds that take 5 minutes to grow, refill your generator, and upgrade your workstations. Issues with framerates was also a major problem for me. *(btw turn on FSR and turn off Frame Generation. you're welcome.)* Chests in the world taking 2 minutes of your available immunity time just for looking at them is a wack mechanic, although the puzzles to unlock them are a breath of fresh air.

The storyline and writing isn't bad, in my opinion, and I love the idea of mixing different blueprints together to make the Serum that you want/need for certain situations. The world looks fantastic, and I like how the items look.

Look, Serum has great potential, but in it's current state, and with the devs stating that they're currently "facing issues with development", I cannot recommend it. It's giving off the feeling of the first few stages of abandonware.

review:
UPDATE: Unfortunately I have had to update this review to not recommended. Not because the game is bad as it stands, but because it has been abandoned by the dev and publisher. I cannot, in all good conscious, recommend a game that will likely never be completed and released from early access. A lot of wasted potential here. My actual review below has been left intact in case anybody is still interested.

At this time of writing this review I have just received an in game message to let me know that I have completed all of the current content the game has to offer (early access).

So far I'd say I'm pretty impressed by what's on offer here. While this is 'yet another' survival game in what might be considered by some to be a tired genre these days, I feel Serum offers a good twist on the usual formula. Early on you find a basic recipe for Serum which is used to keep you alive against a widespread infection called the Blight. The protection this gives you is measured in time and can be viewed on your arm counting down as you go (but not counting down when at base camp). As you advance through the world you can see the effect it is having on nature and wildlife, as well as humans who have succumbed to it. As you progress, you learn additional affects for this Serum and can have up to three equipped at once. Some of these affects can have a profound impact on your survivability in combat as well as allowing you to break certain walls, or double jump or see in the dark. I really like this system and the core gameplay loop of venturing out, gathering materials for base and weapon upgrades and dragging them back to camp while also advancing your story quest while out and about works really well. There's also an experience system tied to crafting the Serum so you unlock additional effects as you go.

As for the base, don't be expecting anything too crazy here - you won't be freely designing and placing things where you want, or building in game versions of the Taj Mahal or anything like that. The layout stays the same, you simply upgrade what's there. 

For me the weakest part was probably the combat. It's not that it's bad per se, you have light and heavy attacks, block and perfect block, dodges etc plus different damage types which work better against certain enemies than others. The problem for me is that it feels a bit floaty at times. I've definitely played worse but feel the combat would benefit a lot from more impactful feedback, visually and in terms of audio. Another criticism I would levy is that the game is pretty buggy in places but certainly not unplayable, no worse than most other early access games to be honest.

I've completed the current early access content in approximately 13 hours and thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. If you like survival games and are looking for something a bit different then this is well worth a look in my opinion. I look forward to returning at a later date to see what kind of content they can add to flesh this out, and see how the story line wraps up.

review: Solid 5/10. I don't regret playing through the game but asking anything more than 20 dollars is too much. Game is held back very hard by inconsistent mechanics, annoying audio, and poor optimization. I did not know what the bad reviews were talking about until the second half of the game. Once I got there my frames never climbed above 25. It feels like they just forgot to optimize the last zone of the game and combined with some weird bugs, the whole game felt like it was being held together by duct tape. First half of the game is also wildly different in terms of game play compared to the second. In the first half you are pressured heavily by the timer and healing is not super easy to access so you don't have room to bring serums that give you extra abilities or resistances without constantly having to retreat back to base and spend resources on more serums. This makes combat quite scary, yet more meaningful. Group fights are deadly and most enemies resist the damage type of the starter weapon. Then you get upgrades for your serum making the timer pretty much irrelevant and you get the spear pretty early on which is the correct answer to almost every enemy in the game. Healing becomes easy and cheap and the weapon upgrades and serums exponentially increase your power. By the halfway point you'll have access to movement speed boost and health regeneration which makes you an immortal speed demon. Not even the final boss out damages the health regeneration if you try to avoid his attacks even just a little bit. Your weapon upgrades allow you to kill everything in 3 hits or less and you even get the bow which enemies are too stupid to react to when they get hit by it. After a while it feels like you are just dealing with the games shenanigans with 25 fps to boot while going mach 1 around the map. I would be lying though if I said it was not satisfying to completely obliterate everything in my path for a while and I loved the more desperate survival feel of the first half of the game. The beginning felt like metro last light juggling my time to be on the surface and looting things, as well as just using melee weapons instead of guns to take enemies out. The different serums are really cool but many seem to just bug out and don't work. Halfway through the game I maxed out the double jump serum and then it never worked again for the rest of the play through regardless of resets and save loading. The UI seems to just lie to you about effects all the time and there is super annoying ambiance that plays like every minute and you cant turn it off without turning off all sound effects. This game would definitely be a lot more satisfying to complete if the combat actually made you think and the optimization wasn't ass. This game makes me wish more video games came out prioritizing playability first and content second

review:
It's early access, I get it. But some of the core mechanics are so flawed that I just cannot recommend a buy at this time. I wanted to like this game so badly, I have been looking forward to it for months. Argh.

Gameplay loop is good, the pressure of the timer introduces a fair bit of urgency/stress and really propels the game forward. Voice acting is passable, which is an achievement in these times all by itself. Game doesn't stink of DEI yet either, but I only played it for an hour. On it's face just seems like a straightforward survival game with a cool loop. I thought it was visually impressive as well.

The bad part of this is the timer runs while you are reading docs that explain the story, and running while in the settings menu, and these particular details aren't urgency so much as terrible design, in my opinion. At least for a singleplayer game. That just isn't fun. Gotta run to the bathroom or grab a drink? Better exit the game first. For a game whose story is partially told through documents you find laying around, you better think twice before actually reading one unless you are close to an absorber. Half your time with be spent figuring out the interface at this time anyway, at least early on in the game.

Devs, for God's sake, fix the buggy absorber. For such a critical component of the early game phase, it is just baffling to me that a timer would be running during unskippable dialogue that lasts way too long for the timer, while standing in front of an absorber and being unable to use it because of the unskippable dialogue. All the while timer is ticking down. This alone made me refund the game. Sure, you can still use serum during moments like these, but it's just a bad mechanic to force me to do so while standing 6 inches away from an absorber.

The gate puzzles need a tutorial. It seems obvious to get the green line from one side of the screen to the other, using flowgates that you can rotate, but both times I solved the puzzles I was confused at how completing the flow one way would fail, but completing a flow the other way would succeed, when both times the flow reached one side of the screen to the other. Not to mention the W/S (presumably Y axis) component of the puzzles, which made no sense at all, and as far as I can tell had no impact on the puzzles whatsoever. You really should throw together a tutorial for the puzzles. And pause the timer while reading it.

Most importantly, the combat is flat out *terrible*. I felt completely disconnected from my targets. There was no impact to any of it, I mean at least sync the blows of the machete with the sound of hitting a target. It just felt so soft and underwhelming. IMO there needs to be more impact, better sounds, and at least some feeling of connection with the target I am attacking. The combat in this game is almost as bad as the 'combat' in Icarus, and that alone is so impressively bad it deserves some kind of award itself.

Lastly, the encumbrance mechanic was when I tapped out for good. The interface was bad enough as it is, but I could not figure out how to divest myself of extra weight in the time I had left on the timer. Largely due to how unintuitive the interface is. Cutting my move speed down 95% so I couldn't get to a chest to unload what had made me encumbered to begin with, coupled with no idea how to do it from inventory, and no meaningful tutorial explaining the mechanic is just chef's kiss level of annoyance. 

As a side note, I am convinced whoever designed the interface hates both me and the entire human species. Maybe Ultron designed it to confuse and demoralize us. Maybe the design plan was found in Hitler's bunker and was specifically created to baffle people into a zombielike state so as to easily conquer them while they stared slackjawed at the monitors in front of them. Or maybe it just needs a seriously fresh perspective applied to it.

To be clear, I really liked the framework of this game. There are just so many poor design issues, my God. But for the reasons above, no way I can recommend the game in this state. I will seriously consider giving this another shot later, principally when the combat is more refined. Good luck, devs.

review:
Let me start by saying, "Serum" has potential. The devs are super receptive to feedback, which is always a good sign. But this game needs a bit more time in the oven. I'm running a 4070 Super with an i7, and I can't get a steady 50 FPS no matter how many settings I lower. I can run Hellblade 2 at 90 fps so it's not my hardware.

One big issue: the inventory tooltips, or rather, the lack thereof. When crafting, there are these mysterious symbols representing materials. It's like trying to decipher hieroglyphs without the Rosetta Stone. Devs, please, some labels would be nice!

Now, about the gameplay. This game loves its timers. Timers for growing, timers for needing more "Serum"". But it's not fun when you're far from home base, desperately trying to complete an objective, and you hear that dreaded "Beep... Beep." If you've used more than 3-4 serums, just accept your fate. You won't make it back to base, you can't re-inject yourself, and you drop all your loot. It's like a cruel game of "Groundhog Day,"but with green serum and bad optimization.

And the controls. Oh boy, the controls. Having an item wheel with no option to pause or slow down time is like trying to juggle flaming swords while riding a unicycle. Tedious and frustrating doesn't even begin to cover it.

I see what they're trying to do, and honestly, I think in about 6 months to a year, "Serum" could be a banger. But for now, it's a diamond in the rough. I'll be keeping an eye on this one, hoping it evolves into the game I know it can be. I'll update this review if there are worthwhile changes but as of now, I'd hold off. But maybe I'm just an entitled gamer and need to "Git gud" and also shell out for a 4090. Just the opinion of a random Steam dude. Grain of .02 cents and all.

review:
Neat concept, nice graphics and almost felt fun but needs more time before being considered for early access.
Survival crafting game with a neat exploration gimmick with the 'serum' timer. However...

- Fails at being a fun exploration game - combat is way too janky, enemies randomly gang up on you out of nowhere, hitboxes and timing of blocking don't make sense, and you can get stuck doing puzzles while an enemy attacks and kills you.
- Fails at being a fun crafting game - look like there's an idea for a neat tech/serum tree but items are tedious to store, and breakdown/use is confusing and not intuitive to begin with.
- Fails at being a fun story. The whole story seems like an afterthought and there is no building of the characters...which is a shame because it feels like a neat core concept which could be a fun addition to the genre. Would be willing to just chalk it up to early access issues if there wasn't an end to the story/or it needed some development but the problem feels deeper than that - it honestly feels like there's no real story to begin with which is a bad sign.

Refunded, will consider revisiting in a about a year if there have been some major reworks.

Howdy Howdy guys. I hope everyone is doing well. Unfortunately, this is the first review I'm ever writing and at the time of this review I would heavily suggest holding off here. I had a chance to play this before release and was excited that things would be better at the EA release. There are definitely some interesting concepts here regarding to the Serum mechanic and gaining abilities through experimentation and having to balance your toxicity.

That being said, there are a whole bunch of QoL that prevent this from being in a state of playability. First and foremost, the tutorials are not handled well at all and do give enough context with certain mechanics. It explains that you can gain abilities through Serum but never goes in depth on what the abilities do or how to utilize them. They are attached to hotkeys when you do get them but it is buggy at best if they will work. I tried breaking a wall with the wallbreaker ability, for instance, and it took me 4 times before it actually worked. And each time I used the ability led to a 20 sec cool down.

Performace is still not great and no matter the settings there was always some level of stuttering. Inventory space is limited but what is more egregious is that when putting stuff in a storage box you can only put in one item at a time and cannot send stacks of items to your box. Furthermore, at the time of writing, there are not hotkeys to send stuff to the box. You have to click on the item you want to send to your box and then mouse click the button to send to box. If you have a stack of 47 electronics that means you are having to click the stack, then click send to storage, and then click on the stack again to repeat 47 times if you want to store stuff. You will fill your inventory out quickly so until something changes, you will be doing this alot.

Combat has not improved and was on the weaker end before the release. Attacks don't fill impactful and if you commit to an attack you can't cancel into a block. You have to be methodical about it which isn't a terrible thing but attacks feel faster than they are blocking after an attack takes some time to follow up with.

Honestly, I want to like the game and I don't need my hand held for a survival crafting experience but at the same time I want to be able to clearly understand what is happening  without having to wonder if what I'm doing is just bugged. I wouls say come back later after a couple of updates and see if things have smoothed out.

review:
This game has an interesting concept that I like, but I honestly can't recommend it at this time. I do understand that its early access so I'm gonna talk about the good, the bad, and the ugly that this game has.

TLDR: Game has a cool setting, gameplay mechanics are frustrating, game is buggy, and QoL is extremely lacking in this game. Wait until its more developed and check reviews before purchase.

The bad (Why you shouldn't buy this game): I encountered a game crippling bug about 3 hours into the game playing casually. This was encountered while doing the stepping into darkness quest when I died to a dullard sneaking up behind me. I was halfway through the quest when I was no longer able to turn on the electrical boxes needed to unlock the door holding the blueprint. I tried restarting the game and that didn't work so I decided to just return to base and ready up for the next quest. Turns out I was unable to even do that as I was no longer able to interact with any of the crafting benches and was effectively soft locked due to a relatively minor mistake of allowing an enemy smack me from behind. In addition to this bug, there are bugs where reloading a checkpoint allows for ranged enemies to hit you through the walls before they are able to load in, and there is at least one wall in the shipping container town you can just walk through.

The Ugly: The story has an interesting premise, the execution of it seems a bit janky though, immediately calling an unknown character over the radio by name is a little jarring after a slightly odd animation of inspecting your hands for some reason when you pick up the radio. The player character does in fact have a reason to know the name of the radio contact and its frequency, but this is tucked away in the journal that I would have never encountered if I hadn't been looking around in the journal fragments for hints on how to get to the floral research facility. Only other oddity that sticks out to me is that Natasha (I think that's the name of the creature you encounter in the floral research facility) is mentioned to potentially have boobs for some reason? Maybe I missed similar quips in other enemy entries but this almost felt out of pocket with a lack of establishing the character as someone to make such quips. Either you should establish that they make these comments regularly about the things that try to kill them, or just remove the comment that basically destroys what I'd imagine is supposed to be a tense moment of you hiding from a mutant you are clearly not ready to fight when you look back at it.
Since it'd be easier to just list the QoL issues I had, here's a list
-Inventory management sucks, moving things from your inventory to storage is tedious as you have to re-select an item once the previous stack has been moved over one item at a time. Collecting plants from the hydroponics tables is annoying as you need to select the individual plant and harvest individually to the point I just stopped bothering during my short play through.
-Ladders are extremely annoying, seriously, having to put an input E to interact to get on makes sense, but having to climb up slowly with the sprint making it only barely faster, only to hit the top and stop to have to hit E again to start a slow animation to get off the ladder is frustrating and basically resulted in me finding any other way to get up or down from things if I could to save time. Thankfully ladders are generally avoidable, or rarely required.
-Combat, basically I did my best to run by everything I reasonably could, or if I needed to fight, did so boringly cheaply or by trapping enemies on geometry or in one case, the ground itself. The player fights slowly, enemies are kinda stupid, dodging isn't taught to the player and was discovered by accident. Dullards are way too tanky and hit way to hard. This is likely to encourage players to use Serums that give blunt resistance, but its honestly easier to just run in circles around them to lock them into a spinning around attack thats easy to avoid (while other attacks seemingly home in on the player) and just click until bad guy horizontal. Actual placement of the enemies is alright up until you reach the container town's greenhouse, where you get spammed with ranged enemies to just run past or do what I did, and kill them individually in the dark. The floral research facility however is a much different story, locking doors behind generators that activate the plant enemies. This is a great way to force the player into combat, except the execution is god awful as they also have Dullards which require your attention to safely fight while you get peppered from several angles by plant enemies waiting for you to turn on generators. Once you suffer your way through that you get more generators with more dullards, plants, and now tentarats for even more ranged damage. Get too far away from a Dullard while you're dealing with this and they will run back to their spawn point and instantly full heal once they reach it, prompting you to continue to retreat for net zero progress, or risk further damage chasing them down if theyre low enough to kill. This full heal happens regardless of how close the player is or how much health they have, once you proc their return to spawnpoint behavior they are going to blindly run back to heal. If youre lucky youll get them stuck on something they can't reach you behind and just kill them for free. Enemies do respawn but very slowly thankfully.
-Healing items such as bandages and painkillers should tell you that they are usable, not just 'don't use them' resulting in me scrapping a lot of supplies that would have made my life easier.
-Respawning is basically worthless in most situations. You can just quit to menu for free and then reload the last checkpoint which the game gives you plenty of. Its better than death being overly punishing, but losing your items because you died is easily bypassed by just jumping back in time and not having to deal with making serums to get your old stuff and continue on. I do appreciate though that respawning lets you keep weapons and serums though, this makes death a bad thing without being punishing with how bad combat is. I discovered this by accident when I overshot with my mouse and returned to menu when attempting to respawn, and then kept doing that afterwards.
-As mentioned by other reviewers, the games optimization needs some work. The gates work as good loading zones and hide this loading decently well, the biggest thing is just performance while actually playing. For clarity this game was being run on a hard drive and not an SSD.
-Pausing the game does not pause the timer. In game menus make sense, but if I'm hitting escape I've grown accustomed to being able to get up and take care of something.

The Good: I don't want to leave the review off with nothing but frustration and talking about the games failings. Its an early access title that appears to be shooting for triple A status/quality and is priced accordingly. I thought briefly about refunding but was getting enough fun out of it to keep playing up until my softlock encounter. The story premise is really strong, the enemy designs are interesting and fitting for the mutation theming, learning how to craft items by scrapping them is a great fallback incase you scrap an item you need later or cant find it. Resources respawn at I feel appropriate timings and the hydroponics farm has the potential to be massively useful if it weren't for how time consuming it was. The timer mechanic feels well done, giving players an incentive to return home eventually as well as making time a manageable resource. Pausing the timer at the home base as well is a massively good move. The visible changes to the players hands and arms as you distort more with each serum use is a good touch. I hope to see this game do well in the future.

review:
Well, there are some serious QoL issues here that make you question what was the idea behind the implementation.  They didn't change it after player feedback during the demo, so not sure if feedback during EA will have an impact or not.  With that said, there's somewhat of a game here, [i]IF[/i] you can get past the jank.

---Cons---
- Doesn't seem to have a map, but haven't played long enough to see how much that matters
- The controller implementation sucks, as you use the controller stick to move an on-screen cursor, this doesn't impact character movement, but menus are a PITA
- Some in-game hints/prompts show keyboard commands when playing with a controller
- Blocking works for like 1.5 seconds, so you have to time it JUST right
- Have to use the item wheel to switch or use everything - no hot-keys, except for skills you gain later into the game
- No pause in a singleplayer game - yes, I know, this one is ridiculous
- Random issues where I get stuck on nothing and can't move or I can't interact with interactable things in the environment - the issues usually resolve themselves eventually
- Inventory mgmt. is bad - no right-click to move, no shift-right-click, no drag-and-drop - you select an item, then push a button...to move ONE item at a time (not a stack)

With all of the above, plus a timer, you can begin to see where they intended this to go, but was that the right decision.  It feels like they either were planning to make a multiplayer game or add multiplayer later (still might) - the ONLY reasons I can see for not having a pause in the game, other than to simply be a dick and keep that serum timer running.  FYI, even in the puzzle sections that timer is counting down, so don't look at the puzzle too long.

+++Pros+++
+ Interesting premise
+ A new game to play (yay)

I'm going to say that for most people, meaning the average consumer, this will be a pass at this time.  The QoL issues are just a tad too distracting - using the controller for inventory mgmt. is just horrible, better to switch to mouse & keyboard, but similarly, combat with the controller feels janky and your 5 seconds of stamina don't help that out at all.

Ascend was one of the only games I actually remember playing when I was younger on the PC. So, In my hype to experience it again at a later age I was like "Hey, I've been meaning to up my FPS Game and this stuff is both familiar, and nostalgic somehow!"

My blind, gullible behind stood no chance against it! I was blindsided by filthy con artists, charlatans, deviants and vagabonds!

But in all seriousness, dropped alot to buy this game only to find 90% of the servers were bots and I was no where near as good as I thought I was. Gameplay loop is spectacular admittedely, but nowhere near the previous games and lacks basically everything besides the actual FEEL of the game. No vehicles, less gamemodes, worse soundtrack (Same one in every match but... Dull, only picking up when you get to hold the objective for a few seconds because your teams farming skill kills, which tbf, is way more fun). 

Wanted this game to be good, very good. Unfourtunately, everything down to the DLC is a scam. 

DLC is a year pass for skins, by the way. You are guaranteed a new skin each day for each DLC you own.. Unless you don't play a select number of games to *earn* the skin you paid for. And if you don't play on that day, you lose a day you can't get back. So if you aren't playing for 120 days of the 364 it gives you, that's 120 skins you can't unlock in your funny new video game. Why? Screw you, that's why. 

Refused to refund me for anything, too. Actually harpooned me in. Anti cheat is also Whack (Denuvo), so don't worry about filthy pirates getting in! They've got to make sure you've spent your money, after all.

Typically I'm optimistic but with this company, this is a passing trend for them, which sucks, because they clearly have talent. Too bad all they wish to churn out is slop.

I will actually list some of the positives though!

Fun gameplay loop
Classes are kinda funny, bit pointless sometimes, but funny.
The artstyle looks nice if it doesn't remind me of reskinned unreal assets. The guns, however, do look pretty nice and functional for the setting.
Maps are pretty well put together for the movement system, though the most popular one is a big bowl, so, do with that as you will.
Game punishes you for using full auto spam weapons by making them basically horrible unless it's for finishing someone off. The weapons themselves, besides these, are stupid fun to play with.
Finally: The destroy the base concept is pretty good, but underutilised. Bases need to be bigger and a little more complex instead of being slip in, slip out, the moment you get to the enemy spawn. Especially since you can just repeat it until it blows up with no penalty, as it doesn't really have any way of stopping you from doing so.
