review:
Revised review after completing the game, and getting all achievements.

I am still not recommending this game as is.

HOWEVER. Several complaints I had, had in game solutions built in I had not yet acquired or discovered.

Priorities when starting this game should be to get money to build a Heavy Plane
Recommended build for this IMO is the Damage Control fuselage, Balanced Wings, Extra Filters Pontoon, Workhorse Engine, Quick Repair Propeller, Highlighter Ornament and finally, the remote copter equipment. For dealing with the Submarine boss, use the Torpedo Fuselage.

The heavy plane make virtually everything in this game easier/better. It harvests crops with bombs much, much better, it's guns are far more powerful, and with the fuselage just taking damage makes you money... good money.

Second priority, visit all islands to find the bars, and recruit all of your crew. Once done, do not neglect their pairings/quests. Once you do these quests all characters get a third skill, and eventually replacement of their bad skill with a good one. Some of these skills are VERY valuable.

Third thing to let you know, you will be FORCED to fight the final boss upon achieving 5 star fame.

Mouse flight is not recommended. It over corrects banking and what not massively. I would suggest using a controller or a flight stick.

Now that all of that is out of the way, I think you'll enjoy the game more... what little of it there is. There isn't a ton of content in this game, and once the final boss is done, and character quests finished, that was it. It doesn't take long. That said, I squeezed 43 hours out of a less than 30 dollar game. I think I would have spent much less time in game if I had of figured out the heavy plane benefits earlier on. I spent a lot of time in this game being very frustrated. The game can be slim on hints, and descriptions of many things are not descriptive enough.

Devs seem hard at work to fix bugs(there's many) and improving the game. I hope to change tthis to a thumbs up in the future.

review:
Brew Barons

AI voice acting. And bad writing. It really, really hurts.

It's a cool-ass concept for a game, don't get me wrong. Very pretty, too. In that sort of 'Valkyria Chronicles' way where everything looks pastoral and idyllic and the machines look very... Punk? Hard to describe, really.

That being said, the main core of the game is fairly decent, if a bit lacking at times. You fly around collecting ingredients for your alcohol, then you turn those ingredients into alcohol, then you either stock your own bar, or sell it to the other bars. I do kind of wish each system was more in-depth.

For example, harvesting apples off a tree is just... Shooting the tree, then flying kinda-close to it which vaccuums up the apples. Collecting potatoes involves bombing a potato field, then just flying kinda-close and vaccuuming it up again. Part of me wishes there was a bit more... Danger? Mechanical depth involved? War Thunder plane controls mean flying and controlling your plane is dirt-easy, meaning the core loop is basically impossible to fuck up in any way and is pretty repetitive.

The combat is... Something? I tried it a few times and it felt very... Slow and dull? Maybe I haven't unlocked extra weapons down the line, but the dogfighting wasn't particularly exciting.

The actual map is... A bit too large for how slow your plane is, too. There isn't enough interesting scenery and obstacles to justify how big the map is given just how empty it is and how slow your plane is, and how little there is to do WHILE you're going from island-to-island.

My biggest gripe, though?

The written dialogue and the voice acting is downright atrocious. I could get over a kinda-okay-ish gameplay loop if the game had interesting characters, chatter, dialogue, and potentially voice-acting. Maybe I'm just an old Ace Combat player who thinks every plane game that isn't Ace Combat is shit, but man. If you're going to give me all this downtime and repetitive gameplay where I'm not really doing anything as my plane slowly trundles along to my destination, the least you could do is toss in plenty of chatter between your pilot and copilot, or radio chatter from your plane back to your bar.

What voice-acting that IS in-game has the most stilted dialogue known to man. None of the speech feels natural. Everyone is overly verbose and bland in a way that doesn't make sense. It's like the most boring and uninteresting dialogue known to man, compounded with an AI voiceover that's just completely flat and dull, with the game taking way too many lines to explain something incredibly simple more often than not.

And the tutorial. Man. It's rough. It's opening is good- I like the idea of getting to know your seaplane by taxi-ing it around a canal for a bit, but that's literally the only good part of the tutorial. Everything else is just... Frustratingly slow and has way too much explaining going on for mechanics that are relatively simple.

I'll likely play the game to completion and maybe re-review then, since apparently this game only takes around 20-odd hours to finish in its current state (This estimation from the fact that a player asking for help on the final boss of the game in the Steam forums had 18 hours in it). But man, these first few hours really aren't... Enticing.

Now, this game is one of those 'Amazing idea and concept' but 'Meh executions'. What I mean by this? The whole game idea's amazing, and the fact you're allowed to fight in an old type plane is great--but the gameplay, its performance,  its scope, and the AMMOUNT OF GRIND just doesn't make it a worthwhile purchase. Heck, its two main selling point, the brewing and air fight, are a bunch of let down that just isn't fun. The game felt too slow for a plane game, map too big to traverse that it became boring, and the brewing while fun the first few times it became an annoying and boring drag. It also did not help that running the pub is so basic and not enjoyable that it almost made me wonder why adding it in the first place. 

I have mixed feeling with the plane editor but mostly disappointment. In hindsight it's pretty good, you can change colors of your plane, add banners, etc. etc. But then you have to PAY for for every little things, and it's not cheap either. Why do painting my plane cost so much? Why not just make it free? THEN, I find out not only I have to buy expensive modules for my plane, and you can accidentally miss-clicked and buy a module you don't want with no way to undo it (It autosaved too as far as I know), I need to find parts and PAY AGAIN TO INSTAL THE DAMN THING. I HAD TO BUY IT FROM A CATALOGUE, FIND MY OWN PARTS AND PAY AGAIN TO INSTAL IT. It's one thing if it's cheap, it's not. 

The writing, AI Voice, and other nitpicks aren't that great either. Though I do enjoy when one of the pilot parent kept pestering her by calling while she's co-piloting.

It's a frustating and disappointing experience, which is sad because I WANT this game to be good--I love planes, and to be able to be a pilot with a partner while running a booze business sound awesome. The game just can't live up to its concept. So I cannot in good faith recommend this game.

review:
Mixed thoughts, i love it, but needs balance <3

I think the game is well-made, especially since only two people worked on it. It's really admirable, but I have mixed feelings about the current game balance.

In short: if you're up for flying and sweet graphics, risk a little money. Maybe the game will get much better if just a few things are changed. But for everyone else, don't be disappointed if the game is too demotivating at the beginning. It just needs a bit of fine-tuning! 

I have to rate it negatively for now because, at the moment, it's mostly not fun for beginners.

My toughts about The Brew Barons in long form, I would like to love it, but at the moment, there are too many little things that cloud the big picture.

Starting difficulties:
When you start the game, you already have some starting budget, but that can quickly disappear due to stupid mistakes:

The one-click shop: If you buy something in the upgrade store or just want to look, every click can bankrupt you because there is no query whether you really want to buy the certain upgrade; it is bought immediately. This is not very well implemented.

The Crash of your cash: 
If you crash, you have the relatively slow flight behavior, and then you have a problem if you already have little money because repair costs are too high at the beginning, and you are virtually stuck and can do nothing more except skip 12 hours and hope someone buys something in your bar to get money. Anyway, I haven't found a real solution without restarting the game to solve this.

Flying: 
The flight behavior is a mixture of realistic and arcade; unfortunately, it's not much fun. Visually, it's great, but you can change a lot with a few things in the controls or basic start setting, but unfortunately, not everyone who buys the game at the beginning will want to waste some time on the controls.

Crafting: 
The problem with the crafting, how should I describe it? I thought at first maybe the magic develops more in the crafting than in the flying, which couldn't really convince in the long run, but unfortunately, the bar and the brewing of alcohol are the weakest points in the game at the moment.

The problem is that you might think you've done everything right and maybe farmed all the components for 30 minutes (yes, in this game, everything is collected and harvested by plane, which can sometimes be a bit annoying due to the clunky and sluggish mouse controls, leading to crashes). You mix everything together, and in the end, you get rum or vodka, but the buyer doesn't want it. Maybe you've collected everything with your last money and have no money left for fuel, and you're totally broke. You simply don't feel like investing time in the game anymore because it doesn't reward you.

Even going back to check what's missing while brewing interrupts the brewing process and is seen as bad and annoying from the user's perspective. If I throw something into the pot and then quickly need to check something because I forgot how something was required or similar, I don't want to start over from the beginning. Also, the brewing process should not start automatically at 100 units; that's not so great for the user and is very annoying, at least at the beginning.
I mean the game is called "The Brew Barons," but what's not really fun at the moment is brewing things!

Work or fun:
It doesn't feel good; the game feels more like work than fun. Unfortunately, in a simulation, the game or loot should at least be basic or satisfying, or so many incentives should be created that I can still somehow try it. But right from the start, there are limits placed in the environment (Exploration).

Exploration: 
For example, I want to explore something, but on the next island, I'm already told that I need to upgrade my propeller to harvest. So, you fly for fun and to make new deals, explore aimlessly and want to take something with you right away, but you can't. Money, time, and nerves are wasted because flying takes time. It's just not a good game start.
I think many will be attracted by the great graphics and the many small and loving details, similar to the Porco Rosso anime or perhaps to a target group of people who like to play the Truck Simulator and chill out but with airplanes. Unfortunately, both are disappointed in the current gaming experience.

Controls: 
As mentioned, everything feels very sluggish and realistic, but maybe the default settings can be set up in such a way that you don't have to change the keys and thrust settings forever: Set the thrust to maximum sensitivity, swap CTRL and SHIFT with W and S, and it's a bit clearer and easier because at the beginning, you or quite a few who don't start directly with a gamepad use the mouse and keyboard.

The Positive:
Great graphics, many loving details such as the change of pilots when they get tired or the design of the bar (although there could be more), or the design of your own bottles (it would be nice to be able to view the bottles later, unfortunately, that wasn't possible anywhere). Great approach, as it could attract logisticians, crafters, and airplane and anime enthusiasts, or even explorers.

Conclusion:
But at the moment, it has big problems convincing players from the start because the grind is too demotivating, and at least at the beginning, the effort is too high, and the sense of achievement is too little to sustain in the long run. Perhaps the developers should work on this again to find better balancing that is more motivating and create such details as instant purchases in the shop or better clarity in brewing or better reference points so that recipes succeed and are also bought by customers in the game to simply improve the entry and not demotivate too much.

I hope the developers take action and receive support from you because it's a great idea to fly around, craft, discover, and even face some challenges in combat. Thank you for the great idea.

review:
First off, I gotta say that I appreciate the devs sticking with the tried-and-tested War Thunder control scheme. On top of that, it really has a lovely concept and art style.

AND NOW WE COME TO THE PROBLEMS. I think I'll just address things in the order I noticed them in-game. The plane has insane weight to it. I don't mean it's going to fall out of the sky at any moment, but rather the time it takes after a maneuver for the plane to stop drifting towards the direction it was going towards prior is insanely long. It makes harvesting fields, during which you will do many loops to turn around, extremely tedious, as over the length of three fields, your plane will still be pulling to the side. On top of that, this game features the biplane with the worst roll rate in the history of mankind. It genuinely makes it terrifying when at the end of an Immelmann, the assistant tries to correct your orientation; you will pull to the side massively, and it takes just way too long while you constantly lose altitude. (I speak of manually flying an Immelmann, not using that upgrade for it).

Now to the upgrades. A whole lot of the parts seem situational at best, maybe even just gimmicky. I would have preferred being able to fine-tune the performance of my plane more while being able to balance my cargo capacity more. Instead, I can get pontoons that will economically ruin me or wings that will cause harvesting wheat to damage my plane.

Decorating bottles. God, it really is an adorable detail. You create your own badge for the bottle, select a nice shape and everything. And I thought, great! This will define my products, and then I can produce them, and the bottle will always look like this - it'll be great! Well, sadly, after that editor, you will never see your bottle again. So it's just another gimmick at best to finish the production chain with that. And remaking your recipes from the Products list? That's currently broken. Speaking of broken, let's talk about the UI. From being able to softlock your game from changing the place you want to go to in your building while the fade-out after pressing exit plays, to the alcohol mixing process ending up in some weird unstable states that disable the use of the brewery. Polishing is badly needed.

The core gameplay loop, in my perception, is just way crappier with all these issues. If I wasn't wrestling with my plane while harvesting, and the brewery didn't softlock me about ten times in five hours, I am sure it could be a LOT MORE ENJOYABLE.

But in its current state? Damn. I want to love this game. I want to enjoy my time in it. But the flight model just needs some real tweaks, and the UI needs some polishing (and please fix the producing from the products list). Would I like more upgrades? Definitely. But I think there are way bigger issues than just a lack of content here and there. I wish I could recommend it, but I can't. I hope the devs read this and fix this game up ASAP - because I think this genuinely could be an absolute gem.

review:
It feels like each of the components of this game may have been play tested, but not the game as a whole. Open world games depend on meaningful reasons to explore, which is where Brew Barons is the most lacking. One would assume that collecting new recipes and materials to grow your brewing empire would be the reason to venture out into the world, but you will run out of reasons to brew almost immediately. You can fully stock your bar very quickly and contracts from other bars come in extremely slowly, and often require ingredients which I was unable to find even after exploring most of the map. The game is beautiful and it's clear that a huge amount of effort went into developing the game mechanics, so it's all the more glaring that so little attention was put towards the gameplay itself. 

Biggest suggestions:
- Have the bars send you many more contracts with a wide variety of required ingredients, add other main objectives such as multistage quests that are not dependant on your characters
- Add more world minigames like the sunken wrecks, things for the player to do while moving between main objectives
- Make the range to identify world items and events much larger and keep them on your HUD much longer
- Incorporate combat with the pirates into the tutorial, or provide some sense of what the player can take of for combat
- There is no reason to be able to discover recipes with a single ingredient

Hopefully the devs flesh out the game parts of this game, but the amount of work that needs doing makes me feel that it will be a year or more before Brew Barons is actually in a state where it ticks the minimum requirements for an open world game.

review:
[h1][b]WARNING: The developers have broken Steam's genAI usage disclosure policy by using voice AI and not informing it so.[/b][/h1]

[b]TL;DR:[/b] Lazy UI design, awful writing, inexistant voice acting... not worth your time, let alone money.

Despite being a flight-arcade game, controller support is questionable and wasn't tested. Right stick is literally mouse look instead of being used for controls with an option to toggle free-look. And the right stick sensitivity is so bonkers that even mid-way push is enough to make the screen rotate so fast you get nausea (or might be the excessive bloom, that comes with a SLIDER).

Although "bloom with a slider" being basically a Knight of the Apocalypse on visual design, that part is actually nice. Not breathtaking, since everything blends together without anything distinguishable. But it's serviceable, and fits the game's price. But the UI and UX design is basically non-existent. It's large boxes with small texts, and sub-menus under sub-menus. Nothing is streamlined and everything is obtuse to use. Repairing is a SLIDER, transferring cargo seems like you'll be moving 30 different items at once, so you have huge empty spaces, sliders and buttons for quantities, drag and drop, and so many other things that make you question "why not just have an option to see a list of things to take, and one option to unload the plane?". Maybe later the game will try to be complicated by requesting a long session of "pick this here, pick that there, drop this many yonder, and the rest take back to base" to justify such a bothersome UI.

The writing is bland and boring, and the story is questionable. You get introduced to the city via exposition dump right after hitting New Game, with the pirates being the antagonists who shoot people and sell brew, and you're going to fight the pirates because you are the Brew Barons... who will shoot the pirates and sell brew. Talk about a hostile takeover. Maybe instead of doing a shallow exposition dump on what exists on the archipelago and who are the antagonists, and just explain the gist of what caused the pirates to reign and leave the rest to be discovered later? Have the characters talk to each other during the long no-fly tutorial (that is slow enough to not warrant full attention of the player) that tasks you with taxiing an hydroplane while people outside your hearing range back talk you for moving a wingless plane around with the most bizarres quips, like "are they using the plane as a boat?". But when you finally get the characters talking (besides the awful lack of voice acting since it was done by a genAI), you'll be glad that they aren't the ones delivering the story.
But now you question yourself. The story is badly delivered with the worst writing you've ever seen. And no, I don't think it's an issue of translation. I've seen badly translated games with great stories, and it's easy to discern the good storytelling inside from the translation oddities of a bad translation, and that's fine (more accessibility for a story, and translation can be fixed later at least). But the writing and way the story is presented feels like... someone didn't actually wrote it. It feels like someone prompted ChatGPT to come up with everything and just slapped everything together (being then credited as writer).

The voice of the characters being done by genAI was justified by the developer on the Steam forums as being done like that because "we couldn't afford actors, and when the player is occupied flying, and stopping to read would be difficult, so we had to use genAI". And that is how you tell that the developer didn't understand the problem and doesn't care about deaf people. If you have too much information to deliver during a critical time, delivering by audio doesn't change the fact that it is too much information. If that is a problem, you reduce the amount of information by streamlining it. Don't say "To do a fast turn, you need to roll the plane inwards to the center curve, pitch into the center of the curve, and correct with yaw if you're getting too much height". Say "Remember, Roll and Pitch to turn!", and either later drop that using yaw can correct a turn too. The rest of the details the player will pick by trying.

I don't like being critical of new and small developers (especially a combo of the two). But when everything is put together this lazyly, with this many corners cut, with this little thought put into it... it's gets really hard. And then there is the whole genAI usage disclosure policy violation, and story and dialogues that don't feel like they were written by humans, and that makes it easier to be hard on them. It seems like it didn't take long for genAI to generate people who think they can do anything faster, cheaper and easier, but I was expecting one of the big publishers do that first... not a small one. As a control and automation engineer, seeing a form of automation lowering the quality of the resulting works this much, I can only say that it's predictable and sad. Let alone the exploitation of those who didn't agree to be part of these genAI databanks, seeing how the users of the tech are incapable of judging if what came out of the tools is good... is just sad. If the genAI users are THAT incapable of judging the quality of the results, don't expect the fitting algorithms to move the tools forward. It's only downhill from here.

review:
Got through essentially the entire first area;

One of many games in this new era of sloppy 'simulators'.  I will not lie, it is the most polished one (alongside supermarket simulator) on the market today, yet still falls victim to many of the same annoyances and issues that prevent me from fully falling in love and ruin it's playability for me personally.

The car physics is not perfect, but is OK for the purpose of the game. The game world actually has quite good detail for the scope, however it is quite 'dead' and uninteresting (with seemingly only one, randomly generating, wreck to collect at a time). It has a bar with no purpose or ability to socialize with NPCs. Everything interesting happens at the dealership. This is where the majority of the issues lie; the game loop (and complete lack of anything to break out of this boring monotony). There is a vandal (that is only annoying), but this made zero sense (as you're unable to close the security gate to your own dealership at night) so I turned it off.

You will go meet people to haggle over used car prices at their houses, which I think is an interesting concept, but this is quite literally nothing more than a fetch quest with some generic 'haggling' with ZERO randomization (each NPC has the same haggling 'skill'). All of the 'haggling' skill and activity is solely determined by your offer compared to the game's 'value' of the car, and gets incredibly boring and annoying by Week 2.

The bills in the game seemingly aren't tied to anything. The game makes you think they are, but endless testing (days of selling cars/having employees vs. no activity) seems to indicate the game just generates random values within a range based on your dealership upgrades/workers/day for all bills (not explicitly tied to employees). When combined with the generic, uninspiring task-based storyline in-game (seems directly lifted from other simulators) forcing you to progress in these upgrades, you will face a growing financial burden with almost zero benefit. 

You still have to give workers individual orders (you can't just drive a car into the body shop and they automatically start, which would actually be worthwhile), and micromanage every aspect of the (growing and increasingly unmanageable) dealership, while reaping less profit over time. If I deal with an increasing amount of stress in a management game, I expect a higher level of return, which simply isn't the case in this game (although an attempt is made through the weird car pricing formulas and model mixes/unlocks as you level up, but this is a nonfunctional solution in my experience).

For the sake of the length of this review; I'm not going into detail about the lackluster mechanics and repair loop of this game either. If you are BIG into cars and realism, steer clear of this game as it very much aims for simplicity over realism. I'll just say, after replacing ~50 batteries I stopped bothering. If you are more into the mechanical elements; Car Mechanic Simulator is leaps and bounds closer (this game assumes every single car uses the same type of engine, wheels, battery, fuses, etc. which PISSES me off).

I believe the devs HAVE offered the option for a 'sandbox' gameplay where you can turn aspects of the normal gameplay off and simply repair cars, but this mode only possesses the boring repetive repair and hagging loops and offers even less in terms of long-term entertainment. This is not a functional solution to the story criticisms IMHO, and I would prefer adjustments (or even different story 'modes' if the dev wants to keep the current implementation).

All of this creates an incredibly unsatisfying and annoying core gameplay. I don't know if it's due to game engine limitations (various assets thrown together in unity) or rushing this into a release before actual testing of the game loop itself. Considering all the other borderline AI slop simulators that the dev's are tied to, and the DLC coming out; I have zero faith the core issues of this game will be reformed. 

If you buy it though, make sure to enjoy the multiple ads for other games the dev has worked on within this. Probably the most interesting and redeeming part of this game /s

review:
I will recommend this game based on the gameplay, but I cannot recommend this game for its engine/camera work.

The progression arc is interesting and fun.  Plays like a lot of other "simulator" games and the economy flows/works well.  

However, the use of lumen and Unreal 5 seems to be relatively poor in optimization.  Without DLSS, it suffers from the same "flickering" problem prevalent in other games using UE5's rendering systems.  But moreso than that is the jarring camera angle/work.

It's most noticeable when doing body work when the camera suddenly stops when you click to sand/putty/etc anything.  The sudden stop, for some reason, causes a bit of motion sickness.  I'm not sure what it is, but for me I just couldn't manage it without feeling some amount of nausea.

If the tools simply followed the center cursor as an anchor and allowed us to turn the camera like with all of the other non-body-work tools, it would be drastically improved.

Also there seems to be a significant amount of stutter/jitter that happens as things render in at distance, even with a higher end PC like mine.  if it were able to be better optimized, this game would get high marks from me, but currently I can't seem to weather playing it for more than an hour at a time.

Even still, someone without my boomer issues would likely enjoy this for what it offers.

review:
Car Dealer Simulator looks gorgeous and starts strong: the one‑man, used‑car hustle feels right and the early restoration loop makes sense. But the game quickly funnels you down a single path and the late game turns hollow. Selling is trivial—lots clear in seconds even above market—and there’s no real demand, negotiation, or sales floor energy. Staff are static and micro‑managed, with teleporting behaviors and no actual salespeople, while customers pop in and out without a buying journey. The experience tilts oddly toward tow‑truck logistics, culminating in the seven‑vehicle hauler as the marquee upgrade instead of land, showrooms, or operational depth—so you never truly feel like you’re managing a dealership.

What’s missing are the pillars of the business: building placement and lot planning; trade‑ins with appraisal/reconditioning; financing and F&I; new‑vehicle ordering delivered to the lot (lower margins, higher volume for late‑game pacing); accessories and service/parts; and role‑based staff with skills in sales, finance, and tech work. Layer in market conditions and customer intent (shoppers seeking specific vehicles), price elasticity, and inventory that doesn’t evaporate instantly, and the sim could blossom. As it stands, it’s a beautiful shell that misses the mark on dealership management.

review:
Im absolutely gutted to write a bad review for this game, because it has the world of potential under its feet. I thought it was an early access title, then realised it wasn't and I was playing a final product (Albeit with updates incoming but not the point).

First, why its SO GOOD:

- Addictive.
- Finding a bargain and making money gib dopamine
- Felt like genuine progression for the first few levels with huge progression on the horizon....

....But its at a few levels in you realise, that what you have been doing, is pretty much it for the entire game. Buy a car, do it up (Or have one of your mechanics do it), sell it for profit. Rinse, repeat. There isn't a game beyond a certain point.

Also - Fuel Station at home? a 100+ car park? Who the heck needed those? You sell cars the same day you put them on sale, and you are individually responsible for moving them around. Imagine if you had 100 cars to run around to each and every station!?

You can buy a Tow Truck and its upgrade for $60k which makes picking up cars only 10% easier as you can carry two, but you can't pickup two large ones, so negates the point completely. Furthermore, you can tow large vehicles with the base standard trailer hitch you get.

I found car sales pricing to be extremely patchy. I would buy one "Porsche" and make it perfect, sell for £60k, the next for £80k, even though the mileage and year were extremely similar. Sometimes I would get random beaters that fetched in immense cash, and others that weren't worth the hassle, but figuring it out was actually very difficult.

Automation would be nice here - Create a production line eventually where you can oversee it, what comes in (Quality vs Quantity), oversee pricing vs competition and the market, etc.

I really wish the devs the best because this is a cracking effort, but getting to this point in just a short few days has left me gutted.

review:
This is another of those games that deserves a 'Mixed' review, rather than a positive or negative. It's a game that whilst fun at first, does quickly fall into the mundane repetitiveness that many of these "Simulator" type games seem to follow.
Lets go through what the game does well first;
- Fun game play and basic to understand
- Graphics are okay, standard for this type of generic 'simulator' titled game
- Consistent updates from the dev's and they are adding new content into the game as per the dev log's. 
- Is quite a fun game for the first 10 hours or so, this does wear down in line with the repetitiveness of the game play but is interesting to start
- Game concept is fun, I like the idea of being able to run my own car dealership and build on that existing foundation to a bigger company
- The amount of jobs you can do is quite a nice variety (I.E. Mechanical, bodywork, washing etc.) this is quite a nice concept which at first does keep you quite busy in the game.

Now, the not so good;
- The game play, whilst interesting at first, does become incredibly tedious with the player having to repeat the same 4/5 jobs for each car. Washing cars becomes tedious fast as there is no variety to the amount of dirt / rust / damage to individual vehicles, with most of them having a preset amount of both which every car follows.
- Car selection is very limited and basic, with the core element of the game revolving around the buying and selling of cars, shouldn't this be a high priority for variety?
- Working on the cars is very primitive and lacks detail. Whilst this isn't the core element of the game, if they are implementing this as the main route to make more profit on your vehicles, shouldn't this be more interactive rather than just the same repetitive part disassembly routine
- Its too easy. There are no mistakes to be made, selling dodgy cars doesn't have any effect on your dealerships reputation, and its impossible to lose money on a car unless you purposely sell it cheap. Doesn't really give the game much depth in terms of difficulty and makes the act of making profit on cars seem less rewarding.
- Lack of dealership upgrades cosmetically. Whilst I understand this game is all about being the Tom Skinner of car sales, why does it have to look quite so shit? Can't we at least spend our "Hard earned" cash on making the place look a little nicer. The whole thing just feels unfinished and a bit rough because of it, and really limits the progression for the player.
- Inventory size. Why is my inventory so small that I can only hold a very limited amount of parts at one time. When you are consistently repairing cars you do have a lot of junk parts build up in your inventory, which quickly becomes a pain when buying / selling additional parts.
- Lack of story line / progression. Whilst the game does try to implement a feeling of a story line into the game, it is incredibly weak and menial, and after level 7 reputation is reached, really means sweet FA in the long run. This makes it quite hard to see a progressive element in continuing to buy / sell cars, and removes any sense of objective from the game.
- There's something about this game that just feels very unfinished. I'm not sure if its the total lack of depth / progression / detail in the game, but it just doesn't feel like a well made game. It is very in-line with the current trend of releasing simulator titles with bog standard assets and low grade production quality, whilst the game is fun to play, it just doesn't stand alone in the simulator category as one of the better games.

Conclusion;
Overall, I'd give this game a "Meh", its not good, its not bad, it's just "Meh". Is it worth the £17.99 in the steam store? Absolutely not. Should you give it a go if its on sale for -50%? Yes. But at this price, and this lack of depth / detail, its really not a game I can recommend. If you are looking for a game that has a far deeper mechanical / sales / progressive element to it, go for car mechanic simulator 21', its a much better game at a much fairer price. Whilst I look forward to the future updates to the game and seeing what the dev's can add, for now my opinion would be not to buy Car dealer simulator until the glaring issues with the games have been addressed.

review:
I don't usually, if ever, review games, but this one has inspired me to. I have only played about 14 hours so far, but I think that's enough to have an educated opinion. I will update if needed as I play more as I haven't unlocked many of the end game mechanics and my opinion may change.

Summary: 3/10
Overall I think the concept is great, but it's not fully fleshed out and leaves a lot on the table. Everything about the game seems half-baked and rushed. There are strange design choices all over the place and the game mechanics are super shallow. A decent time-killer, but it lacks the depth of a polished game that you will play again and again. Leaves a 'what could have been' taste in my mouth after playing, and honestly feels more like an early-access title, not a full game. 

I do enjoy the minigames even though they lack depth, and the mechanic/repairing aspect is pretty good (not Car Mechanic Simulator good obv). The graphics are decent, but the game seems un-optimized no matter what settings I use. The map is relatively detailed but very small. The game has poor sound effects and and even worse driving physics. The a.i. traffic is ok and the world has a good amount of (too many?) npc's walking around. The game has a boring, awkward and repetitive bargaining minigame, with little depth to the financial simulation. The business aspect of the game is way too easy, with seemingly no risk of going out of business. Some variety in design would do this game a lot of good. It seems like more time was spent designing the npc's than designing the cars themselves. The car models are nice, but not enough variety in trim/model and not enough vehicles. It really just leaves me wanting more.

That said, I have some questions for the devs....
Shouldn't there be more risk/reward in rolling back the odometer? What if I don't want to be a sleazy car dealer and prefer an honorable existence? My reputation should take a hit if I rip people off. 
Shouldn't there be some risk/reward when fixing bodywork? Why is body damage only rust damage, and always in the same places? No crash damage whether existing or player made? No broken windows/windscreens, body panels or electronics? Car interiors play no role whatsoever? 
Why do we not have more information on car prices (such as average selling price, average listed price etc) to better inform buying decisions? 
Why so few vehicles (not a priority for a car selling game?)? 
Shouldn't cars get dirty sitting around? Wouldn't they need to be washed and waxed again after body work? How about some weather? Hail/weather damage? Window cleaning/detailing? Wheel cleaning/detailing? 
Shouldn't I be able to make a bad buying decision? Shouldn't I be rewarded for taking better pictures? Nice license plates, shouldn't I be able to customize them? Do tires exist? Rims? Accessories? Fluids? Can't we get some different trim levels to vehicles? 
Why do people line up to buy so easily? Shouldn't dead inventory be more of a worry?
Why can't I customize the appearance of my shop/character? 
What's the point of having grab points for gas nozzles and pressure sprayers if I can just access them from the hot menu?
Why can't I buff the wax before polishing? The oscillating sander from the bodywork minigame could provide that, and it's already in the game. Just lazy. It would have been SO MUCH FUN to buff the wax and watch the shininess increase, fr. 
Why do the body work/washing minigames autocomplete at a certain completion %? Wouldn't it be more interesting to have it be more challenging in some way, like you can miss spots and not get 100% so easily? 
No car auctions? Trade-ins? Financing and credit checks?
Shouldn't I be able to buy a new car for myself to use? Or at least have a reference as to the new car prices?
Why can't I change the color of vehicles? 
Wouldn't a working odometer on the dash have added some immersion?
Have the devs ever owned/bought/sold a car? (lol)

Then, I notice (in game, no less) that the developer is releasing a few more games in the near future that are seemingly just re-using assets to make more car-themed games, that in reality, could (or should) have just been DLC for this game. Garage Monkeys could have just made a game called 'Car Life' and put all the game mechanics in... from their upcoming Car Cleaner Sim, Car Rental Sim and Car Crime Sim (even Gas Station Sim). I'm guessing that this is some kind of business decision, but it comes off as a cash grab strat and is unappealing. Even an ATS strategy for DLC/content would be better.
Car culture isn't easily replicated if the developers aren't passionate about it, and I suspect that these devs are not 'car people'.. GTA VI will most likely have better vehicle minigames and mechanics. Perhaps all of this was by design, and they were simply aiming for a very casual game, but I can't help but think of what could have been.... 

I wanted to LOVE this game, but I only like it as a friend, and only on sale. 
I would actually recommend Car Mechanic Sim instead, as it's the same buying/selling refurbishing cars without some of the minigames and is a more complete game in general, and it has actual car brands and accurate designs and mechanical aspects, with better driving physics (barely) and mods to boot. CMS just needs a car wash and an inflatable flailing arm man at this point.

Like with so many of these $20 titles, with a little more work and care it could have been a smash hit for $35-$40 and people would have bought it in droves. Too bad, so sad. 
Maybe I should get into game development.

review:
The game starts off promising, but it quickly turns into an exhausting grind with no real sense of progression.

Even after hiring employees, you're still doing 90% of the work yourself. Their presence barely improves efficiency — for example, to wash a car, you still have to drive it to the wash bay, assign the employee, and then wait 2–3 real-time minutes for them to finish. The same goes for every step of the process: you must meet with the seller, buy the car, personally drive it to the mechanic (who only works if you already have the needed parts), then wait another 3 minutes for repairs. Then it's off to the body shop for another 3-minute rust removal and repaint job, followed by the car wash again, then the photo booth, and finally to the sales area. After all that, you still need to go into the office and manually register the car for sale.

None of this can be automated or delegated, and every single vehicle goes through this same drawn-out routine. Meanwhile, once the store is open, you can sell 5 cars in under 5 minutes — meaning your lot is constantly empty because prepping even one car is such a time sink.

This game feels like busywork disguised as simulation. There's no real management here — just repetitive manual labor, stretched out by timers. It’s more tedious than fun.

If you’re like me and enjoy simulator games, trust me — there are better options out there.

review:
At first glance, this game seems promising. A fun and chill car-flipping simulator: buy a rusty wreck, fix it up, repaint it, sell it. Simple, right?

Wrong. Reality hits hard, fast, and painfully.

You start with your first car in a rotted-out garage. The task? “Paint the restored parts of the car body.” Fine. I walk around the entire car, repair and paint everything. Triple-check every panel. And still — the game won’t let you proceed. Why? Because somewhere, a tiny, microscopic section of a part is “not painted” according to the game.

Even with the scanner tool, it’s nearly impossible to find. Sometimes the prompt appears but pressing it does nothing. Sometimes there’s no prompt at all. You stand there staring at a fender or a rocker panel corner from every possible angle like a desperate detective — and nothing happens.

At that point, you realize it’s not your fault. The game is actively working against you. And this isn’t a minor bug. It’s a hard stop that kills all progress. You can’t skip it, override it, or move on. You’re stuck because the game refuses to register a millimeter of paint.

This completely kills any motivation to play. Instead of enjoying the process, you end up stuck in a loop of pixel-hunting frustration. And this happens during the very first task of the game. What’s waiting later?

Summary:
	•	Concept: Great.
	•	Execution: Awful.
	•	User experience: Infuriating.
	•	Bug handling: Nonexistent.
	•	First 30 minutes: More annoying than fun.

Until this is fixed, I can’t recommend this game — not even for free. It’s not worth your time or nerves. I came to enjoy flipping cars. Instead, the game flipped me off.

review:
The game is fun while it lasts, then falls off a cliff. The progression system is unfulfilling as there is no real story or incentive to continue the game past level 10. And no, it does not take long to reach level 10. The map is small, un-interactive, and displays roadblocks which could lead a player to believe that sections of the map would be unlocked with progress, but as of right now they're just closed off. 

The driving physics are wonky, but forgivable. Some of the animations for vehicle repair and transport are visually unappealing and tedious. Overall, it is a well-made game that fulfills a good portion of the excitement us sim players feel at the prospect of engaging in some curious endeavor like owning a car dealership. However, the experience ends way too soon and isn't engaging enough. 

I'd love to see more diverse geography, vehicle selection, and gameplay in the future. Being limited to one vehicle with the capacity to tow 2 vehicles max becomes very annoying once you build up significant amounts of cash. You might want to buy many vehicles and perhaps load them on a car hauler with higher capacity, but this unfortunately does not exist in the game. Perhaps that could be a task designated to an employee in the future. Also, there is no way to spend cash for your character such as acquiring a house, a personal vehicle or starting up additional dealerships and buying out competition. So there really isn't much incentive to progress in that regard either. I'm really hoping to see enhancements to progression in patches, DLC, sequels, etc. At that point, I could definitely see myself engaging more here.

UPD. Okay, I admit, some work has been done since the initial review time. There are less bugs than before, true. However, the characters still sound and behave like being struck with a terminal case of cerebral illness. The menus and UI are still inconsistent. And, on top of that, instead of adding more cars to this car dealer game, the dev team concentrates on... the figurines feature!
No new cars, nope, nope. They definitely won't be spoiling the fun of selling the same dozen vehicles over and over again. Figurines for everyone! 

This is a perfect... tech demo. I was able to complete it in less than 20 hours, which for such kind of game is too fast. It became kinda boring after the first 10 hours. 

The game shows a great potential and is fun to play, but right now there is a lot of issues:
- strange game economy. Basically, the higher you pay initially for the car you purchase, the higher profit you will yield. The only thing affecting the initial car price seems to be the year of manufacturing. Which isn't totally illogical, but... still feels off somehow.
- even if the car you purchase is fresh and costs a fortune, its mechanical state will be awful (you will still have to replace almost every damn part). No exceptions.
- the game has a very small variety of cars. In such a game, you'd expect to see 10 times more different car models and series
- a lot of small quirks and issues that show too openly that there is a lot to fix and add. Missing character animations, very strange dialogues (most of the characters talk and behave like they are mental).

This game may become absolutely great. Sometime later. Maybe.

Now that I have played over 24 hours and reached Reputation 10, which feels like "the end," I wanted to write this review.

I played the demo of this game about a month before release, and it made me very excited for the full version. I couldn't wait for the opportunity to expand my dealership, "Freakin' Nice Cars." This game is very addictive, but it's not actually good. This seems to be a pattern for many Simulator games these days: there is a repetitive pattern that gives you just enough dopamine that you get carried away in the cycle, but there is not actually any creativity or diversity in the gameplay. Before you know it, you're deeply immersed in the game but you're not really having any fun. I kept waiting for something to happen, it's almost like an idle game, but the payoff never comes. In fact, I don't think the barricaded sections of the map ever opened up. So you're stuck in this blighted town, buying and fixing lemons for hours and hours.

Maybe there's updates planned for this game, but as it stands I would not recommend anyone follow in my footsteps.

review:
TLDR: I really wish they had a "mixed review" button. This game has so much missed potential I wanna give it a thumbs up but I can't.

Sound: overall the driving sounds are "good enough" but nothing spectacular. The voice overs for the NPCs during haggling is comically bad though the voice for the story guy is pretty good. Then there is the music. There are 4 radio stations two being reggae and urban which are out of my scope to review. The other two fall somewhere between rock and country and frankly are much better than you would expect from a game like this, if you played Road 96 and liked that sound track you will be very happy with this one.

Driving: I wanna be nice here but this is just bad. ALL the cars handle the same and that handling is just barely serviceable. You can stay on the road but there is only a faint feeling of being in control the cars seem to glide across the road more than they drive and the slightest bump will send you flying.

Graphics: The graphics are a bit campy but overall i like the feel. However, this game needs some optimization. According to steam my PC is in the top 15% and this game still runs like I'm on a potato. It's laggy and drops frames constantly. OH, an when it autosaves (which seems like every 2 minutes) it completely freezes for 1.5-2 seconds

Game play: the messed up part is there are really 2 different game play loops to this game.

You buy cars off of a website and sell them through the dealership and there is a haggling minigame at both ends. Overall they did a good job with the haggling system but it doesn't take very long to figure out how to min/max the crap out of it. I really don't think they can fix the min/max problem because if they change stuff you will just figure it out again. I'm not complaining, I actually enjoy this mechanic, I'm just stating facts.

Now that you have the car:

There is a mini game where you can do body work grinding rust away, applying body filler, sanding the filler, and painting the car. The first 3 steps are pretty repetitive and all feel pretty much the same, but at least an early upgrade makes them go pretty quick. Painting the car is one of my favorite things to do in the game. There is just something about the way the paint is applied that I find very satisfying. 

The car wash minigame is basically playing Pressure Wash Simulator FOUR TIMES ON EVERY CAR!!! At first you will only be able to soap and rinse the car and much like Pressure Wash Simulator you gotta take a bit of time to get in the small corners and hose stuff down for a second on rinse. After a while you can upgrad to add wax and polish which I find almost as satisfying as painting a car especially when you use the X key to highlight the car something about the wax animation is just on point.

Car repair: This is basically a dumbed down version of Car Mechanic Simulator. I kinda like that it's dumbed down a bit, if I wanted more detail I would play that game instead. Early on you are kind of a hack who can only tape over holes in the exhaust, but as the game progresses you can do more. One of the complaints you will hear about this game is that there aren't power tools (at time of writing anyways) and you have to click the mouse drag it up/down then reset and repeat a time or three. I get some people would like to click and buzz bolts loose but I actually think this mechanic gives the game some charm. My only real complaint about this part of the game is that ALL the cars are exactly the same at least Car Mechanic Simulator had a few variations on certain parts.

The early game play loop is buy a car, repair/wash, and sell and feels quite rewarding. You will, however, hit the max level of 10 in 15-20 hours and be able to hire employees to do the work for you if you wish. This is where the second game play loop comes in. Once you start hiring employees the game becomes a time management game and there is no way you can do everything. You become a glorified valet. You have to take a car to the mechanic tell them each item you want fixed. When they are finished you have to drive it over to paint and body and tell them to work on it. NO, you don't just drop it off and they do their thing you gotta tell them to get to work on every car. Finally, you take it to the wash bay and like paint/body you have to tell them to get to work. Throw in dealing with customers and trying to fill the parts recycling bin and it becomes a complete mad house during the day and at night you still have to go buy cars for tomorrow. You are insanely busy and no longer have time to do the rewarding things of building cars that you enjoyed early game. I honestly like to start over more than playing the end game stuff.

Another complaint you will hear is that there isn't enough variety of cars. I think there are 13 car models. Though that isn't a huge number it's enough to give some illusion of variety and really I don't see what having 50+ car models would add to the game at this point.

Brand-specific or generation-specific components

🎯 Recommended | 15.2 hrs played
⭐ "The grind is real—but so are the upgrades."

If you liked Gas Station Simulator, this one’s a no-brainer. It’s built by the same devs and delivers a similarly satisfying loop of “buy low, sell high, upgrade relentlessly.”

You start off flipping basic rides, but the real hook is in upgrading your garage and offices—unlocking new tools and tiers that make the whole thing click. It's a slow burn at times (XP gain especially feels front-loaded then sluggish), but when that next upgrade hits, the dopamine hits harder.

The realism isn't the point here, and honestly? That's fine. It’s not a car dealership sim for purists—it’s a chill, low-stress progression game with just enough strategy to keep you hooked. You can toss on a movie, click through some deals, and let the hours melt.

Pros:
✔ Addictive upgrade loop
Balanced economy
No major bugs so far
UI is clean and intuitive

Cons:
XP progression curve could use tuning
Needs a "double-click to hold" option for accessibility
The "thug" mechanic needs a toggle

If you enjoy laid-back tycoon games with a satisfying sense of progression, this is well worth full price. If it’s on sale, it's an absolute steal and you would be silly to miss out on it.

EDIT: So I am changing my review to a thumbs down. The base game is still decent, but the fact that they would charge $18 for DLC that should absolutely be part of the base game is simply ridiculous and I cannot support it in any way.

review:
I Survived 20 Hours in This Digital Dumpster Fire

Car Dealer Simulator — a game so unforgettable, I forgot it while playing it.

Let me start by saying this: I finished *literally all the content* in 12 hours. If you’re looking for a quick weekend game before you slip into existential despair, this might be it. And hey, if you’re a masochist who loves mindless grinding, you can pad that up to 15–20 hours to get all the achievements!

Let’s talk *features*. There’s a bar. That’s right — a fully modeled, glorious bar. But can you order a drink? Nope. Not even a sad pixelated soda. So it’s basically a decorative hostage situation.

Cars? Oh yes, we have cars! A whole whopping *7 or 8* different kinds — because who needs variety when you've got... mediocrity. The houses? They look like someone said, “Let’s model an entire town after abandoned horror movie sets!” Every building is a Pinterest board of decay.

Now the NPCs? *Chef’s kiss.* They walk through cars like they’re ghosts. Clipping through your ride like it’s not even there. And the voice lines? About five of them, all shouted at max volume on a loop like a broken animatronic in a haunted Chuck E. Cheese. Immersion? No, just repetition.

And the character models? I'm convinced the devs cloned one guy and just slapped different shirts on him. Sometimes you'll see triplets — or entire family reunions — chilling on your lot like it’s a glitchy Thanksgiving.

Final verdict: Save your money. This game feels like it escaped the alpha stage in the dead of night and snuck onto the full release page wearing sunglasses and a fake mustache. Early access? It needed early access, beta testing, and probably an exorcism.

⭐ 1 out of 5 — and that one star is for the sheer comedic value of watching three identical dudes phase through my sedan.

Missing end game mechanics. Trying to stock your max level dealership with one tow truck is extremely tedious. Many of the mechanics of the game become tedious but there is automation like hiring employees. Getting new cars, that all on you. Plus you have to load every car manually. 

Inventory management is a nightmare. You cannot filter anything. During the end game I found myself digging through dozens of rotors trying to find the good quality ones over all the dead ones. Just have to click one at a time. 

The tow truck upgrade isn't much of an upgrade as now you have to get out to load cars but it is easier to drive loaded with better gas than the pickup. Cars missing a non critical components like a tail pipe are non driveable. All the "damage" that vehicles have is purely a numbers game, it has no impact on the driving of the vehicles. Having to use the computer for everything is a huge pain when you have to move cars and activate employees to work.

review:
It's a no from me, and I'll tell you why.

Short answer, it's clearly not a finished product.

Long(!) answer;

This game needs a lot of work, both in content and bug fixing.

It starts off entertaining, but everything you do becomes a chore real quick.

Buying cars:
You buy cars by going to the pc in your office, you cannot do this from your tablet (weird design choice if you ask me).
You then go to the seller and haggle for it. Most of the time you can almost cut the price down to half of the asking price.
When you've purchased the vehicle, you get back in your car, you then toggle your towdolly's extenders by pressing X or else you cannot put the car on it. Very necessary "realism" in a game. You then drive back to the dealer with the newly purchased vehicle.

Washing your car: 
You want to have your cars nicely presented to your customers so obviously you want to wash your car.
Well, I hope you enjoy doing that cause there's 2 steps (later even 4), to do so. 
First you apply a layer of foam to the whole car by holding the sprayer and walking around you car.
When that's done you can water it down by switching to the water and hose all the foam off.
After your first carwash upgrade it'll add wax and polish to the mix.
Have fun running another 2 rounds around your car while applying those.
This was fun for the first time but the second time it already became annoying.

Fixing your car:
From the start you can replace some parts and others you need to upgrade the workshop for.
First off, the dismantling of parts is very tedious. Takes about 1 minute for the harder parts while clicking and waving your mouse. Another weird design option, since Car Mechanic Simulator already showed the perfect way how this could be done.
But hey, they can't give you an electric wrench from the start now can they? Those are very expensive...
Another weird mini-game is taping up your catalytic converter, which also becomes not fun to do very fast.

Getting rid of the rust:
Here we go again with having 4 different tools to do the exact same thing with 4 times in a row.
First you use the sandpaper to get rid of the rust on your car, this can take up to 2 minutes depending on the amount of rust.
Then you take the spatula to spread some putty or something on all the places you just sandpapered. 
I hope you like sandpapering, cause you can now do it again on all the places you put the putty on.
And lastly you have to spraypaint all the spaces you worked on again. 
Maybe you've got a clue on how fast this is gonna feel like a second job instead of a casual game.

Selling cars:
Now your car is ready to be sold. 
But wait, first we need to take some pictures.
Open the tablet, select camera, take pictures, every menu in the game is exited by right clicking your mouse, but not this one. On this one we press escape and it brings us back to the main tablet screen so you'll have to click it twice. 
(I don't know who designed this but please stop taking drugs.)
You then go to the office again (cause the tablet is a cheap model and can't handle a website) and select the car and pictures and type in an amount you want to sell it for.
Now you wait for customers and the haggle mini-game starts again, trying to get as much money as you can.

That's a full cycle from buying to selling a vehicle.
80% of the time spent on this cycle is everything but buying and selling the cars. 
Which makes me wonder why they named it "Car Dealer Simulator", cause actually buying and selling cars is what you'll be doing the least and feels like a side hustle.

There's also an inventory cause you have to buy parts to replace on your vehicles. 
This has to be done physically at the shop and you inventory can't hold all items that fit on a vehicle at once. 
So you have to buy some, bring those to your warehouse and go back to buy more. 
Your car doesn't have inventory space, the truck's loading area is just for show.
The warehouse is in a completely different building than anything else so if you need something you'll have to run over to grab it.

You'll reach a point where you can hire workers to do the work for you, which will take some time. 
But even then it's still a damn slog.
Workers will not pick a car by themselves, you have to drive a car to their station and then talk to the worker to make him go to work.
They'll also not take the car out when they're done, so when you come back with a new car, you'll have to get out of the car, get in the car that just got washed, drive that car to the station where the rust will be cleaned off, but there's already a car there, so you have get out of this car, no get in the car that the rust got removed from, drive that out of there. Get back in the car that just got washed and drive it into the rust cleaning station, get back in the car you want to have washed and drive it into the carwash.
Did I also mention that you have to talk to the workers twice? Cause yes, they feel the need to tell you that the previous car is done before you can tell them to work on the next.

Here's some other reasons why I feel this game shouldn't have been released yet;
Driving feels absolutely unresponsive or over responsive. You either can't take a turn or you'll be doing a 360.
The levelling is very slow. I had amassed over 200k before I was able to upgrade my next station.

Positives:

The repair and bodywork mechanics are different from what you might have seen before, for the first few repairs it is interesting.

Teal Deer- I found the game to be more shallow and repetitive then many games in the simulator genre. It also felt more like an early access game especially at the $20 price point. Loading times can feel like the game froze at times, and the mouse acceleration feels way too high. If I keep the game I will update my review as it gets updates as it has only been out a couple of days at this point.

I am really on the fence about this game. First if you are planning on picking it up and using the 2 hours to see if you like it that isn't going to work. The tutorial explains mechanics that while not difficult won't be intuitive so I don't recommend just skipping what it is specifically asking you to do especially since you are on tracks until those specific tasks are finished. 90 minutes in and I have picked up and sold 2 cars. I can see this tutorial being like Skyrim where on multiple playthroughs you just want to skip it or speedrun it. But it is good for walking you through what you will need to do. That said you should take advantage of the demo or YouTube to see if it is something you're interested in.

I am leaning towards the no on a recommendation because at $20 for a fully released non-early access game there are some some things that need to be optimized, and the beginning of the game feels really shallow. With 2 cars I have unlocked car washes (soap up and rinse off), scrape off rust, apply putty, sand down putty, and paint. They all have the same mechanics. Use specific tool from radial menu. Press X to scan car and highlight everywhere you need to use the tool (60-100% of the car so far). Use the mouse to slowly go over every inch of the highlighted area. Then switch tool and do the same. That is 6 mechanics that mostly makes you go over all of the car the exact same way. Next there is the use the magic scanner. See what is in red and decide if you want to "repair it". That involved choosing a specific part spraying it with a magic juice that suddenly made a giant hole appear and applying tape to it. The spraying part is the exact same as all the other mechanics previously described!

I am someone who enjoyed house flippers, Spray Wash Simulator and car mechanics simulator. This feels more shallow then all of those

review:
In its current state, I find it difficult to recommend this game. While the concept is engaging and the overall gameplay is enjoyable, several issues detract from the experience:

· Sound Design: The sounds are monotonous, particularly the engine noises, which lack variety and make all cars sound identical. Also the NPC noises get annoying quickly.
· Sale Negotiations: The negotiation process with NPCs is repetitive. NPCs always react the same way and are overly knowledgeable about the value of cars. Once you understand the system, it quickly becomes boring. Introducing some randomness could improve this aspect.
· Part Repairs: Fixing worn-down parts, especially at the beginning, feels like a waste of time and money. While it's realistic that you wouldn't recoup the money spent, it is unsatisfying. Focusing on cosmetics seems to be a more viable strategy.
· Car Physics: The car physics are lacking. Although it's realistic that steering becomes difficult at high speeds, the game fails to convey a sense of speed. Driving at 100 km/h feels barely different from driving at 50 km/h. Additionally, driving over curbs often causes the car to jump unrealistically.
· Random Events: The game lacks random events, making it feel repetitive quickly.
· Open World: The open world generally feels a bit boring and lifeless.
· Filter System: A better filter system when searching for potential cars would be beneficial. For example, an option to show only cars with poor visual condition would enhance the user experience. Or sorting them by price ascending.
· Performance: Performance varies depending on your machine. While it's not terrible, it is far from optimized.

Overall, I would suggest waiting for some fixes and updates before diving into this game. With some improvements, it has the potential to be much more enjoyable.

review:
Car Dealer Simulator – More Rust Than Shine + (Reply to Developer @ Bottom)

The first hour had some charm, but the fun wears off fast. The gameplay quickly becomes repetitive and sluggish, with clunky mechanics and poorly designed menus that lack basic quality-of-life features. Working on vehicles feels like a chore rather than a rewarding experience.

The haggling system is particularly grating—repetitive, unbalanced, and ultimately not enjoyable. After four hours, I found myself flipping the same handful of cars repeatedly with no real sense of progress. Investing time in repairing vehicles feels pointless; it's faster and more efficient to do the bare minimum—rip the trade, remove the rust, and flip. Anything more just slows you down with no real payoff.

I wasn’t expecting a masterpiece, but this is the first game in a long time that managed to bore me stiff within an hour. There’s potential here, but in its current state, Car Dealer Simulator is more frustrating than fun.

-------------

Reply to developer on my review:

Thank you for the thoughtful response.

I gave the game a fair shot—8 hours of playtime—and ultimately found it lacking in depth and engagement. The core gameplay loop feels stagnant: buy a car from someone down the street, clean it, maybe make some light repairs, and sell it to the next person who walks up. That’s essentially the entire game.

Making meaningful repairs takes too long relative to the small profit increase, and the repair menus are clunky and not intuitive or satisfying to use. Because the process is so time-consuming, it feels like you're only ever working on or selling one car at a time, which kills momentum. Even when you unlock employees, it doesn’t add real depth—you're just delegating the same shallow tasks, which leaves the player with even less to do.

Progression is also painfully slow. While increasing the reputation multiplier might speed things up, doing so only reveals how little content is actually there once you reach higher levels. The negotiation system, while not inherently broken, is overly simplistic: go up or down 33%, adjust by $1 for a few turns, and either strike a deal or walk away. There's no real nuance or strategy involved.

I think the game has solid bones—it looks good, and the concept has potential—but right now it’s more of a car wash and basic negotiation simulator with poor driving physics. It misses out on a lot of what makes the real-life dealership business exciting: auctions, trade-ins, financing, customer management, seasonal trends, and the unpredictability of the used car market, service center, and new car franchise dealership with a manufacturer. There’s so much more that could be done here.

In short, I wish I had spent my money elsewhere. I really hope future updates bring in more variety, strategy, and engaging mechanics, because there’s a solid foundation here—but it currently feels empty and repetitive.

review:
[h1] Release day not recommended. Significantly worse than the demo, with multiple softlock problems, a drastic graphics downgrade, and absurd control problems. [/h1]

When you buy a game blind, you're taking your chances. Maybe it'll be good, maybe it won't. You have no way to know because you haven't played it yet. But when you play a demo for a game, you like to believe you have a decent idea of what the finished product is going to be like. Or so you hope.
Having played the demo, I had my reservations about the full game. But my concerns were with how the additional content would be implemented, not the core structure of the game. That's why I did something I almost never do and bought this game on release day.
Wishing I hadn't.

[h2]Some positives[/h2]
There are some praiseworthy elements.

[h3]Lots to do [/h3]
Compared to the demo, there's a lot more to do in restoring and repairing cars. There are a lot more upgrades to buy. In theory, there's a lot of distance in this game. Considering I got softlocked an hour in, I can't say for sure.

[h2]Lots of negatives[/h2]
Okay... here we go.

[h3]Terrible controls [/h3]
Walking is bad, driving is a joke. 
Your walk speed is somewhere on the level of an Olympic speed-walker, and your sprint speed will have the Flash doing double-takes. Default mouse sensitivity is so high I'm pretty sure my character broke his neck looking around.
But driving is ridiculous. I'd go so far as to say the developer may never have actually driven a car. The turning radius on your vehicles is wider than a lorry, which for a subcompact is a little crazy. Braking and cornering makes you feel like you're driving on ice, and since the game's town clearly hasn't seen any precipitation since about 1704, that doesn't track. Any attempt to brake will leave skid marks (your tires are apparently made of crayons), yet stopping doesn't seem to want to happen.

[h3]Softlocks! [/h3]
Yes, multiple. 
The first time was in trying to go get my tutorial car. The game wouldn't show me where it was. I ended up deciding it was a bug and starting over before I figured out what was wrong when it happened again: because I hitched up the tow dolly before being told to, the game was... waiting for me to hitch up the dolly before telling me where to go. Which I'd already done and the game wasn't registering the state of the resource. Okay, fine. Kind of an amateurish mistake but whatever.
But when I did what I'd always done in the demo and queued up two cars to buy, I managed to break the tutorial and softlock the game. Because I couldn't progress until I'd fixed exhaust system holes - which the scanner and game agreed numbered zero. Since there were no holes, I couldn't fix any holes, the tutorial couldn't advance and... we're softlocked again. This time unrecoverable, which meant having to start over [i]again.[/i] Definitely not a good sign.

[h3]Graphical bizarreness [/h3]
The demo looked decent. Somewhat simplistic graphics, sort of a 2008 look, but passable. The full release game looks worse. There's [i]static[/i]. No, it's not some weird post-processing artifact; I'd turned it off. It was some kind of odd shading or ambient lighting issue that only happened during twilight. 
Foliage suffers from jittery shading, contrast on vehicles you're working on is inconsistent at best, and it just looks cheap even when compared to its own demo.

[h3]...and the audio [/h3]
There's no nice way to say this. The voice acting is atrocious. I turned the voice volume off because I couldn't stand it. I'd done the same thing with the demo, but I'd hoped the demo had placeholder audio and for the full version they'd swap it out for better. They didn't.
Vehicle sounds are cartoonish and flat. Level balancing is inconsistent at best, so you will have spikes of substantially loud effects compared to the general volume. 

[h3]Optimization? [/h3]
This also runs worse than the demo. My setup is pretty dang beefy, and even turning down the settings from the Autodetect choices, it was still lugging somewhat and spooling up the fans higher than anything short of Satisfactory and the like generally does. 

[h3]Timescale problems [/h3]
Might as well address this, too. Time flies in this game. In the demo, a day would end, the clock would halt in late evening, and while you could keep working you couldn't buy or sell new vehicles. Well, the clock no longer stops. Not only that, but it runs [i]way[/i] too fast, meaning that the experience you got in the demo is not what you get in the game. You get a much more inconvenient, unfriendly time model to deal with. 

[h1]The Bottom Line[/h1]
It doesn't feel finished. This feels, sounds, looks, and plays like a game that's still in EA, and the fact that there were two softlocks before the tutorial was even done isn't a good sign, either. 
I'd really wanted to be able to post a review that said "Hey, it was just like the demo only better!" but I can't. It's a bad sign when you'd rather have the demo than the full-release game, but that's what's going on here.
It has a lot of potential, but hold off until the bugs get squashed. 

Not recommended.

review:
This is the most mixed of mixed reviews I've ever really tried to write. I honestly don't know if I recommend this game or not, but I'll try and keep this short and coherent to maybe help you understand my thoughts.

The game is both addicting and incredibly frustrating. It's half esport team management sim, with scouting, signing, and training players as well as getting sponsors and building a performance venue. The other half is a moba simulation card game, with like 30 unique heroes, a bunch of player related skills, and a whole host of items to learn and play with. I do sort of feel that these two ideas are at odds, it's hard to trade away a player who isn't doing well when that also means you lose all the investment, strategy, and knowledge you had with their personal cards/heroes.

I want to give this game credit for being unique. It really does play like nothing else I've ever found, and when everything goes well, hours pass by in the blink of an eye. The caveat there is pretty massive though. The game's English translation is bad, and while some games could get away with that, a management sim + complex strategy game really needs to be better about communication, from tutorials, to card descriptions, to even just the difference between "Next" and "Skip". That's a big problem, but it's not the reason I'm on the fence about this game- the reason I'm on the fence is how the game can't decide if you as the player are just watching your team play their matches, or if you're actually using your skill and knowledge to play for them. You spend most of the time in game with the moba sim, playing the game, but the strategic depth wears pretty thin pretty quick and a ton of the game is out of your hands, either with randomness or just there's nothing you can do. Attacks can just plain miss and often do, you don't get to decide what cards your players have in game, and you don't have any control over where they move on the map- laners will always run to their lanes no matter what. This makes a lot of game states where the only solution is "lose the game and hope you get lucky with the randomness of the the management sim this week", which is not a terribly enjoyable feeling.

Overall, while there is a lot of fun to be had with this game, there is a lot of bad to go with that good. You need a ton of time investment to just understand it, and then the game just becomes a very mixed experience. For the time you need to put in and the amount of frustration from this single player game, I think you don't get enough back and you should put your resources elsewhere. If you like the unique style of this game though, I can understand wanting to push through.
