review:
This game is really fun and addictive until it isn't.

The concept is great and scratches an itch I didn't knew I had. Art is okayish, I don't even mind the AI character art of the players that much, I just wish there was more variety. It's 99% the samey looking edgy oversexualized young adults with hair/clothing. There are some things however which just add way too much to my frustration and made me eventually stop playing. I'll list them here in order from least annoying to most.


[h3] 1) What the hell is happening [/h3]

This game is incredibly good at hiding information. You increase your athletes stats after every match. There's things like, "offense" and "defense", which should be pretty self-explanatory. But then there's stuff like "farming" - that might be the rate at which the athlete gains gold but I'm only guessing. "Mechanics"? I have absolutely no idea what that is. The number also doesn't mean anything to me. The 43 Mechanics stat just increased to 45! Is that good? Does this guy now have an advantage over other players? I don't know. 

In any case do these numbers seem to have absolutely no impact whatsoever in the actual match. I just had a game where...

- Top Laner with 60 offense playing Definitely-Not-Nunu which I have been buffing the whole match hits for 200 in teamfights
- Jungler with 50 offense playing Tiny Splinter Cell Wukong which I ignored the whole match oneshots enemy tanks for 2500 damage

Where does this insane difference in numbers come from? They almost have the same attack rating! Their active buffs have no indication for +% damage! What is going on?

By the way this is only if you're lucky. Most of the time the enemy teams Flying Gatling Brain that is 5k gold behind suddenly oneshots one of your champions every round for no apparent reason. "Wth this is OP", you mumble to yourself. "I gotta make sure to pick that champ from now on." So you lock him in first thing next match and what do you know - he's the worst load of horsesh1t you've ever had in your lineup. Insert [final boss vs. final boss when playable] meme here.


[h3] 2) Unfair match endings [/h3]

I've noticed two different ways for the games to end which feel really awkward. 

One is an extremely farmed toplaner pushing without end, destroying every tower and eventually hacking away at the nexus while none of the other lanes seem to give a single hoot. Now people actually having played games like League of Legends might recognize this as a thing that happens in reality - but not one that goes on for fifteen straight minutes in a professional tournament setting with several team- and dragon fights inbetween. Eventually the nexus falls to one guy with everybody else still farming on other lanes.

The other is a full-hp 5 man team having broken through every tower, standing before the nexus which is at 2 hp while 3 guys of the opposing team are still dead and the 2 alive with 40% hp have no way in hell of defending against this onslaught. The match has gone on for quite a while so with it about to end any second now the game naturally decides that it's time for the FINAL FIGHT™, revives and heals everybody to 100% and then pits them in a completely unrelated 5v5 teamfight until one team is wiped out. More often than not this ends in the team which was 2 auto-attacks away from winning losing the teamfight. And more importantly, the whole match.

Both of these scenarios suck, no matter if they happen in favor of yourself or the enemy team. If you win, it feels really cheap and undeserved. Not very satisfying.

If on the other hand you lose, it's straight up rage inducing because there is nothing you could have done to prevent this.


[h3] 3) Systems upon systems [/h3]

This is not such a big deal in the first few ingame weeks, since the only thing you do between matches is leveling up your heroes, have a google translated chat with your athletes here and there and maybe look at the showcased players of the week. 

As time progresses however, an insane amount of weird systems and mini-games get piled on top, to a point where it gets annoying real fuggin fast. 

I wish there was like a central hub from where you could decide what you would like to do after each match. Maybe you don't care for any of this stuff and just want to proceed to the next match. That would be great. Instead you have to click NEXT through every single system and mini-game like a power-point-presentation, if you want to or not.

Suddenly I have to talk to some a-hole shoeseller sponsor and discuss whether he is a better deal than our fried chicken cook. Yeah I guess, more money = better so I fire fat Colonel Sanders and sign a contract with shoe lady. NEXT.

Some intermission screen informing me that today's a "rainy day". Seems to have no visible impact on the game. Well, okay. That's nice I guess. I like rain. NEXT please.

Some puzzle mini-game to raise my athletes stats. Two even have "critical success". Thank you, very cool. Where's my match. NEXT please.

Now I have to roll a dice for each players mood for the next game. I have the chance to improve the relationship between two single teammates from 😡 to 😠 because apparently everyone hated each other from the very beginning. So I'm sending these two incredibly hot young animu teammates of opposing genders off to a candlelight dinner. No, I'm not making this up. Now they both hate each other slightly less while the rest of the teams content for each other is still the same. Yes. Great. NEXT please.

Then my coach has leveled up or something and now apparently has some stats too or something. Oh god, I don't CARE. NEXT!

Then there's three conversations in a row to click through, one where the coach talks to a literal owl that flew in, something something Harry Potter reference. I don't know, I just click-spammed to get through this sh1te before my ADHD brain forgets about the two new champions I actually wanted to try out. NEXT NEXT NEXT YES NEXT COME ON SHUT UP!

Then there's player spotlight, yes, great, none of my guys are there, whatever. NEXT. Another spotlight that looks the same as the one before just with different people in it. Holy hell, this is getting worse than YouTube ads. GO. AWAY. NEXT!

Then I have to build a venue. A. WHAT. WHY? Dude we are like 6 people in this office and now we have to provide money for an eSports arena for some unwashed teens to sit in and watch us play? Can't someone else do this? Apparently not, so I now have to decide on things like ticket pricing and wether to put in a commentator booth or just some plants which both have the same effect on the overall quality of the venue. Oh god is the NEXT button now finally not grayed-out anymore? Thank god. Now it's surely match time.

Lolno. Do I want to hire some more athletes for whatever reasons? Well no, thank you, I'm quite happy with the ones I raised myself through all of these tiresome minigames. Still I have to click through 4-6 pages of scouting/hiring data to get throug this part. Also contracts from my guys apparently have expired so I have to click a big RENEW button for each one to keep them playing. What was the purpose of this? I don't know. I can't click NEXT yet because apparently I have too many medals. I don't know what that means but who cares at this point.  So I click on things until the NEXT button eventually becomes active again. NEXT.

Finally I'm told  about the upcoming match. Clicking through 5 more laner vs laner comparisons, then 1-2 final VS screens and I could already proceed to the ban-phase. But at this point I lost all drive and interest already.

----------

Don't waste your money. Maybe get it on a 75% sale. Fun for a few hours but there's better optimized games that have way more respect for your time than this one. The way it is now it's just too tedious and from the looks of it they have no plans of changing things because they're already working on a DLC with even more stuff. Lmao. Good for them, I guess.

review:
I'm pretty mixed on this one. It's absolutely a fun game, but it needs another layer (or three) of polish before it's truly great. I'm putting it down after ~12 hours (plus some afk time) because it's gotten a bit too repetitive and easy, and I don't feel any desire to start again from the beginning on a higher difficulty. Ultimately, I'm putting myself as a No because I think this game should be a lot better than it is. However, if it seems exactly up your alley and you've got money and time to burn then don't let this review discourage you from checking it out. 

Pros: 
- Simulates the MOBA formula surprisingly well
- The voxel art is pretty good (it actually delivers on the teaser trailer really well) 
- Has a good depth of tactical gameplay (i.e. in the matches themselves) 
- Champions designs are cool and they feel distinct and nuanced
- Pick/ban and team comp building is challenging and rewarding 
- The minigames are generally pretty satisfying

Cons: 
- AI art is everywhere and ruins the experience a bit
- Translation is pretty bad, like others have said, though the important bits seem to be translated better. The only egregious examples tend to be the small visual novel decisions between matches, which hardly matter. 
- The deckbuilding aspect is pretty nonexistent. Once you have a good deck, there's little incentive to swap out cards. Same for multiple players - you can achieve flexibility with champion cards, there's no need to have substitute players 
- The minigames don't mean much. The small optimizations might be important at higher difficulty, but the game felt trivial on easy just based on the games themselves 
- The systems aren't explained well, and this combined with the last point means I stopped paying attention to basically anything but playing cards in games. I never lost a game this way (on normal)

This game is simply too random.
Real moba games at a professional, esports level such as LoL or Dota have almost no randomness at all. This game was supposed to be a simulator of such games from the coaching side, i.e. strategic and management, meanwhile there is almost no actual management, it is limited to 5 clicks every match and possibly another five if you want to hire another player.

The actual game is 90% a card game, very random. The deck has 5x3+5x3 cards +3x5 passive effects for each team, it is hard to plan anything here.

The behavior of the players is completely senseless, nothing is simulated here, these are the most ordinary scripts in the world of following simple paths and random ticks counting whether and how much damage someone will receive, and with low health, return to base and loss of pace.

So for example, you can split push one lane all the way to the nexus and the enemy team won't retreat to defend it, they will stay in their lane and you can end the game like that.

And if the game goes on for too long, a deathmatch is forced. Even if none of your towers are destroyed, you will lose the game if you lose that one teamfight. So neither objectives nor towers matter.

This also means that only one strategy pays off: 5 characters for late game and teamfights.

Back to randomness: even teamfights are random, characters don't focus their attacks on the most important target, or even on the tank protecting those targets, they just attack randomly.

I've lost too many fights with 5 opponents with 1% hp to be able to say anything positive about this game.

Jungler? He won't gank anything himself, he can stand next to an opponent with 1% hp pushing a tower and he will ignore it. You have to take all actions yourself by playing cards.

[b] I do not recommend it, it has nothing to do with coaching, it's just a random Chinese card game, the English translation is poor, the mechanics are too random, the game runs terribly slow. [/b]

Now? Now it's entirely RNG. A gotcha mechanic spits out random players. Then you have to spend, and I kid you not, casino tokens to 'influence' them. fighting every other team in the game for them. Okay. Why not. Ignore scouting. Trade for players you want, if you can afford it.

3) Translation? Not even once.
I've played and understood many Machine Translated games. This game has to be poorly translated on purpose. Everything is nonsensical gibberish. Meaning even the dialogue trees are RNG based.

If these core issues get fixed the game will transform from another shitty casino rouge-lite into one of the best team fighting strategy and management games ever.

There are a few more things that bother me personally.

-Versatility. 
When the game launched players only had access to one trait. So. That is why this goes here instead of being an insurmountable problem. Cus this shit sucks. It is RNG based. Do you have an idea for a player with 3 different play styles to seamlessly assimilate into every meta? To bad. You'll have better luck scouting them then spending 2 seasons bringing their stats up to game speed... Yes. That is a joke. 

-The A.I. 
Playing on hell difficulty. In game 3 of worlds. If the CPU loses here they lose it all. They spend an entire turn playing gathering momentum. Their next deployment phase comes up. 23 strategy points to spend... My butthole puckers. Then the A.I. proceeds to spend all 23 points to move all their players to gank my solo lane... while I had two of their players over-watched. So it was a 3v5... Where they were attacking a player not involved in the objective fight that was happening the same turn... They lost 2 players in that fight. Which caused them to lose the 2v4 for the objective... My Mid lane made 1,500 gold in one turn. And it wasn't even my turn... Causing them to snowball. Giving me the win. Great job devs. Nailed it.

All that nastiness aside. I love this game. While it does fail as a tactical team fight management game. It does succeed as a casino rouge-lite, tactical team fight simulator, simulator. Basically. If you like thinking about playing games as much or more then actually playing the game. This game might be for you.

-The graphics, sound design and U.I. are well done and charming. Yes. There is A.I. art. And what is worse is the fact that not only is it extremely poorly done. It is also completely unnecessary.

-The base heroes are great. A few duds. But with enough foresight and creativity you can turn them into hyper-carries.

-The rest of the management outside of what has already been mentioned is amazing and flawlessly implemented.

-They finally got picks and bands up to a Gold rank moba standard. At least on very hard difficulty. It is genuinely fun now. Before you just banged your head against the wall until your opponent beat themselves.  

-There are about 4 billion options. You can, almost, completely customize your entire experience in this game.

-The newest Rouge-lite mode. ;) It is really good. Player development is based off winning only. No worrying about trophies, KDA or MVP scores. 

-Worlds is meh. The teams in premiere league are so poorly translated their player names just appear as empty boxes. And the World rankings info tab is also glitched to where every player is shown to have lost 99 games, each season, every season. BUT! Tier 4 skills are cool. And being recognized as being #1 is always very nice.

-Building unhinged team comps of the most absurd heroes. Then going 90-0. The synergies and counter-play in this game is spot on... I just wish the CPU understood more of it.

Fin:
If you love spreadsheets, senseless min/maxing, and/or theory crafting. AND don't mind having the game continuously demean and disrespect your time and intelligence. Then you could consider picking this game up on a severe discount. If you are looking for a fun, casual single player MOBA experience. This ain't it chief. This game is less strategy and tactics. And more RNG and risk management. 

P.S. DEFINITELY Ignore the DLC's. I bought the 1st one and immediately turned it off. Lazy, thoughtless greed. Heroes and items thrown at the player that don't fit in the game. They feel like they are from a different studio. It is bad. One of the heroes has an ability that just feeds me free kills while costing the CPU 6 sp. Foso's Libra record against me is 0 kills for her to 17 free kills for me... Working as intended devs? I literally never use any of the heroes. They are unimaginative and sucky. ew. gross.

Hope this helps.

review:
I can only really recommend the game on a sale, at $20 I think it's still too unpolished to justify that price.

The main aspects are unclear mechanics and missing information. Despite getting to the points threshold to start actions at the same time, one team will always go first, with no clear determinant. Stats such as health, AP, how they scale, and even what order the heroes attack in a fight are all missing and this can be frustrating. This sort of information should be given in-game so that drafting isn't a coinflip as to whether you've screwed yourself because all your heroes go last in a fight. Some more granular information (and control) over what your 'athletes' do would go a long way to making you feel like an actual manager. While there are some nice updates planned to make the transfer system better (a sore point right now, your youth academy and scouting are essentially pointless), I do hope this gets looked at.

My main point of frustration with this game, however, is having moved onto the higher difficulties, the game starts to utilise scripting, when the probabilities start going wack mysteriously more often ([i] especially [/i] when one of the only stats the game purports to show you is probabilities in the first place!), rather than the having the AI make smarter decisions. It truly is wild just how often suddenly you'll find that your side will stop hitting the low health target with a 40% presence, or the enemy repeatedly beats the odds and keeps attacking your carry with a 8% presence. Overall, this has made what was an interesting concept into a frustrating experience, and unfortunately just going back in difficulty isn't really worthwhile when I've been smashing the AI throughout. Then again, I've been smashing it in the harder difficulty too, just having a more frustrating rather than enjoyable time while doing so. Guess it's not that different from actual MOBAs. Genuinely, just stop lying about the presence percentage and this would all go away, it's ridiculous having a 0.00005% chance scenario happening every few games because the AI is clearly not following the shown percentages.

So overall, I'd suggest either waiting for a sale, or for the game to reach a better state. Don't get me wrong, it's an excellent timesink if you wish, but once you get into it, you realise there's quite a gap between its current state and what it should be.

I like the game but I would not recommend it in its current state for $20, it lacks a lot of polish as far as SFX, and the system of directing 5 MOBA players what to do using a random hand of cards is clunky at best. You don't have a lot of control over modifying the decks your players use between fights. Another small gripe is that some keywords are not explained and you cannot hover over them to see what they do. 

Example A: You see one of your heroes is getting collapsed on and want them to recall or retreat but if you didnt happen to draw a card that turn that gives that command, there is nothing you can do to prevent it from happening.

Example B: My top laner started with a "roam together" action card that is useless on a solo laner and every time its drawn its a dead card in hand. 

Another problem is not being able to give macro instructions to your team. Your top mid and jungle could be pressuring the enemy nexus towers or nexus and your jungler is farming camps, theres no way to get him to group or assist in pressuring one of the lanes. 

The game has a pretty lazy way of handling the issue of all your heroes being at random places all the time, by having teamfight cards or teamfight events that everyone participates in automatically. 

The shell and general concept of the game is addictive and the core gameplay of watching your heroes automatically do stuff on the map is very fun and satisfying, for a game like this the devil is in the details and a bunch of small problems add up to an experience that isnt worthwile and doesnt feel like a finished product worth $20 sticker price.

There is only the one autosave at the start of each day, meaning any crash say 50+ rounds into a match will nuke anywhere from 30-60 minutes of progress you then have to redo. They really should add saves inside matches, or at the very least, right before match start. But as it currently stands this is too annoying to bother with. For the actual game review, read below.

So, barring QoL improvements (Like a way to speed the game up), minor balancing concerns, and a dodgy translation, EG is way better than I would've expected. It has that "One more turn..." thing down that often keeps me awake longer than it should, there is an amount of content here that puts most other management games that just wallow in EA for eternity to shame.

The healthiest parts of the game are hero variety, which is probably the most important part. The management aspects team-side are pretty basic and mostly consist of deciding stat-spread for individual players and who gets some extra focus. I do think player development could be a bit more interesting.

On the card side, hero cards are fixed, while the "Roguelite" part of the game comes in form of player cards. There, the variety is a bit lacking, and usually most roles have a few obvious choices you're gonna be sticking to. Game and role passives have way more choices, but there too a couple of them are just obviously better than the rest.

As mentioned at the start, the biggest thing the game needs is QoL and polish, I really hope the dev outsources the translation or gets the community involved. Speed up options would be nice, including a way to skip fights (There is just no point in watching them, you can't do anything anyway). Otherwise, the game is already great and hopefully only getting better.

review:
ive got a lot of feelings about FACEMINER. its a game that makes you think on several very prevalent issues in our modern society. but the game itself can feel like a bit of a drag to actually play.

FACEMINER is a very blatant criticism of ai usage and the effects of ai usage, like the environmental and economic factors. theres also themes of cyber security, specifically once you unlock the ability to purchase facefinder cameras to harvest your own data. the game itself is an interesting form of criticism.

the story is heavily told through the various emails you receive. most of the emails are incredibly short. some are messages from the FACEMINER administration on things like work efficiency or claiming the negative effects are just fearmongering. other emails are from other FACEMINER employees discussing the ethics and effects of their work. a lot of emails provide nothing to the story, just standard emails about mundane stuff. its both an interesting and incredibly boring method of story telling. 

its interesting in the way that it allows you to see into the lives of your fellow coworkers. some seem to be hysterical and outraged at anyone who opposes their work, others fearful of the world theyre creating others are jaded and dont seem to care. these are all very real responses to the usage of ai in modern society, so i definitely think it was important to be included. however, your inbox very quickly gets full of messages. notices about efficiency or expenses, rank up emails, babbling between employees, messages from people opposing the work of FACEMINER, etc. it all just gets jumbled up. and since the inbox is the method of storytelling, all this nonsensical data makes it hard to keep track of the story. 

the gameplay loop is also a bit boring. you can select how fast you want your game to go or if you want to play an endless game. even on the quicker speed, the game still takes ages to actually reach the ending. and endless isn’t even all that fun– it’s the same exact game, just without an ending. there’s no new infrastructure or offsets to switch things up. which, gets frustrating even in a standard run. things get more expensive exponentially. it’s really easy to dig yourself into a financial pit or to basically keep your game at a standstill. 

one major bone to pick is that you have to pay to save your game. you get a free autosave after ranking up, but in order to save, you need to pay. and like all other upgrades in the game, saving becomes exponentially more expensive the more saves you make. it’s honestly just a nuisance.

the game does use ai for image generation. specifically, all datasets are made up of ai-generated faces. it uses nvidia’s ffhq dataset to generate these faces. while the devs claim it’s for thematic purposes (as well as it would obviously be tough and expensive to legally gather enough faces to create the datasets). but how many of the people whose faces were used in nvidia’s dataset consented to their faces being used? and since the ai is trained on real people who may or may not have consented to their images being used for ai training, it undermines the criticisms the game it trying to make. at least, in my opinion. the game’s whole point is to criticise ai usage through the unethical gathering of data and the effects it has on the world. if the game’s face data was gathered unethically, then FACEMINER has become what it set out to criticise. it ‘s a slippery slope.

all in all, a summary of the story is just “ai bad”. do i think it’s got a good story? yes, if you’re willing to do some digging to read the important emails. do i think it’s fun? no, not really. once you’ve made it to mid-/late-game, you’ve done basically everything but get the story’s finale. most late-game features, such as the emissions/offsets have barely any upgrades. if you’re interested in the criticisms this game has on ai and a cynical worldview, then maybe you’d enjoy the game. but it’s definitely a type of game you dont actively play, you just check in every now and then to upgrade it and let it run on its own.

review:
This game doesn't know what it wants to be. I would put this in the automation genre, but it doesn't let you design layouts for anything, so it's kind of barebones in that genre. You just click upgrades and balance stats. I would put it in the mystery thriller genre, but there's really not much narrative to this game. You get some emails to read, but that's about it. I would put this in the clicker genre, but you barely have to worry about the clicking of faces at all after a few minutes in the beginning of the game, and no other clicking mechanism is ever introduced. It is most closely related to the clicker genre, but I wouldn't recommend it for that.

Some aspects of the game are basically missing. You may see some footage of video where it's spotting faces. That's not gameplay. There's no video footage of faces other than a little video clip in the documents that serves no gameplay purpose. I also found the emergency transmission windows annoying and not at all realistic... to the point where they were the same videos over and over with no rhyme or reason to when they show up.

That said, the Win95 theming is done extremely well, and I hope it gets expanded on. I want to see  improvements to the music player. Maybe add a Winamp upgrade? Also, it'd be nice if early days GPUs were introduced to help with mining the video feeds. I could also see part of the narrative being that you have to upgrade the OS to support newer video codecs but you'd give up your anonymity in the process and have to waste more power on a newer OS. None of that is done here. Everything takes place on a semi-convincing Windows-like OS that doesn't have Paint and doesn't let you edit documents. It also doesn't have a command line interface, something I expected to see considering the focus on energy consumption.

What's unclear to me is whether or not the hardware is on your premises or networked into as an agent. I think that's the weak point I noticed before anything else. It appears to be a situation where the hardware is in a solar farm location nowhere near your real home, but when it overheats, your own computer overheats, so that breaks that illusion. Which is it?

Overall, I like the game, but it feels shallow. It could be a ton better. It doesn't feel particularly special. It is, however, a little bit relevant to today's AI-related problems. It's an interesting base for a game that could evolve into something special later, but right now, it's just not enough to do to keep things engaging. I suffered through the first playthrough just hoping it got more interesting, and it never did.

review:
Decent incremental, but not really worth it.

It's got the cute Win95 aesthetic going and it's got some mechanical depth that's initially interesting, but the depth disappears by the mid-game. There's three paces you can choose from when you start which decide what kind of idle game you want this to be, and I chose the 'normal' one. I had unlocked everything just about an hour or so in, and the remaining hour was spent just watching YouTube and mindlessly buying upgrades while I waited for the game to give me the ending it kept teasing me with.

On that note, actually: the game's plot and ultimate message.

Going in, it seems pretty on-the-nose: a warning about the dangers of modern technology - specifically AI - and the impacts that it has on the world, which could ultimately kill us.
Except then you actually get past mid-game and the company you're working for is actually essentially just a cult that's running its business to willingly heat the Earth up because it'll apparently mutate humans into some ascended form or something. Also, none of this is actually happening and it's just a training simulation for the real thing.

It's just so weird, and that in combination with how the gameplay suddenly tapers off makes me feel like one of those things where someone has a great concept, but they're only able to build out half of it before they ran out of idea.

For what it's worth, I did mostly enjoy the few hours I spent on it. But not enough that I'd say I really got $8 out of it, and I think that's my real sticking point here, especially because I can't see myself going for another run.
If this was ~$2, I'd probably recommend picking it up.
As it stands, though, I just can't.

review:
I almost want to recommend *Faceminer*, but the question isn’t “can you play it” so much as “should you?” Up front, it has an interesting premise and a bit of charm. The retro interface feels authentic and gives the impression the game might develop into something deeper. But the gameplay automates almost immediately and never evolves, creating an incremental idler that plateaus within an hour. The story tries to build mystery around who wants these faces mined and why, but it never really pays off that curiosity in either answers or impulse.

*Universal Paperclips* is the closest comparison: both games are about destroying the world through automating a single mindless task. Beyond that, the difference is obvious. *Paperclips* begins with a single button and keeps evolving—each new stage shifts the goalposts until you sit atop your throne of paperclips and realize how far you’ve gone in destroying everything to achieve it. *Faceminer* wants to tell a similar story about obsession and exploitation, but it gives away the moral upfront and never lets the mechanics mirror that descent. You’re told mining faces is bad from the start, so there’s no arc—just repetition. And mining faces isn’t fun to begin with, so why is anyone doing it?

The result is a game that looks clever but feels hollow. Its metaphor for crypto and AI collapses under its own contradictions, asking you to balance progress with environmental guilt in a system that insists you stop. Once you understand the point—and you will, because it’s endlessly repeated—there’s nothing left to play for. It’s a neat idea trapped in a loop that proves its own message: not playing really is the winning move.  And so, can I really recommend a game that actively insists you don't play it?

It's ambitious, and it has a message. I didn't hate my time with it. But for this price tag, the gameplay is too shallow, the experience is too short, and the message about AI is insufficiently developed. If I paid 99 cents for two and a half hours of making the number go bigger, then this would be a thumbs up. But the game costs eight dollars, you can count the number of meaningful upgrades on your hands and toes, and the game doesn't offer any insights or predictions about the current AI situation beyond "AI power usage contributes to global warming" and "Carbon credits are greenwashing."

Even in-universe, the game does a poor job of illustrating the effects of climate change. When it's 45 degrees celsius and the game shows me stock footage of trees burning, that visualization is effective once or twice. They show that stock footage dozens of times, and I already know the planet is on fire when it says the world is 90 degrees celsius. Frankly, it feels like the game is incomplete because the ending is terrible, and there are no more upgrades to unlock after the first hour or so anyway. You just keep grinding the number bigger until everyone dies, I guess. With more work this game could be a gem, but right now it's overpriced for a clicker that starts off strong and then peters out very quickly.

review:
Gameplay is pretty standard clicker stuff without any interesting mechanics. Buy one resource to increase speed, buy another resource to increase capacity for speed upgrades, etc. If you've played any clicker game in your life you can figure out what's going on here pretty easily. 

I think ultimately the point of this game is to try and say something meaningful about the harmful effects of generative AI on the planet. To do so, it uses generative AI, so ultimately the developer(s) of this game are one of those people harming the planet. Big whiff there, pal. 

Visually, the game feels like it's trying to cash in on the Y2K aesthetic that's been popular for a while now with games like Nubby's Number Factory and Hypnospace Outlaw. There's no real [i]need[/i] for those aesthetics here though - Hypnospace Outlaw was about a very specific point in the Internet's history, for example, so the game recreated those Internet aesthetics. Faceminer could have just as easily been a Windows 11 desktop, and it would functionally change nothing about the story or the gameplay.  In fact, it might have even made the message hit harder? Ultimately, this game is a well-meaning but ineffective piece of satire on a hot-button issue.

review:
Great presentation, but there's not much backing it up.

The gameplay is simplistic even by idle game standards. You upgrade your software to mine faces faster, upgrade your hardware to support better software, and upgrade your infrastructure to support better hardware. That's pretty much the entire game, just playing whack-a-mole by dumping money into whatever upgrade is currently holding you back from buying more mining speed. You unlock some more features later in the game, but they're also just things you upgrade in tandem with your mining speed.
Faceminer isn't just simple, it's also static. The game doesn't change in any significant way as it progresses, you will keep buying levels in auto mining speed and its supporting upgrades for the entire game. I was originally going to complain about the game being short for a real game, let alone an idle game, (taking me two and a half hours to finish even on the slowest difficulty) but frankly there's not enough substance to the game to justify making it any longer than it is.

There's a story, but it's not worth playing the game for. While I do agree with every point it makes, it plays out exactly how you'ld expect in the most heavy-handed way possible to the point where it veers dangerously close to being [i]moral art[/i].

While it may look nice, there's not much substance to Faceminer. Take away the slick presentation, and it's a thoroughly mediocre idle game that I wouldn't even recommend playing for free. And I don't know about you, but I wouldn't pay eight bucks just for a fake Windows 98 interface.

Nice soundtrack though.

review:
FACEMINER is the video game equivalent to one of those fancy restaurants where everything looks and feels perfect, but the actual dish sizes wouldn't even satiate a rat. In other words: it's too short for the asking price.

(Audio)visually, the devs made something that I wouldn't roll my eyes at if called a masterpiece. The soundtrack is a banger and the UI of your 1999-based computer OS was done perfectly. I'm also going to credit the story for being a poignant reminder of what happens when you let a group of 1000 obscenely rich folks build datacenters that use more electricity than a small country so they can sell every single detail about us to each other to get even more obscenely rich, but I'll spare you my leftist analysis.

The gameplay, however, is where the game(!) falls flat on its face. I can really appreciate good soundtracks, killer visuals and a tight story/message, but above all else, I want my video games to have good gameplay to separate them from the movies and music out there. Don't expect the exponential growth factor of Cookie Clicker or the mechanical richness of Universal Paperclips. Trust me, we'll get back to that second one.

90% of the upgrades are the equivalent to "take less damage" and 9% are "watch abstract numbers go up". There are very few upgrades that add new mechanics that keep the player hooked. This is because the game's story has an average runtime of 2-3 hours if you pick the standard game length option. There just isn't enough game for me to solidly recommend this title.

Again, I really appreciate what the devs did here and I'm not going to unjustly call this game a cash grab, but it's just too expensive for what it offers. I'd say this is a $3 experience at most.

If you don't care for the audiovisual aspect (which again, this game nailed), I'd suggest giving Universal Paperclips a spin. It's a free to play web game with a surfeit of mechanics with more or less the same message as FACEMINER, although it's about physical resources rather than data. If Universal Paperclips is a bit too much for you to chew, I can also recommend the web-based game Crank, where you, well, turn a crankshaft until you get robots to do it for you, among many more things.

review:
[h1] Buy For The Story and Dev Support. Play Demo For Game [/h1]
[b]TLDR: Its the demo with a completed story. Very little is added mechanic wise, its extremely short, making the 8 dollar price very steep and almost unjustifiable. If you want to experience the story and support the developer, go ahead.[/b]
[h3] Good [/h3]
A unique take onto the genre! The initial start is extremely fun, in typical incremental fashion you stop doing manual work to focus on upgrading instead over time.
Great soundtrack.
Visual fidelity is fantastic. 
[b]Story is written well. Personally it didn't affect me, but I can see how others might think about the game for months after playing it.[/b]

[h3]However...[/h3]

[b]The demo is the entire game, baring the continuation of the story.[/b] If you want to spend 8 dollars on a "You destroy the planet due to your carelessness and greed" type story, go for it. 
[b]There is also no power scaling of upgrades.[/b] Another generator, another cpu upgrade... these have no context. Adding numbers feels inconsequential, but evolving feels good. More cameras? How about a drone. More generators? How about a whole powerplant. Things like these make the game much more impactful and fun.
[b]The diagrams are just diagrams[/b]I really thought that the diagrams might have a gameplay impact but they are just visuals. 
[b]You cannot interact with the emails in any regard at all. Some emails dont make sense ingame either.[/b] "Click click click..." mate you click for the first 10 minutes then its over. "I keep seeing faces" No you keep seeing your resource bars go up or down, the program is doing the job for you. These are admittedly creepy but also jarring because gameplay is so much more different than what these people imply.

[b] Overall, I just find it extremely hard to justify the price point of this game. It is a very, very good incremental game, but the pricing is not good and its why I have to give it a thumbs down.

Rating: ★★☆☆☆ (2/5)

Shawarma Legend starts off with a decent hook — managing your own shawarma restaurant sounds fun and quirky on paper. And to be fair, the first 30 minutes or so are pretty enjoyable. There’s a certain charm to the simplicity, and watching your little eatery grow feels rewarding… at first.

However, that charm fades quickly. The gameplay becomes monotonous and highly repetitive, making it feel less like a game and more like a chore. Before long, it starts to resemble a second job — and not the kind you enjoy. Tasks pile up, and the fun turns into a grind.

That said, the game does get easier the more you progress. As you unlock upgrades and automation tools, your restaurant starts running a bit more smoothly. Automation is definitely a game-saver here, and things become a lot more manageable once you’ve invested in it.

A word of advice: don’t unlock the custom order feature too early. It might seem like a cool upgrade, but without enough automation in place, it quickly ramps up the difficulty and becomes overwhelming. Wait until your restaurant is more self-sufficient before diving into that part.

The music is a bit on the childish side, but it’s also somewhat soothing — nothing too memorable, but it fits the light-hearted theme of the game.

All in all, Shawarma Legend just doesn’t offer enough substance to keep you coming back. It might be worth trying if you enjoy casual simulation games and have time to kill, but there are plenty of better, more meaningful games out there. Unless you're a die-hard fan of restaurant sims, I’d suggest giving this one a pass

review:
The gameplay is quite fun and challenging that turns into nice satisfaction found in completing all the orders you receive throughout the game alongside buying each upgrade. Despite a few upgrades at first feeling more like setbacks, often the later automation upgrades feel much better and make those early days struggling worth the grind. Personally, the only set back in gameplay is found once you complete your upgrades, as the order complexity and numbers have just hit the point where it is more frustrating to play than it is satisfying, despite there being little challenge.

My only true gripe with the game is the use of AI images in both the title and pre-day hub area, alongside the AI music. It's a simple thing, but it both takes soul out of the game and makes it seem lazy. The character sprites, items and area during the gameplay in your restaurant are clearly hand drawn, and I believe that the style has charm, which just adds salt to the wound as that effort could have been extended to the rest of the games visuals and only would have aided in it's presentation. The AI imagery and even the music don't necessarily take away from the gameplay, but it just leaves a poor taste in your mouth. The transition from gameplay area back to the pre-day hub is also jarring.

I just believe that if the dev continues to make games or continues to work on this game, working on removing AI would greatly help the image of him, his brand and the presentation of his games. In the visual art department, it adds a level of cohesiveness to your game if it all feels the same, and to top it off it could all be in a style thats uniquely yours; 
I believe the AI route was only chosen because he didn't want to spend money nor time on the art, and whilst I understand that point of view, It removes from the game. At the very least he could have commissioned an artist (which, would also, further any good image he has)
The same applies for AI music

Despite this, I do believe that the developer has potential as he has clearly made an interesting and enjoyable game and I wish him luck on his developer journey.

review:
I wanted to love this game but I just cannot recommend you spend money on what is ultimately a disappointing experience. 

The game has a great concept with a strong atmosphere, and what I hoped was great potential but the overall experience ends up feeling disappointingly thin. Reading reviews and looking at the blurb I felt that I was promised tension, deduction, and deeper problem-solving. Unfortunately, it never fully delivers on that potential.

The biggest issue is simply its length. Just as the mechanics start to click and the world begins to feel intriguing, the game is over. It ends before it can build momentum or explore its own ideas in any meaningful way. What could have been a gripping investigation feels more like the prologue to a larger game that never arrives.

The story also ends up predictable. Key beats begin to telegraph themselves early, and the ending lands exactly where you expect it to. Without twists, red herrings, or layers to peel back, the narrative lacks the depth needed to keep you engaged or surprised.

The investigations themselves feel shallow as well. Each case presents a problem, but they’re often solved with just a few simple steps. There’s rarely a need to dig deeper, only once or twice was I cross-referencing clues, or genuinely thinking like an investigator. Instead of complex puzzles or branching deductions, you get straightforward tasks that resolve too quickly to be satisfying.

Overall, The Operator is an interesting idea wrapped in a very short, very predictable package. If you’re looking for a brief atmospheric diversion, it works—but if you want a substantial investigative experience, this one doesn’t reach far enough.

review:
I absolutely love this game’s design and idea but sadly I don't think it was executed very well.

Rather than feeling in control of the narrative, most of the game was spent watching the story unfold with little player-contribution. There were different options to choose during conversations, which would somewhat influence the story plot-wise, but given that it's a mystery game and the choice of options available were very limited and surface-level (e.g. will you lie or not lie), replaying it to see what else (if anything) could have happened doesn't feel worth my time.

The story had some small unexpected and exciting twists, however most of these developments were overshadowed by the main plot being very predictable. I think if they had delved more into the individual cases within the game itself and focused less on forming an overarching plot, it would have been much more enjoyable.

The nature of the game put it in a great position to deliver really varied and unique puzzles (e.g. code breaking, crime solving, hacking -- all of which were very fun), yet the quantity of puzzles was seriously lacking. It felt like maybe only an hour out of the 3.5 hours of time spent playing was actually focused on problem-solving and the rest was in tedious over-explanatory conversation. 

I understand this is tagged with visual novel and so maybe the developers intended it for it to be more of a narrative-based experience, but if that is the reason for the lack of puzzles, I would have expected the plot to be more developed and have less of an obvious ending.

TLDR - would not buy. knowing this is a movie you just nudge along.
Linear game, where choices don't matter at all. Interesting story-line, and puzzles you'll only solve once, but not enough to justify paying even half price for the game (from an enjoyment/replay value perspective). It's a one and done, no replay value whatsoever. Better off watching a play-through on YouTube.

PROS, but:
All elements of the game could be built towards a randomized investigative type game (look at "Papers, please" or the game described below and then apply the principles to this type of game play).  
Bomb-defusal mini-game was innovative and tense, could have multiple scenarios play out.

A similar type of game that accomplished this was Sid Meier's Covert Operations. If the type of game-play "The Operator" presents is what you're looking for and you can stomach very retro gaming (this was an DOS era game), would recommend checking out Covert Operations instead.

But again, the story is compelling. Will look to see if the sequel's gaming experience expands in a way I was hoping this game would play out: not as a movie, but a game where the player has actual agency in the world.

To the Devs:
You have a lot of components in hand to assemble a compelling, unique "radiant" type investigative game with an engaging story (or stories) lying beneath the surface to draw the player into the game's world. Looking forward with cautious optimism to see how the sequel(s) plays out.

To simplify (somewhat) integrating multiple endings (and this doesn't have to be visible to the players, or could be some sort of end of day report/summary), continue with the the day to day system, and use the day end to grade the player's actions and, using key flagged actions (as a suggestion: timing when completed could affect endings too - in time, late, way too late, done wrong, etc), lead them towards whatever multiple endings are created in the next (probably third) game.

I didn't care for this. I can see how people would like this game, and I appreciate what the developers were trying to do with the story, but the whole experience just fell kind of flat for me. 

First, be aware that this is a short game. That's not a problem by itself, but you may not want to pay $10+ for a 3 hour game. I think when I see "puzzle" or "detective" tags, I'm expecting there to be more in terms of puzzles or problem solving. In reality, the game plays much more like an interactive fiction, or pure story game. You are in the role of a detective-like character, but really you're just clicking on fairly obvious clues to move things along. You'll probably spend the majority of the game time listening to the game's characters tell you things.

I will say there was one mid-game sequence which I really enjoyed, but overall there is too little interaction and input from the player for me to recommend this for the price.

review:
It's an interesting game and I enjoyed playing a bit of it, but the developer has a specific idea in mind about how it is to be played and I'm not into that.  Specifically, when listening to an audio file, the controls are locked and you can't do anything else.  The developer has said that he wants to be able to focus the player's attention, but that's not how my attention works and it's very uncomfortable.  Instead of focusing my intention, it's like someone powered up a megaphone next to my ear and is shouting, "this is all artificial!  Stop being immersed!  This is a video game!  The stakes are very low because none of this is real!"

The ideal situation for me would be being able to replay all of the audios - including recordings of the "real time" conversations - repeatedly while I peruse the visual and text data.  This is how I have investigated things in the past (though those were technical investigations and not criminal investigations): get everything in front of me and let my mind chew on a bunch of it at once to get into it.

I'm not exactly normal when it comes to my focus and attention, but the make or break question for Steam reviews is, "would I recommend this?"  In this case, I don't.

UPDATE: I'm not suggesting that the dev should change the game to suit me; I'm just saying that I don't recommend it.
name: The Operator

review:
I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

It's on a very different level compared to other detective games such as Return of the Obra Dinn, The Roottrees are Dead or The Case of the Golden Idol. It's also very short, I finished it in less than 4 hours and there's no replayability. Also be very careful with the saves, there are save points and you'll lose progress if you don't quit at exactly the right times. review:
A complete disappointment.

1. The gameplay is primitive and boring. Games like Cyber Manhunt or Orwell do this concept much better, in my opinion—they’re more engaging and last longer. The cutscenes drag on, and while you can see why they're there for certain moments... those moments are painfully obvious within the first hour of playing and after that, they seem redundant.
2. The story is shallow and uninteresting. The main twist is something you figure out in the first hour—[spoiler]namely, that your protagonist is Sasha Cole (thanks to the opening scene, the emphasis on Mia COLE, and the fact that your character starts hallucinating when the agent recalls her love for singing). Once you realize that, it’s immediately clear that your friend is the mole, while the "obviously" unfriendly boss is actually a good guy.[/spoiler] This one dumb decision ruins the rest of the game—there’s no wow factor, no payoff.
3. The lore? There isn’t any. Nothing is properly revealed or explained. They just threw in a bunch of medical and chemical terms and called it a day. [spoiler]Who is the Ghost? Why can he effortlessly kill trained agents? What’s the deal with the Organization? The game explains nothing—guess we’ll have to wait for a sequel instead of getting a proper, finished story.[/spoiler]
4. The ending... It left me completely deflated. [spoiler]I hate "everybody dies" endings more than anything, especially when the game tries to pretend it’s being "nonlinear."[/spoiler]
5. It’s very short. Less than three hours to finish.

review:
The only thing this kind of game has to do right is to have a compelling story with a mystery that's satisfying to solve, and The Operator fails on that count. I was expecting something like Papers, Please or The Roottrees are Dead but as a murder mystery, but the only part of the mystery that is solved by the end feels more like a side story to the real mystery, which is never solved at all. The plot twists and character developments make little to no sense and seem like the developers first came up with some "cool" moments, which they struggled (unsuccessfully) to tie together.

I will say there ARE some cool moments - there is a [spoiler]bomb defusal scene[/spoiler] which plays out like [spoiler]a singleplayer version of Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes[/spoiler]; I played it with my girlfriend, with her taking notes while I scoured the supplied in-game manual, and it was very hectic and tense and fun. But as with most plot beats in this game, the circumstances that led to that scene made no sense to us and ultimately the outcome didn't seem to change anything important. Despite being such a short game, it doesn't really seem to branch much based on your actions. The Operator doesn't even have multiple endings, and the one ending it does have is both bleak, unsatisfying, and nonsensical.

Combine this with the fact that - in the style of Papers, Please - there is a lot of information at your disposal throughout the game, but the majority of it is never used (such as the fact that every character bio has a set of fingerprints, but they never come up at all) and I'm left with the impression that the developers had much greater plans but just ran out of time/money and decided to release what they had and call it a day.

review:
Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

Choices are ultimately meaningless because an apparently superhuman hitman escapes custody in a high-security building (the story even makes a point of saying how secure this building is when you're helping another character find the passkey for the locker room) and is then apparently omniscient as he knows exactly where to find the director of this highly secure organization during a security lockdown, exactly when to intercept to main character en route to the exit, and is then able to ascend from the parking garage to the eighth floor to eliminate the supervisor/insider contact of our benevolent hacker companion all apparently without facing the slightest resistance from security in what is basically this universe's FBI HQ. Did the mole have him memorize the layout of the entire building? For what reason? After all that you're treated to a series of newspaper headlines letting you know that absolutely every ally you had over the course of the game is either dead, imprisoned, or missing. All tension goes out the window and it just turns into a cascade of tragedy for no clear reason. It's just so unbelievable to me. Maybe if it was clear from the start that this was more like a part 1 to a larger story or something, I would be more forgiving, but I expected a satisfying conclusion when I bought the game. Not super-hitman destroys everything because *dismissive raspberry sounds*[/spoiler]

With all that said, I do think the developer has a lot of potential. The puzzles were interesting and solving them felt really satisfying.

review:
I really like the genre of mystery games but The Operator felt like it fell short in a few categories for me to recommend this as is. I think they tried to do some interesting things, but I found the story to be a little too 'on rails' for me, and a little too short for the price point. 

One way I'd describe TO is to imagine the intro to a story where you're shown a vast map of the world with a story about it's history and maybe even a quick introduction to the strange artifact you'll be using to navigate the world... And then to only interact with 3% of the map, and to gloss over the history, and the artifact is just a paperweight that we'll never use more than once. That's fine but it does feel like someone went through a lot of trouble to flesh out this world only for it to shrink down to a tiny slice of what they'd made. 

Personally, I'm also not a huge fan of the story. I think they tried to go in a series of different directions at the same time (are you going to play it by the straight and narrow? Are you going to go rogue?) and it all led to the same one place so none of your choices really mattered. The big reveal hinges on you believing that the game's limitations are intentional and not a contrivance of some grand design, so the payout for their big reveals never really felt as good as they could've been. 

So... yeah? I think the story's a little weak/ watered down, but it lives in a frame that I could see the developer building into a bigger/ broader story that would be fun to play. The bones are here for something that could be a cool mystery game, but I'd sooner recommend 'The Roottrees are dead' if you're looking for a better/ more rewarding mystery to sink your time into.

* There's a lot of moments between the actual gameplay bits that feel like time padding, like I would have skipped if given the chance. 
* The writing is just ok, nothing special. The characters could be fleshed out a bit more, I think
* Without spoiling anything, the ending is pretty unsatisfying imo.

Overall, just an ok game, but could be great. I hope the developers continue to grow.

I would recommend this game on sale. Otherwise probably not worth it. I've played the game and gotten all the achievements but like many of the comments this is more of a story than a game. Some of the puzzles were neat and I had hoped they would return but with such a short story it doesn't. 

It leaves a lot of things for a potential sequel? So it feels kind of underwhelming. There is no multiple endings or resolution to the current ending. I'd hope a DLC or something might be able to fix that but as it stands now. It's a one time/or two time play that leaves you underwhelmed.

name: The Operator

review:
Promising game but fails to deliver. 

The game barely allows you to look for answers or solutions yourself as you must mostly rely on asking other characters for help, including during some of the most high-stakes moments of the story. This makes playing the game a rather passive experience, something you definitely don't want while playing a so-called "detective game"

It occasionaly introduces some interesting mechanisms (i was looking forward to trying the [spoiler]chemscan[/spoiler] again after learning how to use it), but then fails to include them throughout the story. Overall, it doesn't really let you "deduce" much past the first few days.

The ending is pretty abrubt and unsatisfying, as it leaves a lot of plotpoints unresolved and comes off as a bad cliffhanger for a second opus.

Overall, the game seems to be more preoccupied with its storytelling (which was not bad!) than with its gameplay (not great). Could've been a pretty good short film, but I don't recommend it as a game. It doesn't seem to trust their player or itself enough to rely on more complex game mechanics than simply "clicking the button when asked".

If you have cash to burn and need to kill 3 hours then maybe, but to be honest I'd recommend dozens of games before I suggest this. It's a real shame considering the promise it started out with.
name: The Operator

review:
To the question of whether I'd recommend this game: it depends, but probably not. 

Full disclosure up-front: I knew nothing about this game, nor had I done any investigating as to what the game was ultimately meant to be, so my reactions here are likely influenced by it not being quite what I expected or really wanted. 

The Operator is a ultimately a fairly short, story-based narrative dressed in the clothing of a detective game, rather than a detective game where you work through puzzles and solve mysteries. 

The game's mechanics and design were an interesting approach to storytelling, but felt quite underused, which probably goes more to my expectations of wanting a detective puzzle game with a greater variety in cases to solve. In most instances a new mechanic was introduced for one section, only for it to never be used again. 

The story itself is passable. I've consumed my fair share of content in the thriller, detective, mystery and conspiracy genres, and nothing here felt fresh to me in terms of the plot; you could see where the story was going from a mile away and the ultimate outcomes fairly early on. 

If you want a mystery story with conspiracy elements woven in, then this is probably worth a go. If that's not what you're in the market for, then you can probably give this a miss.

review: Maybe I'll change this review after playing a little more, but I'm personally not a fan of a game that forces you into situations that make no sense for the character you see. I'm sorry, but [spoiler]no federal agent on their second day is going to hear from a criminal and just agree to a deal. Or at least I am given no reason as to why they would do that other than to progress the plot, and that feels like sloppy writing. Heck if that's the case why even give me the option to tell the truth or lie before. If Evan is so after the truth that he doesn't care, why would he talk about Hal to his supervisor? That would feel better than this. I don't mind visual novels/linear story lines, but I do mind it when a game acts like you have choices and you don't. [/spoiler]
name: The Operator

review:
The game has a great concept and some thrilling moments. The developers did a fantastic job immersing you in the feeling of being a "cog in a machine". The music, interface design, story theme, and execution were excellent. I especially enjoyed the quiet moments where I could read through various documents and explore the backstory and world the developers created.

That’s why it pains me so much that all this hard work feels utterly underutilized. You’re essentially handheld and dragged through a linear story, with little to no impact from your choices. There are intricate mechanics that seem fun once you struggle through their first use, but they are never used again. It is just a little bit more "game" than a "interactive movie".

I don’t want to be cruel—I can see the developers put a lot of effort into it—but it was just far too short.

review:
Really solid, interesting gameplay mechanics and plot premise completely and utterly ruined by subpar writing creeping throughout the entire game from start to finish. Twists are entirely predictable, some (not all) characters react unnaturally to events, "intelligent" characters completely act against their own interests, game acts like you should care about characters you have absolutely 0 bond with, very rushed last chapter which does not work because of the aforementioned missing character depth. 

I assume LOTS of players will strongly dislike the last 5 minutes of gameplay, and though I like the general idea and premise of it, I think it's execution was badly done and almost insults the player for having used their time playing this game.

TL;DR really really strong mechanical and conceptual bones, terrible terrible writing
name: The Operator

review:
I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

review:
This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

review:
Amazing production value on this game. All my issues that I had upon reflection were basically nonexistent at the time of playing, and only upon reaching the end of the game did they solidify in my mind.

Namely, that most of the puzzling aspects of the game are more guided setpieces. 
The potential of things like the terminal, the GUI, etc, are limited to exactly one interaction.
The ending is a big open wound and comes very abruptly -- just as, in my eyes, the story was just starting to ramp up.
And said ending essentially undoes most of what you did in the game, narratively.
Your ability to interact with the game UI is usually heavily restricted unlike other "hacker" type games that use this presentation style.
In short, everything but the presentation quality is a bit undercooked. Get it on sale, if anything.

review:
The game markets itself as a mystery and conspiracy genre piece which it lives up to. It is very text-based in the vein of Hacknet where you're attached to a computer terminal for the entirety of the game (voice acting present though). Outside of one really great and tense sequence it's mostly clicking through simple instructions and doing some deductions to progress. It's interesting and compelling but the playtime is lacking to fully explore the concept. The store description mentions working on many cases and assisting agents but everything done is very attached to the central story where some more diversity in content of the cases would be appreciated to pad out the fantasy of doing the detective work and better utilize the mechanics introduced. I wish it was easier to play though certain sections of the game to make different choices without playing through the whole game again.

I would recommend this game on sale but at full price, it's too quick to finish to enjoy completely.

[spoiler]Mystery is actually kind of predictable and because there's so much to do with the main story, everything is obviously a hint for the ending twist. Like Arkham Knight, it's easy to guess the twists before they happen which mutes the impact of those moments.[/spoiler]

review:
The one thing I liked about this game was that you get to defuse a bomb, that was pretty cool. Aside from that, the puzzles are just clicking where the game tells you to click (or, after figuring out an obvious reveal, trying to figure out which section of which video you can click for the game to accept it as 'proof' of the obvious reveal). The whole game is made up of 'choices' like "Will you work with a wanted terrorist who has hacked into your computer? Please choose 'Yes' or 'Yes'." You're searching for a mole in your federal department, and in order to do this [spoiler]you access a bunch of confidential information and feed it to an outside person whose affiliations and identity are unknown. Literally ... being ... a mole. To find out that the "mole" is the director of the organization. He's not a mole, he's just doing his job in a way we don't like.[/spoiler] 

The game ending is particularly just bad. After a 'twist' reveal that was basically obvious from the beginning, [spoiler]you, your friends, and your allies all are framed and/or die horribly. That's the ending. A bunch of newspaper clippings about your friends being murdered or sentenced to life in prison after you got shot in the head and framed for murdering your boss.[/spoiler]

I kept waiting for the game to actually become interesting, and when it became obvious that it wasn't ever going to become interesting I just finished it because I was already so far in that I figured I might as well. How do you make a government conspiracy mystery game boring? I don't know, but The Operator sure managed it.

review:
The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

review:
The Operator feels more like a short demo than a full game. The entire experience is over in just a few hours, making it hard to justify the full price—definitely one to buy only at a discount.

The game revolves around solving a single case from start to finish. While that might sound intriguing, it quickly becomes clear that they could have added a few standalone missions beforehand to build up engagement. Instead, you’re thrown into one investigation with no variety.

The tools available for solving the case are extremely limited. Some mechanics feel underdeveloped, and many tools are used only once, making them feel pointless rather than integral to the gameplay.

Overall, The Operator is a bland and forgettable experience. It lacks depth, variety, and replay value, making it hard to recommend.
