However, in terms of a puzzle game it never feels like it ramps up. The story is broken up into such small pieces that there's no real need to sift through different possibilities. Every step towards solution seems pretty obvious. There are fun mechanics introduced and then only used once. You're never really challenged to combine the skills or info you have gathered over the course of the game. In the end it feels like a kind of short visual narrative with a fun interface. If they made another one focused on more difficult scenarios and a wider scope I would probably try it.

Also, nobody had cell phones or digital cameras in 1992/3. Not sure why they chose to set the game in that particular time period, it makes a lot of the technology feel very out of place.

review:
This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

The "puzzles" are really more reading things in order or straight up being given the answer, and you can't even do anything with any other connections you find early on. And speaking of that, you find a LOT early on, because nearly everything is super obvious. There was only one puzzle that I genuinely was impressed with and one tool that I found really cool within another puzzle. Otherwise, the game is very linear even though it seems like it isn't, and nothing you do really matters. You can't make your own decisions or find your own connections between information. The game just walks you through each step and only allows you to do anything with that specific thing at that time.

Other than the somewhat lackluster gameplay, I personally found the ending to be extremely disappointing, because it basically answered everything you already figured out for yourself and answered nothing you didn't. The main story doesn't even really end, it just gets cut off--and in a really unrealistic way, too. It seems to be an obvious sequel setup, but in doing so it doesn't ever truly "end" this game.

The game is also very short, maybe two hours at most. Shorter even than it seems from the reviews. I wouldn't waste my money on it.

review:
A great game had it come out about a decade ago. There's nothing the game does that other games don't do in greater depth and with greater innovation and interest. Tools and mechanics are all used at a very basic level, and there's no integration of multiple tools or strategies on a case to reach a conclusion as in other games of this genre. 
For example, a truly innovative element of the game is the use of a spectrometer tool, wherein information on a sample must be looked up and entered precisely in order to derive lab results. However, the tool is only used a single time. Other games in this genre would have made it a permanent element of the game moving forward, integrating it alongside other tools and resources to solve cases. This game uses it once, then abandons the idea entirely.
There's a bomb defusal scene which is fantastic... until you realize that the information is static rather than being generated. The plot and story are ok, with some nods to the X-Files and 90s conspiracies along the way, but again nothing really new or innovative beyond what's already been done in similar games. 

In sum, this is a great demo for a game that came out in 2013, but better, more complete, more elaborate, more creative games already exist that do the same things.

review:
I almost never leave reviews, so bear with me.

I was kind of enthralled by the demo: I loved the idea of drawing connections, of looking something up in one database and comparing it to the next database and finding it on a list retrieved earlier.  Then...well, I'm [i]not[/i] going to say is "bait and switch"; I think the demo is a fair representation of the game.  But the game did go in different directions than I'd hoped: for instance, the connection-drawing is in many ways the core of the game, but there was a lot of stuff around it: dialogue choices, minigames  ("oh, look, mastermind"), occasional long cutscenes.

At its core the game is a thriller, which is not really my genre.  (There's literally a "Them", which I think is the same as "The Organization", which is what you get if you ask LLMs to summarize the thriller genre.)  I could have guessed that, probably, but there's so much that seems to pay homage to [i]The X-Files[/i] (the FBI in the 1990s, the typewritten location captions, your boss is literally named Skinner for heaven's sake), and one of the first cases you get is alien-abduction-based.  This ended up being way more "thriller" in tone than X-Files was.

But to be clear: I didn't hate it!  I wish Steam had a scale more subtle than "yes/no", because I want to give it a "qualified yes" or maybe a "no, but if it's your thing, then yes".  There's a lot to like here: the atmosphere (even if you could practically see the words "cue dramatic music" at major plot twists), the interface, even a lot of the writing and plot.  Much of the voice acting is good; I really liked Pendell and Walker; Andrews less so.  (The two coroner reports, even less.)  And the [spoiler]bomb-defusing scene[/spoiler] did a great job with the tone.

Ultimately, I don't [i]regret[/i] playing it.  I also just don't recommend it unless you're looking for a thriller.  In which case, enjoy!
name: The Operator

review:

With that being said, as many other reviews have mentioned, the story is incredibly short. It lasts around 3 hours and could use a bit of "fluff," as there is no replay value outside of achievement hunting. I feel that if the story added [spoiler] one or two [/spoiler] days and provided [spoiler] a few additional cases that are both unrelated and related to the main story [/spoiler], it would greatly enhance this near-perfect game and justify the price point.

Given the current length of the story, I would not recommend buying the game at full price. If the game is on sale, then I would consider purchasing it, provided you understand that you will complete the story in 3 to 4 hours and that you likely will not play it a second time, as the story follows a fixed, very short path.

review:
I enjoyed the game and, right up until its ending, I was sad that it was about to end.

The ending killed it for me. It wasn't a bad twist, it was how forced of a tragic ending it was. If you don't mind spoilers, see below:

[spoiler] Everybody dies. Well, okay, one person is on the run from the law and another is imprisoned for life, but everybody else dies with extra fluff added to the details of what happened to twist the knife even harder that, after everything you did throughout the game, it was all meaningless because you failed. Might as well have had Patrick Star read me the extended cut of the Ugly Barnacle.[/spoiler]

The intensity of the tragic ending was so dramatic, I went online so I could see what I did to get the bad ending because it gave me such bad whiplash. Nope, no bad ending. Just one ending. It didn't earn or build up to leaving me holding an empty bag of misery. It has extra secrets, but because its ending left me feeling the way it did, I don't feel like I have any reason to TRY and learn more. It doesn't feel like there's a point to learning more outside of satisfying the curiosity I was feeling right up until the game kicked me in the crotch.

If you don't mind stories that abruptly end tragically, literally everything else about the game felt solid. I almost want to give this a recommendation. However, with the ending leaving me feel like nothing was accomplished but a few hours burned down the hole, I feel like I can only recommend this with "Play it at your own risk."
name: The Operator

review:
The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

review:
I'm only giving this a thumbs down because I believe this is marketed incorrectly. I loved the game for what it is, a visual novel. But this is not necessarily a detective game, and I'd argue not even really investigative.
The game follows one story line, and kind of fools you into thinking your choices matter when they really don't. For example, I attempted every dialogue option to not work with HAL, but that didn't matter, I had to work with them anyway.
The tools used are awesome; facial recognition, Human Database, lab analysis. But we only use some of these things once or a few times at most.
Don't get me wrong, the story is fantastic, and I genuinely loved my time with it. I agree with a lot of the other reviews that this should be way longer, but overall, I think the game is marketed incorrectly which is where I can't recommend it. I, and it seems a lot of others, went into this with the idea I would be solving multiple cases, using the technology multiple times, maybe even an endless mode where there's multiple variations of possible cases. 
I do think it's a great game, the immersion into the FDI computer is fantastic, the art style/graphics are perfect, everything ran smoothly. I mean genuinely top marks across (most of) the board. But it did leave me wanting more, I really dislike that we only used some of the tools once, and my choices didn't matter. All that being said, I absolutely would purchase another game from this dev.

review:
This game has an interesting premise and it has been made well. The graphics are good and the audio is top notch in my books.

But unfortunately it's... hmm, how should I say it... easy? Or not even that, hand-heldy! Like, it doesn't really let you do much anything of worth outside of one high stakes scene that is timed. But that it not what 99% of the game is.

It's kinda like this game is backwards from what you would expect from a logic puzzle game. It's the Agents or other people that call you aka the NPC's aka the game itself that do most of the detective work. And you, the player, are the computer whose job is to do the tedious work of checking. You get one single question to answer from the field agent and the answer is never that hard to find. In fact it's almost never necessary to collect and compile information as an active researcher and there's basically no need to take notes. Most of the times you just click on the right, kinda obvious document and do the thing and then answer so the plot may thiccen.

And it's not like the setting of the game, you being the computer guy helping detectives in the field means it has to be boring. There could have been more you could do. But most of the intrigue in this game comes from chat interactions, not from actual action you get to do.

Like for example, there are two things that could have been so fun to get to use as active participant, as part of a larger puzzle YOU need to solve yourself, the chemical analysis software and the bomb defusing manual, that only get one use. And also, no love for the vehicle database, just for people database. But like, just being able to do more than to just find out an answer to one question at a time, being able to take notes and to make actual deductions? Would have been fun. Think of Mainlining as an example.

It's just that, there is so much promise. This game was instant purchase for me as soon as I found out about it, as a fan of mystery and "hacking" genre of games. But it just didn't really deliver what I hoped for. And I'm kinda bummed about it.

name: The Operator

review:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

review:
I'm [i]really[/i] glad to have a game like this where the story isn't just "surveillance bad".

The mechanics are good though sometimes it can be hard to scan things even when you know what to scan. Special ways to solve problems are generally only used once and can be decently complex and fun because of that. They're usually a refreshing change and can be [i]incredibly[/i] intense. I just wish certain things would be randomized between attempts.

Now for the story. Like I said, I'm very glad it didn't go for the usual story this type of game attracts. It's a fairly decent plot with likeable, well voiceacted characters and let's you figure out certain things early without being utterly obvious.

The problem is the ending. The rest will be in spoilers, though I'm not gonna say anything specific. This is basically just for people that are really adverse to any kind spoiler, no matter how small.

[spoiler]The story is very good at making you think that your choices matter; though they ultimate do not. The stakes feel astronomical in multiple situations, but turn out to be utterly meaningless in the end. And there's no easy way to say this, but:

The ending sucks. Ruining the rest of the game levels of bad.

For starters, there is only one, even if it might seem you'd have at least 2 paths to go down. On top of that it is abrupt, doesn't make any sense and the person responsible for said ending was probably meant to seem really intimidating and constantly in control. This is not the case and the person ends up looking incredibly incompetent and only seems to succeed because everyone else is even more of an idiot.

I can not overstate enough that the entire game was fun - only for the entire mood to be ruined at the end, seemingly just to set up a sequel that could've easily focused on a different conspiracy. I genuinely do not know how it was fumbled this badly.[/spoiler]

review:
The game kind of struggles with what it actually wants you to do and who it wants you to be.

To get started: I really wanted to love this game, because I like researching and playing detective. However you are given a set of tools and expectations to be resourceful, while actually non of it works outside the main storyline. 

As a package it is nicely crafted and for a while it has you engaged, but at some points it expects you to really take control and go beyond the objective ... but only in the exact path the developer(s) have set out for you. The developer(s) haven't realized that it becomes very frustrating, very fast that the game doesn't allow you to explore or make combinations other than that what they exactly have programmed you to do. So encouraging you to think beyond one case, but at the same time limiting your possibilities very much gets your frustrated easily. Sure there is a subpath that you miss sometimes, but you only miss it because all your other attempts to try something different aren't supported (like you can't call anyone on your own or analyse something that isn't supposed to be analyzed). If you don't have any room to play / experiment, you stop doing it and than at some point the game will make fun of you and point out that you have missed something.

Same goes for the dialogs. The game keeps asking you to select an answer while none of it really matters, it is all linear! Again it learns you to make choices, but the choices don't matter so why are they even there than? Just for a single different line of text to go back to the main story path again?

I'll try to give it a go some more when I am less frustrated. But for now, it has got me fed up.

review:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.

review:
I would prefer to give this game a 5/10, but unfortunately, that's not possible on Steam, so I’m rating it negatively for interested buyers to see.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

review:
I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.

The Operator has a lot of good things going for it, the premise and story are interesting and the puzzle gameplay keeps itself fresh so nothing feels tedious. Special mention must be made about the high quality of the sound design - both the voice acting and the choice and timing of the music stings are excellent.

The biggest problem with The Operator for me is that it all falls apart just as it was gaining momentum. The last set of puzzles lack the sense of discovery from earlier, the game abruptly ends leaving a bunch of unanswered questions, and you're left feeling like nothing you did mattered.

This feels like the kind of game that should have multiple endings or changes caused by the player decisions, but there is nothing like that here. This is a specific story that you're being taken on a ride for - one with a pretty obvious "twist" - and no replayability.

If this was a prologue or chapter one of a larger game I would feel more favourable to this, but in its current state I wouldn't recommend this unless it's at least half price.

review:
While a very polished and well-crafted experience, this game has a number of fatal flaws that undermine and eventually irrevocably cripple your enjoyment of it.  Firstly, it's incredibly short.  I do understand that this tends to be the case for these kinds of games, crafting content for them is much more effort intensive than it is for other genres, but even by the standards of other games in this genre, you get very little playtime compared to its cost.  This is further exacerbated by a complete lack of replay value, as the story is completely linear and has no alternate endings, though there are a few pieces of content not central to the story that the player can find through their own initiative.  If you take nothing else from this review and do decide to buy the game, buy it on sale, the existing content doesn't really justify the price point.

To get into the real reasons this is a negative review, as money alone wouldn't have been enough to get me to write this, we need to first revisit the game's linearity.  The game does provide the illusion of choice, but none of the choices the player can make matter, and acting as though they do will inevitably see the game yanking on your leash and railroading you back to the single story it wants to tell.  This linearity continues to the mysteries that form the game's content, as they are designed so that the player is forced to solve them linearly as well.  Rather than providing multiple angles of attack, players must solve one specific part of a mystery before progressing to the next one, so for the most part you don't get that feeling of everything coming together as multiple clues and leads snap together into a single image, though there are exceptions to this.  I can't get too much into the ending without spoiling players, but it was abrupt, unsatisfying, and served to terminate any remaining sense of agency I had.  Everything I had accomplished was undone in an instant, in a way that felt, frankly, disrespectful and contemptuous to me as a player.  The entire point of a game, the thing that fully differentiates it from other forms of media, is that the person consuming it has agency, is not simply a passive observer but actively engages with and shapes the piece of media that they are consuming.  Of all the games I've played, this embraces that principle the least, and suffers for it.

The ultimate sin of The Operator, however, the one no detective game can be forgiven for, is its predictability.  I am in no way talented when it comes to mysteries.  When I play a detective game, read a mystery novel, or watch a movie in those genres, I am generally unable to put together the pieces ahead of time and figure out the twist before it is presented to me.  This was not the case with The Operator.  I was able to determine most of the major narrative twists well ahead of time, because they were fairly obviously telegraphed.  There were a few that were well done, and there were some that would have been very good if other obvious elements hadn't telegraphed them ahead of time.  Anyone playing this game will likely figure out its main narrative twists well before they are presented to the player, and that is truly tragic.

review: I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

Not really a game, more like a short visual novel.  

The puzzles are simple, you press a view buttons and they are very hard to mess up at all.  The writing is okay, every character feels like a plot device rather than an actual person, and they only speak to you in the tone of that plot device.

Interesting idea but definitely needs more fleshing out for this price, if you thought this game was "be a detective that helps solve cases while there is a mysterious plot slowing unfolding in the background" you are mistaken.  This is a game that instantly throws you into the conspiracy plot and gives you no wiggle room to escape from it.
name: The Operator

review: It's by far the shortest game i have ever played. I went to it slowly and didn't surpass the 4 hours mark. That's unacceptable, especially because the mechanics were there and it just lacked more content.  It felt like an introduction but then it suddenly ends. The story is meh, pretty obvious and with a little more inspired writing it could be less predictable. I really wanted to like the game because it had nice ideas like the *nix inspired console and other interesting things. The people finder was used a couple of times, the chemical analysis only one time, this can't be meant seriously.
name: The Operator

review: It was a fun game up until the abrupt and very unsatisfying ending. This is a very short game that ends on what should be the completion of the first act.
name: The Operator

review:
Maybe my expectations weren't set properly but I was going into this game hoping to fill the shoes of an FBI operator : 

- Analyse photos, videos, samples
- Search and match data accross differents sources
- Analyse piles of documents or suspects conversations
- etc.

in order to make some deductions and help ongoing investigations. 

This is what you get for the first 25% of the game. 
After that, it slowly shifts into a narrative driven experience, where your choices don't matter (the game is programmed to end one way), the scenario is at best foreseeable at worst blatantly cliché. All the investigation mechanics that you were taught are thrown out the window and never used again. 

The scenario felt like drinking room-temperature water. It's uninteresting, not particulary pleasant and completely forgettable. Overall it feels like a huge bait and switch
name: The Operator

review: Great game, interesting story. But it ends far to quickly and abruptly. At the end I felt unsatisfied and craving for more.

review: Very short. Not as mysterious as they would like it to be.Dissapointing. Gameplay is fun, but its over in a flash. Should probably not cost as much, seeing as you finish it in a couple of hours.
name: The Operator

review: An interesting idea that has trouble finding pace, the story seems like it's told in 10x speed and holds your hand pretty hard. Would recommend if it was on sale, but not at full price for how short it is unfortunately.
name: The Operator

review:
Quite disappointed with the game, barely 3 hours and no complexity in the storyline or gameplay. 
The first part of the game is very good (the demo and a bit more), one expects a 'Papers, Please' style with routine investigations hiding a deeper secret. But in the end, you get 4-5 pseudo-investigations and then a very linear sequence of scenes with very little research and an ultra-simple plot... 
The few original interactions are nice but used only once... 
Adding more investigations without impacting the main storyline by reusing the tools would have really added a lot to the game...
Not worth it or I had too many expectations (and a slightly exaggerated game description on the store page)
name: The Operator

review:
Game has good base features, such as databases and interactable video/image search functions, as well as references to certain lab and analysis tools. There was also good voice acting and character designs.
However, I had not realized game was such a railroaded linear story line with no real choices or variation in gameplay. Several points where game takes control from player and forces unnecessary video or audio cutscenes that do not add well to the experience or even the story. Certain events forcibly squish the interactable area of the screen, making it difficult to maneuver through the various game elements needed to continue. Not friendly to slow readers, as whenever a new line of text appears, it forces the log to the bottom, forcing you to wait until the whole conversation is over to double check the one thing you wanted to check in the conversation, such as spelling of a name you want to look up.
Would not recommend for anything more than $4.99
name: The Operator

name: The Operator

review: The game is good, and it's fun to play, but I don't think the story is enough to justify buying it full price. The ending being a cliffhanger sucks, as I was expecting some sort of conclusion to any part of the story and got none. We learned one crucial piece of information about ourselves and then the story ends. I hope any additional chapters/episodes of the story are free because this story is incomplete.
name: The Operator

review:
"The Operator" is a good game, except it isn't actually a game... It is more of an interactive film, where your choice doesn't actually matter, for example, despite several attempts to play for the agency, I couldn't do so, you always have to side with some renegade hacker("HAL"). The game just locks in dialogue options, so you can only comply to progress further in the game. When she reveals her identity, you can't report her, which proves how choice doesn't matter in this game, even the dialogue options aren't that much of a choice, as the respondents largely react similarly. Also, many actions in it don't have consequences, like you can mess up all the tasks hundreds of times, and the game just tells you you are wrong, not the characters, the game, like, you can (in some cases) just blindly click the screen and eventually you will get it right. Or with how you can mess up the bomb diffusal and subsequently kill a federal agent, with no consequences. 
Generally, the game is well made, and I have not found any bugs, but the crippling lack of player agency, and no consequences for wrong choices just make the game unplayable, and I would, therefore, not recommend it to other people, as a game at least. As I said, this isn't a game it is an interactive activity, that uses the mechanics of a game.
name: The Operator

review:
Good, but far too short.   When the game had finished, it felt like I had just completed the tutorial, I was just getting the hang of all the things I had access to... and then it... ends... abruptly. 

The quality is amazing, but there is just not enough content.   Just enough content to put you over the 2 hours refund window, but not enough to really be worth it for the price. 

I was going to give this a thumbs up, but I think I'll stick to my first though of a thumbs down... Zero replayability (other than achievements) and just enough content to stop people refunding... I don't want to see more "released" games like this on the market.
name: The Operator

review: Great concept with the same bad execution that Hypnospace Outlaw suffers from. name: The Operator

review:
The Operator has such a great premise and the systems are polished and well-executed.  Unfortunately a lackluster story, simple puzzles, and an egregiously short playtime means I cannot recommend the game.

Your choices don't matter, every puzzle has one solution, and most of the aforementioned well-executed systems are used exactly once.
name: The Operator

review:
Very neat concept and potential gameplay, but sadly extremely linear, none of the "investigation" mechanics require any kind of investigation, most of them are used literally only once in the game, and after the start it felt like I just had to find the one thing the game wanted me to do rather than actually connect dots and investigate or research anything.
There's some interesting unique dialogue you get when you DO connect some dots that aren't required but it doesn't feel encouraged, and there's some unique stuff you could probably get from the 2-3 achievements I didn't get but I have no motivation to play this again despite how short it was.
The plot is extremely "by the book", it's very predictable and honestly boring. Wasted opportunity.
name: The Operator

review:
From the get go you are thrown into the games story line and it does not stop. The pacing does not allow you to sink your teethe in to what I thought would be a fun and interesting game play loop. 
Instead of playing an agent who starts to slowly unravel a conspiracy through your own investigations and discoveries, you are just railroaded into it by the characters that force themselves on you.
I really like on the surface what they put together. The presentation is fantastic; but for me the pacing of it all just threw me off.

review:
This isn't right, I should be giving this game a positive review. This game caught me fresh out of watching an episode of Monk, so I was up for a good detective game and for the most part, it delivered. The investigating, the story, the puzzles to solve, all solid and well designed.

But that ending... &$!" THAT ENDING! Without spoiling too much, no matter what you do, whether you succeed or fail certain tasks. It always ends the same. You die, the bad guys win and nearly everyone on your side is quietly eliminated. We then get a jump to the present day with a potential cliffhanger, but it comes off as nothing more than sequel bait. I mean, come on! At least in L.A.Noire, you still foiled the conspirators' scheme. This is just a huge middle finger to the player.

Needless to say, I did some digging. This couldn't be how the game actually ends right? There has to be a good ending you need to meet a certain requirement for.
Turns out I'm not the only one doing this, but all the players have dug up is a hidden message that comes up if you enter a password into a file before you're supposed to know it.
It doesn't really explain anything.

What an utter cop out. Hey is any gaming channel working on a Top 10 worst video game endings? I think we've found a good contender.

(Edit: That jester award is probably from that guy in the forums who's going around harassing anyone who shares my opinion. Guy just can't take the idea that people see this game's ending as awful.)
name: The Operator

review: At that price, I would have hoped  for at least twice the length (I did 4 hours while taking my sweet time, and there are unskippable scenes inbetween chapters that are closer to loading screens), as well as multiple ending (especially since [spoiler]the only ending is a bad one[/spoiler]). name: The Operator

review:
I'm pretty conflicted regarding my thoughts on this game, if there was a neutral review that would be my rating. 

On one hand the game is very polished, especially for an indie game. It's OST really sets the mood and switches at the perfect time to give you goosebumps. The mechanics are pretty fleshed out; providing a decent challenge while also not being so hard that would require one to search up guides on them. The story is also really thought out and you will get invested into it very quick.

The unfortunate problem I have with this game is that it's extremely short. You can tell by the average 3 hour playtime in the reviews. Additionally all the content + mechanics that the game will throw at your are pretty much in the trailer. (There's only like 10 cases in total) Additionally, all game choices seems to not divert things from the main ending, which means that the game is not very re-playable. There may be some secrets as hinted by the credits achievement or that can be activated by a certain specific sequence of events, but they aren't readily accessible and would require probably some video tutorial guide.

And that leads to the big question, should you buy the game? I honestly can't say in good faith that it is worth it to buy the listed price ($14 USD). If you have a good amount of spare money to spend on games, then go for it. But for most people, I'd recommend holding out on purchasing the game unless it has a heavy sale.
name: The Operator

review:
[h1]Meh[/h1]

This is one of the games where I wish there would be a "Meh" option.

I plaid the Demo and was looking forward to the games release as this sort of "operate and solve puzzles from your PC" ones are much to my liking. 

Unfortunately the game itself was quite linear, very few and quite easy puzzles and the story sort of foreseeable. 

Choices matter a little bit, but as soon as you had your play through you will only see the results at the very end. There is no save function, no chapters, so if you wanna try out other choices you will have to go through the exact same stuff another time - which is a bit boring as the story is very linear.

Perfect game if you want to click a few buttons every once in a while and not think to much.
name: The Operator

review:
Ok look....I was really hoping that this would just be a game where you are an operator and you're helping agents finish up their investigations and what not...that type of game would have a lot of replayability...it would have a lot more time in it and what not. 

While this game is GREAT...it is absolutely TO SHORT for the price they are asking. You can finish it in under 2 hours if your attention is full on the game, especially if you played the demo. [spoiler]You continue where the demo left off which leaves you only 3 days in the FDI instead of the full 4 days if you play it from not continuing the demo.[/spoiler] I have kids so I finished it in about 3 hours because kids never let you just give all your attention to a game you are playing. 

**SPOILER ALERT**

[spoiler]The story has a "cliffhanger" ending but the ending leaves you feeling absolutely crushed and unfulfilled. Everything you worked for....poof....gone....there is a scene after the credits as well that may leave the option for a possible DLC or next game but hopefully they make the possible DLC free or make a possible next game much longer so that it feels like it's worth it.[/spoiler]

If the game is on sale for like $5 then it would be worth it...don't buy it for the full price because as it is absolutely not worth it in that regard unless you want to support the team in making games in the future.

name: The Operator

review:
kinda wish i could leave a "mixed" review because i don't hate this game - it does a lot of cool and interesting things and scratches a little bit at an itch left by hypnospace outlaw and home safety hotline, however the game is extremely short (a casual run through is about 3 hours, i can imagine someone who understands and quickly solves all the puzzles immediately on their first playthrough could potentially complete it in half that time,) the game introduces multiple puzzle mechanics that it uses exactly once and never returns to, and it has zero replayability - there is only one ending, the nature of which i imagine many will find unsatisfying due to the negative outcome for the player character and his allies. this is in spite of the player SEEMINGLY having some control over the events that take place, but ultimately have no impact on the end of the game. the feeling i got by the end of the post-credits sequence was that i had just paid 16 bucks for just the prologue to the "real game" which doesn't exist.

speaking of prologues, if you played the demo and were drawn to the game due to the extraterrestrial / ufo themes that dominate that portion of the game, you'll be disappointed to know that this entire element is dropped immediately after the portion of the game covered by the demo ends, and never comes back. i'm not going to call this intentionally misleading, but i imagine a non-zero number of people who bought the game will walk away disappointed due to this fact.

finally, the game is a bit buggy and softlocks in multiple places - i recommend you follow what the game expects you to do in the exact order it likes, as getting ahead of yourself, either through experimentation or actual foreknowledge, can potentially end your entire run and you'll have to start over.

review:
I wish there was a sideways "Maybe" finger.

First, let me make this clear. The game is amazing. It's well-made, the suspense is thrilling, the puzzles are great and it keeps you riveted to the screen.

So why don't I recommend it ?, it's 3 hours of entertainment with 0 replayability for 15$. 
In comparison, thats a months subscription to a game like WOW, or a full game thats a year years older with dozen of hours of playtime if not more. Or put in another way, it's WAY overpriced for the amount of total playtime. 

Wait until it's 3-5$ and get it, but with 0 reason to ever replay it, since all events are static and it only has 1 ending, it's literally not worth more.

review:
I was enjoying this game... right until the last mission. Spoiler-free explanation: Feels like a waste of time.

Spoilers ahead.




The game felt incomplete. The ending feels like a Diabolus ex Machina, which instead of leaving me feeling intruiged, left me disappointed. Doesn't feel like the time I spent in the story even mattered.
I get that the Organization is extremely powerful, but that does not translate well -- to me at least -- as an ending to a game. The one trope I absolutely hate is the "All For Nothing" trope, and unfortunately this is the exact embodiement of it.
This would work for a much longer game as a Prologue. This doesn't work as a game in and of itself.
Shame. I was looking forward to this one.

name: The Operator

Was it fun? Yeah, I guess, but very, very linear and just lots of systematic clicking.

I'm utterly bemused that THIS is the final released version of the game.
